papers.title: Signed Wasserstein distance for room impulse response comparison
papers.summary: The nature of room impulse response signals is often adverse to a clear evaluation of similarity: they are sparse, rapidly varying, signed signals resulting from the complex interaction of room reflections and phase relationships. Therefore, conventional point-wise metrics may be sensitive to small temporal shifts and provide poor loss surfaces for optimization. In this paper, we propose an optimal transport-based distance for RIR similarity that explicitly accounts for the structure of impulse responses, inspired by the signed Wasserstein distance formulation. Optimal transport provides a natural framework for this problem, by comparing signals based on how their underlying distributions are displaced rather than requiring a one-to-one correspondence. We evaluate the proposed distance against commonly used audio baseline metrics through a series of room-parameter perturbation studies. The results demonstrate the advantage of using the signed Wasserstein metric for geometric evaluation tasks and show a promising performance for room parameter optimization within a differentiable Image-Source model.

explain.tldr: A new method to compare room impulse responses that handles their sparse, shifting nature better than standard metrics.
explain.plain: Room impulse responses—the acoustic fingerprints of spaces—are tricky to compare because they're sparse signals with rapid changes and phase shifts. Standard metrics that compare point-by-point often fail when signals are slightly time-shifted. This paper proposes using optimal transport, a mathematical framework that compares distributions rather than requiring exact alignment, adapted specifically for signed signals like impulse responses. Tests show this approach works better for evaluating room acoustics and optimizing room parameters in acoustic simulations.
explain.why: If you're modeling room acoustics, designing virtual spaces, or optimizing microphone placement, you need reliable ways to measure how similar two acoustic environments are. This metric could improve tools for room simulation and acoustic design.

terms.meaning: A recording of how a room responds to a sound—captures all the reflections and echoes that define that space's acoustics
A mathematical method for comparing two distributions by measuring the minimum cost to transform one into the other, rather than comparing point-by-point
A simulation technique that models room acoustics by treating reflections as if they come from virtual 'image' sources, used to predict how sound behaves in a space

papers.title: Piano2Pop: Expanding Piano Demos into Pop Productions Without Aligned Supervision
papers.summary: We introduce Piano2Pop, a music-expansion task that transforms piano MIDI into instrumental pop productions. Enabled by recent advances in music generation and polyphonic music transcription, our pseudo-supervised approach conditions a pretrained flow-matching model on piano rolls without aligned piano-pop supervision. We train on synthetic piano-instrumental pairs derived from pop recordings, comparing pair-free transcription, including function-selective (FST) and register-density (RDA) augmentations, with a pair-supervised piano-cover generator as pseudo-demo sources. On 476 testing real-world piano-cover/pop pairs, the pair-supervised approach achieves the best Frechet Audio Distance, Accompaniment Prompt Adherence, and spectral shape on real-piano inputs, while FST mitigates piano-heavy outputs in pair-free training and remains a promising alternative. All fine-tuned systems significantly outperform the zero-shot baselines, which suggests a role for task-specific modeling.

explain.tldr: A system that automatically transforms piano MIDI sketches into full pop music productions without needing paired training examples.
explain.plain: Musicians often start with piano demos but need help expanding them into full arrangements. This paper presents Piano2Pop, which takes a piano MIDI file and generates a complete pop production with drums, bass, and other instruments. Since there's no large dataset of piano-to-pop pairs to learn from, the researchers created synthetic training data from existing pop songs and used a pretrained music generation model. They tested different approaches and found that using piano covers as intermediate examples worked best, producing results that sound more like real pop productions.
explain.why: This could help producers and songwriters quickly turn piano sketches into fuller arrangements, speeding up the demo-to-production workflow. It shows how AI can assist with arrangement and orchestration tasks without requiring perfectly matched training data.

terms.meaning: A type of AI model trained to gradually transform one thing into another, here used to generate music conditioned on input
Training an AI system using automatically generated or synthetic examples instead of manually labeled real data
A metric that measures how similar two pieces of audio sound by comparing their learned features

papers.title: PerMix: Anomalous sound detection by predicting the perturbation ratio of mixed samples
papers.summary: In anomalous sound detection based on self-supervised learning, the performance of the detection model largely depends on the selection of the pretext task through which the characteristics of normal data are learned. A common pretext task is to mix samples from different classes and classify the mixed sample as its target class with an angular margin loss. However, this supervision becomes mismatched when the target sample is the minority component of the mixture and the margin remains fixed irrespective of the mixing ratio. To address these issues, we propose a pretext task that directly predicts the perturbation ratio of mixed samples by reformulating the logit so that the angular margin is scaled by the perturbation ratio. In addition, we adopt a supervised contrastive loss modified for mixed samples, in which positive pairs are formed according to the dominant class. Experiments show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on the DCASE 2020 Task 2 benchmark. Our code is available at https://github.com/kaistss/PerMix.

explain.tldr: A method for detecting unusual sounds by learning from mixed audio samples with adjusted training signals.
explain.plain: Anomalous sound detection identifies unexpected or abnormal sounds in audio. Current methods mix samples together and train models to recognize them, but they struggle when one sound is much quieter than the other in the mixture. This paper proposes predicting how much one sound was mixed into another, and adjusts the training signal based on that ratio. They also use a modified learning technique that focuses on the dominant sound in each mixture. The approach performs better on a standard sound detection benchmark.
explain.why: Better anomaly detection helps with quality control in manufacturing, maintenance monitoring of machines, and safety systems—any application where unusual sounds signal problems. Improving how models learn from mixed audio could also benefit music production and audio analysis tools.

terms.meaning: A training task designed to help a model learn useful patterns from unlabeled data, even though the task itself isn't the final goal
The proportion or amount of one sound mixed into another
A training method that encourages the model to make similar sounds closer together and different sounds farther apart in its internal representation

papers.title: Predicting Music Valence and Arousal via Textual and Multimodal In-Context Learning in Large Language Models
papers.summary: While arousal can be reliably predicted from musical audio, emotional valence remains difficult to model due to its subjective and context-dependent nature. In this work, we investigate the potential of in-context learning (ICL) with large language models to advance continuous valence and arousal prediction. Rather than predicting emotion scores directly, our framework leverages contextual demonstrations from an auxiliary dataset to refine the initial predictions produced by a small, task-specific base model. We systematically evaluate a text-based ICL variant using lyrics and generated audio captions, alongside a multimodal variant that incorporates raw audio signals. Using the entire MER60 dataset strictly as a held-out test set, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains, particularly for valence. Text-based ICL improves the valence $R^2$ from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 demonstration shots, while the multimodal variant achieves 0.346 with only 10 shots. These findings suggest that training-free ICL offers an effective inference-time strategy for current language models to predict continuous music emotion.

explain.tldr: Using large language models with example demonstrations improves predictions of how happy/sad and energetic/calm music sounds.
explain.plain: Predicting how emotionally positive or negative a song feels (valence) is harder than predicting how energetic it is (arousal), partly because it's subjective. This work uses large language models in a new way: instead of training them on emotion data, they show the model examples from similar songs, then ask it to predict emotion scores for new music. They tried two approaches—one using song lyrics and descriptions, another using actual audio—and found both worked better than a basic model, especially for predicting valence (emotional positivity).
explain.why: Understanding music emotion computationally could help producers and platforms organize music by mood, create better recommendations, or assist in soundtrack selection. The finding that language models can improve emotion prediction without special training suggests new tools might become available for music analysis.

terms.meaning: how positive or negative a piece of music sounds, ranging from sad/dark to happy/bright
how energetic or calm music feels, ranging from relaxed to intense
showing a language model examples of similar tasks before asking it to solve a new one, without retraining

papers.title: HARMONY: Hierarchical Anchor Retrieval on Manifold for Oblivious-source Machinery Acoustic Anomaly Detection
papers.summary: In standard acoustic anomaly detection (ASD), models are usually trained separately for each machine or domain using explicit metadata. However, in realistic deployments, machine identifiers are incomplete, unreliable, or simply unavailable. Thus, metadata-free machinery ASD asks a single model to monitor mixed machine populations without machine IDs. In this paper, we argue that the main failure mode is not a weak detector family, but representation entanglement. The heterogeneous normal modes overlap in frozen pre-trained feature spaces, making anomaly scoring and approximate retrieval unreliable. We study this problem directly and propose HARMONY (Hierarchical Anchor Retrieval on Manifold for Oblivious-source acoustic aNomalY detection), an anchor-guided geometric repartitioning framework that reorganizes mixed-source features into compact Voronoi regions and reuses this structure for hierarchical retrieval. On DCASE 2020, HARMONY improves mean AUC from 75.40% to 90.00% (14.60 percentage points) over the strongest unified baseline and from 83.90% to 90.00% over a strong foundation-feature baseline. On a single CPU, its hierarchical retrieval achieves a 7.8x speedup over exhaustive search with only a 0.20 percentage-point AUC drop. These results suggest that incorporating explicit geometric partitioning can improve both detection accuracy and retrieval efficiency for ASD. Code is available at https://github.com/Zzyh0208/HARMONY.

explain.tldr: A method to detect equipment failures in mixed machines without knowing which machine is which, using geometric organization of audio features.
explain.plain: When monitoring multiple machines with a single system, you often don't know which machine produced which sound—yet current anomaly detection systems need that information. The researchers found the real problem isn't weak detection, but that features from different machines get tangled together in the same space, making it hard to spot what's abnormal. They propose HARMONY, which reorganizes these mixed features into separate geometric regions (like dividing a space into territories), then uses this structure to quickly find similar sounds and detect anomalies. On standard test data, this improved detection accuracy significantly and made the system 7.8 times faster.
explain.why: For producers and engineers monitoring equipment or recording in complex acoustic environments, this matters because it enables reliable anomaly detection without needing to label or identify every sound source beforehand—useful for live sound, studio monitoring, or field recording where you can't always control or identify what's being captured.

terms.meaning: when audio features from different sources get mixed together in the same space, making them hard to distinguish
geometric territories where each region contains points closer to one anchor point than any other
finding similar sounds by searching through organized levels of groups, rather than checking every possibility

papers.title: MQAScore: Fine-Grained Text-Music Alignment Evaluation via Large Audio Language Model
papers.summary: Text-to-music alignment is commonly evaluated by the global similarity between text and audio embeddings, which collapses all described attributes into a single score and obscures which ones are missing. We instead introduce MQAScore, which verifies each atomic musical concept along five clip-level dimensions (genre, instrument, mood/theme, vocal, and usage) by the probability that a large audio language model (LALM) answers affirmatively to a binary question. To assess evaluator reliability, we construct verification labels from presence/absence annotations and LLM-guided concept substitutions, and propose the Sensitivity-Invariance Ratio, which measures how selectively an evaluator responds to meaning-changing substitutions. Experiments show that concept-level scoring improves both question-answering and similarity-based evaluators, and MQAScore can be a more reliable and interpretable fine-grained complement to global similarity for evaluating text-to-music alignment.

explain.tldr: A new evaluation method that checks if AI-generated music matches text descriptions by testing specific musical features rather than one overall score.
explain.plain: When AI generates music from text descriptions, current evaluation methods give a single similarity score that hides which musical aspects (like genre or instruments) are actually missing. This paper proposes MQAScore, which instead asks a large audio language model specific yes-or-no questions about five musical dimensions: genre, instrument, mood, vocals, and usage. They tested this approach and found that checking individual musical concepts gives more reliable and clearer feedback than a single global score, helping creators understand exactly what went wrong with a generated track.
explain.why: For musicians and producers using AI music tools, this means better feedback on what the AI actually understood from your description. Instead of just getting a score, you'd learn whether it missed the genre, got the instruments wrong, or misunderstood the mood—making it easier to refine your prompts or improve the AI system.

terms.meaning: how well AI-generated music matches the text description you gave it
an AI trained to understand and answer questions about what it hears in audio
numerical representations that capture the meaning of text or audio in a way computers can compare

papers.title: MixJudge: Learning a Language-Queryable Critic for Vocal Mixing
papers.summary: Mixing requires not only applying processing but also assessing the resulting mix. Audio-language models can provide conversa- tional mixing advice, but existing evaluations do not separately test whether they can judge specific mixing issues. Since professional supervision for such judgments is scarce, we construct a curriculum of 11 vocal-mix issues at multiple severity levels and use it to train MixJudge, a language-queryable audio critic. MixJudge shows its ability to retrieve mixing issues, distinguish opposite issues, and order the severity of an issue. Moreover, its judgments transfer to menu selection: given a set of processing candidates, MixJudge often favors versions acoustically closer to a held-out professional version, demonstrating how explicit mixing judgment can support comparison and downstream mixing decisions.

explain.tldr: A system that learns to identify and rate specific vocal mixing problems by listening and responding to questions.
explain.plain: Mixing involves both applying effects and judging whether the result sounds good. While AI models can chat about mixing advice, nobody has tested whether they can actually spot specific problems like too much reverb or poor balance. The researchers created training data covering 11 common vocal mixing issues at different severity levels, then built MixJudge—a tool that listens to mixes and answers questions about what's wrong. It can identify issues, tell opposite problems apart, and rate how severe a problem is. When given choices of different processing options, it tends to pick the ones that sound closer to professional mixes.
explain.why: This could help producers and engineers get detailed feedback on their mixes without needing an expert in the room. Instead of vague suggestions, you could ask the system specific questions about your vocal mix and get assessments of particular problems, which could guide your mixing choices.

terms.meaning: AI systems trained on both sound and text, so they can listen to audio and discuss it in conversation
a structured training approach where a model learns from examples organized by difficulty or category
when a model trained on one task performs well on a related but different task

papers.title: A Learned Musical-Time Coordinate for Piano Audio-to-Score Transcription
papers.summary: End-to-end piano audio-to-score (A2S) transcription is the task of reconstructing a notated score from an audio recording in a single system. Existing A2S approaches usually rely on pre-segmented excerpts, and few handle whole pieces without external segmentation. This raises the question of whether a musical-time coordinate can guide score transcription while also helping the system segment whole pieces. Previous work on jazz saxophone A2S uses an external beat tracker to obtain such a coordinate for score prediction. We introduce downbeat phase, a musical-time coordinate learned jointly with score transcription that represents each audio frame's relative position within a notated bar. With this coordinate, our system can not only condition its score decoder on downbeat phase but also self-segment at bar boundaries and stitch the segments into a whole piece. Evaluation suggests that the coordinate improves metrical structure and supports whole-piece transcription with comparable notation quality.

explain.tldr: A system learns to transcribe piano recordings to sheet music for whole pieces by learning where each sound falls within a musical bar.
explain.plain: Converting a piano recording into readable sheet music is hard, especially for full pieces rather than short clips. Most existing systems need help knowing where bar lines should go. This paper teaches a transcription system to learn 'downbeat phase'—essentially, where each moment in the audio sits relative to the bar structure—at the same time it's learning to transcribe. This learned coordinate helps the system both predict the right notes and automatically figure out where to split the piece into bars, then reassemble it into a complete score.
explain.why: If this works well, musicians and producers could convert piano recordings into editable sheet music automatically, without manually chopping up the audio or using separate tools to find the beat. This matters for music notation, archiving, and making recordings easier to work with in notation software.

terms.meaning: automatically converting a recording of music into written sheet music notation
a learned measure of where each sound in the audio falls within a musical bar (e.g., on beat 1, beat 2, etc.)
a single system that handles the whole task in one go, rather than using separate tools for different steps

papers.title: Optimized Compressor Parameterization for Produced Music in Hearing Aids
papers.summary: Hearing aid compression is typically designed for speech, yet music demands different trade-offs due to its narrower dynamic range (DR) and impulsive transients. This paper investigates whether music fitting benefits from being signal-aware, both in mapping compression demand across signal-audiogram conditions and in tuning its parameters to these combinations rather than inheriting them from speech-derived prescriptions. Compression demand is characterized across eight audiometric profiles, three residual DR severities, and three produced music signals under linear gain. Signal dynamics emerge as a first-order factor: production-compressed music fits the residual DR of the mild-to-moderate profiles evaluated, while dynamically rich recordings challenge even moderate hearing loss. Per-signal optimization of single- and multi-band wide dynamic range compression is then applied to two profiles with the highest compression demand. This optimization improves the Hearing Aid Audio Quality Index over gain-optimized NAL-NL2 baselines while also improving audibility, indicating substantial headroom for music-specific fitting.

explain.tldr: Hearing aids need different compression settings for music than speech, optimized per song.
explain.plain: Hearing aids use compression to make sound audible for people with hearing loss, but they're typically tuned for speech. Music has different characteristics—it can be either very compressed (like produced pop music) or very dynamic (like classical recordings)—so the same settings don't work well for both. This paper tests whether customizing compression settings for individual music tracks and hearing loss profiles sounds better than using standard speech-based settings. They found that optimizing compression per song improved both sound quality and audibility compared to standard approaches.
explain.why: If you produce music or care about how it sounds to people with hearing loss, this suggests hearing aid fittings could be much better if they account for your music's specific dynamic characteristics rather than treating all audio the same way.

terms.meaning: the difference between the quietest and loudest parts of a sound or song
a hearing aid tool that reduces loud sounds and boosts quiet ones to fit a wider range of volumes into what someone can hear
a measurement of how much hearing loss someone has at different frequencies

papers.title: Heard But Not Said: Prompting Understates Temporal Information of Musical Moments in Frozen Large Audio-Language Models
papers.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) understand music, yet struggle to locate a described moment in time. We ask whether this reflects missing temporal information or a bottleneck in how the time span is extracted. Using a paired-query probe built from Slakh2100 stem activations, we attach a state query (e.g., ``only piano and bass are playing'') and a change query (e.g., ``the guitar drops out, leaving piano and bass'') to the same span and vary how much preceding audio the model is shown. Across frozen LALMs, three ways of extracting the span ask different questions: full-track prompting asking whether the model can say when; windowed yes/no scoring asking whether it verifies the moment when handed the segment, and whether it needs what came before; attention asking whether it can find the moment on its own. State queries score above baseline without context, while change queries improve with preceding context in most short-segment models; 30s padded encoders show no comparable recovery. Prompting and attention expose almost none of this. Prompting failures thus understate what LALMs can verify, though not what they can locate, by an amount set by query type and encoder.

explain.tldr: Large audio-language models understand musical moments better than prompting suggests; different extraction methods reveal hidden temporal knowledge.
explain.plain: Large audio-language models can understand music but struggle when asked to pinpoint when something happens in a song. Researchers tested whether this is because the models lack temporal information or because the way we ask them questions hides what they actually know. They created paired queries—one asking about a musical state ("only piano and bass") and one about a change ("guitar drops out")—and tried different ways of extracting answers. They found that models can verify moments better than prompting alone suggests, especially when given context about what came before, but this ability stays hidden unless you ask the right way.
explain.why: For musicians and producers using AI tools, this matters because it shows current models have more temporal understanding than their limitations suggest. Understanding these hidden capabilities could lead to better AI features for finding moments in songs, editing, or synchronization tasks.

terms.meaning: AI models trained to understand both sound and language, kept in their original state without further training
asking an AI model a question or giving it instructions to get a response
a mechanism that lets AI models focus on specific parts of input data to find relevant information

papers.title: Phase-Based Onset Enhancement for Piano Transcription in Ensemble Settings
papers.summary: Piano transcription models have achieved very high performance in recent state-of-the-art systems, but their performance tends to degrade in ensemble settings where the piano is played alongside other instruments. While some approaches attempt to address this issue by incorporating multi-instrumental datasets, the problem remains challenging. In particular, when other instruments produce high-energy sustained tones while relatively low-energy piano notes occur simultaneously, the magnitude components of their frequency representations overlap, making it difficult to accurately distinguish piano notes. To address this issue, we propose an improved piano transcription model that jointly leverages magnitude and phase information, enabling more robust piano transcription performance in ensemble settings. We evaluate the proposed model on two piano ensemble datasets with precise MIDI note annotations, which we obtained by revisiting and extending existing datasets. Notably, we constructed a new piano concerto dataset, PCD-K, by playing a piano part on a Disklavier and recording the audio and MIDI pairs with pre-recorded orchestral tracks. Experimental results demonstrate that phase information is highly effective in improving performance, outperforming magnitude-based approaches in ensemble settings.

explain.tldr: Using phase information alongside magnitude improves piano note detection when piano plays with other instruments.
explain.plain: Piano transcription—automatically detecting which notes a piano plays—works well solo but struggles in ensembles when other instruments' loud sustained tones mask quieter piano notes. The researchers found that looking at both the magnitude (loudness) and phase (timing details) of audio frequencies helps separate piano from other instruments. They tested this on two datasets, including a new one they created by recording a Disklavier piano playing with orchestral backing tracks, and showed phase-based methods outperform magnitude-only approaches.
explain.why: If you're working on tools to transcribe or analyze piano in orchestral recordings or mixed ensembles, this shows that phase information—often overlooked in audio analysis—can significantly improve accuracy in detecting what the piano is actually playing.

terms.meaning: Two components of audio frequency information: magnitude is how loud each frequency is, phase describes the timing/alignment of those frequencies
A piano that can both play notes and record exactly which keys were pressed, producing synchronized audio and MIDI data
Precise digital records of which piano notes were played and when, used as ground truth for training and testing

papers.title: Where Does Timbre Hide? Localizing Speaker Information in Speech Signals
papers.summary: Timbre similarity is a key evaluation target for generative speech systems, including voice conversion, speaker-cloning text-to-speech, and zero-shot speech models. When the generated voice does not match the target speaker, the problem often reflects imperfect separation of speaker-related timbre from content, making it important to identify where timbre information resides and which representations still carry it. Using speaker identity as a measurable proxy, we probe frequency bands, phase/magnitude structure, WORLD source/filter decomposition, voiced/unvoiced regions, self-supervised learning (SSL) layers, EnCodec/HuBERT tokens, and a 45-listener test across Mandarin, English, and Japanese speech/singing data. Speaker information is distributed: 1--8 kHz magnitude and vocal-tract spectral-envelope structure dominate perception, above-8 kHz bands remain machine-discriminative, shallow SSL layers expose compact speaker information, and token leakage depends on tokenizer/layer choice. These findings indicate where generation systems should condition on or transform speaker information, and where content, codec, and token pipelines should audit residual speaker leakage.

explain.tldr: Researchers identify where speaker identity information hides in speech signals to improve voice conversion and voice cloning.
explain.plain: When AI systems generate speech in someone's voice, they often fail to capture the right timbre—the unique sonic quality that makes a voice recognizable. The problem is that speaker information gets mixed up with the actual words being spoken. This study systematically searched through different parts of speech signals (different frequencies, sound components, and AI model layers) to find where speaker identity information actually lives. They tested this across multiple languages and had listeners verify their findings, discovering that certain frequency ranges and vocal characteristics carry the most recognizable speaker information, while other parts leak speaker identity in ways AI systems might not expect.
explain.why: For musicians and producers working with voice conversion, voice cloning, or AI singing tools, this explains why these systems sometimes fail to sound like the target voice or accidentally change the speaker when you only want to change the words. Understanding where timbre hides helps engineers build better tools that preserve or transform voice characteristics more reliably.

terms.meaning: the characteristic tone or color of a sound that lets you recognize a voice or instrument, separate from pitch and loudness
levels within an AI model that learn patterns from raw audio without needing labeled examples, often used as a foundation for speech tasks
the shape of the frequency content created by your throat and mouth shape, which is a major part of what makes your voice sound like you

papers.title: MuseFlow-TSE: Music-Aware Target Speech Extraction via Cross-Source Band-Splitting and Data-to-Data Flow Matching
papers.summary: Target speech extraction (TSE) isolates a speaker's voice given an enrollment utterance, but existing work is validated almost exclusively without music. Discriminative methods are content-faithful yet masking-bounded; generative methods improve naturalness but may hallucinate, drift in identity, and require many steps. We present MuseFlow-TSE, a discriminative deletion, generative insertion framework for music-bearing scenes. Stage-1 is a music-aware cross-source band-split extractor that estimates target, interfering speakers, music, and noise under conservation and music-leakage constraints. Stage-2 is a data-to-data flow refiner initialized by the discriminative estimate, negatively conditioned on interference stems, and run for 1--4 difficulty-adaptive Euler steps with an end-to-end fidelity objective.

explain.tldr: A system that isolates a singer's voice from recordings with music and other speakers.
explain.plain: When you want to extract one person's voice from a recording that also has music and other speakers, it's really hard. This paper presents MuseFlow-TSE, which does this in two stages: first, it splits the audio into separate parts (target voice, other speakers, music, and noise) while being careful not to lose the music; second, it refines the result using a generative process that learns from the first stage and improves the quality. The approach balances staying true to what's actually in the recording while making the extracted voice sound natural.
explain.why: This matters if you're working with vocal recordings that have instrumental backing or live performances—situations where you need clean vocals but can't rely on existing tools that were only tested on speech without music.

terms.meaning: isolating one specific person's voice from a mixed audio recording
dividing audio into separate frequency ranges or source components (like splitting into vocals, drums, bass, etc.)
telling a generative model what *not* to produce, so it avoids recreating unwanted sounds like background speakers or noise

papers.title: Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoding of Sperm Whale Coda
papers.summary: Sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) communicate through short click sequences called codas, whose structure includes the rhythmic pattern of inter-click intervals (ICI) and the spectral composition of the clicks. In this paper, we propose the Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoder (DCCE), which explicitly encodes rhythm and spectral information with separate encoders before fusing them. We evaluate DCCE on three coda-understanding tasks: social unit, coda type, and individual identification. We compare DCCE against strong baselines from literature under a common linear-probe protocol and analyze the role of each channel and training objective through ablations. On 1,383 codas, shared partitions and validation-only layer selection support three random splits and three recording-date-disjoint folds. DCCE with unit pairing and type supervision achieves mean random-split macro-F1 of 0.901/0.865/0.597 for unit/type/identity. Raw ICI remains strongest for type (0.987), and ICI plus temporal mel statistics is a strong identity reference (0.724). An auxiliary identity objective improves spectral-branch identity prediction but does not improve the mean fused-identity score in this configuration. Date-grouped evaluation and four year holdouts expose generalization limits. The results support task-dependent combinations of timing and spectral information, without establishing independent biological channels or general architectural superiority. Code, notebooks, and complete results are available at https://dcce-research-site.vercel.app.

explain.tldr: A machine learning system that separately analyzes whale click timing and sound quality to identify whale social groups and individuals.
explain.plain: Sperm whales communicate through rhythmic click sequences with specific timing patterns and sound characteristics. Researchers built a system with two separate analysis paths—one for the rhythm of clicks and one for their sound spectrum—that combine their findings to identify which whale group made the sounds and which individual whale it was. The rhythm information alone worked best for identifying coda types, while combining rhythm and spectral details helped identify individual whales, though the system struggled to generalize across different recording dates.
explain.why: This work demonstrates how analyzing different acoustic dimensions separately can help identify patterns in complex animal communication. Musicians and producers might find the approach relevant for analyzing or processing layered sound information, and it shows practical challenges in building systems that work reliably across different recording conditions.

terms.meaning: the time gaps between individual clicks in a whale's coda sequence—essentially the rhythm or timing pattern
the frequency content or tonal qualities of a sound—what frequencies are present and how strong they are
a machine learning technique that learns by comparing similar and different examples to find meaningful patterns

papers.title: Agentic Music Post-Production
papers.summary: We introduce MixAgent, an agentic pipeline for music post-production that follows the workflow of audio engineers to build interpretable and editable mixing plans guided by a reference song. A grouping agent first routes related input tracks, such as drum recordings, into subgroups. A planning agent then uses retrieved examples to choose and order audio effects, such as volume control and reverb, for tracks, subgroups, and the full mix. To refine the mix, a detector identifies what needs correction, and a critic proposes numerical parameter adjustments from tracks to the full mix. In our experiments, prompting recent multimodal models to listen and revise often worsens the mix, making reliable correction a central challenge. We therefore build MixCritic, a dataset of 45,657 repair critiques derived from parameters fitted to professional mixes, and train the critic with supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization on rendered audio outcomes. On MedleyDB, learned refinement reduces error by 19% relative to the initial mix, with preference optimization reducing it by 8.4% over supervised training alone. Retrieved examples further improve effects selection, and a human listening test shows that MixAgent gets higher quality ratings than mixes produced by Qwen3-Omni, Gemini 3.8 Flash and GPT-4o-audio.

explain.tldr: MixAgent automates music mixing by routing tracks, selecting effects, and refining parameters guided by reference songs.
explain.plain: Professional mixing involves many decisions: grouping related tracks, choosing effects like reverb or EQ, and tweaking settings to sound good. This paper presents MixAgent, a system that mimics how audio engineers work by first organizing tracks into groups, then selecting and ordering effects based on similar professional mixes, and finally refining the mix by detecting problems and adjusting parameters. The key challenge was getting AI models to reliably improve mixes—just asking them to listen and fix things often made things worse. So the researchers created a dataset of 45,000+ professional mixing corrections and trained a specialized critic to suggest better parameter settings. Their system reduced mixing errors by 19% and outperformed other AI music tools in listening tests.
explain.why: This matters because mixing is time-consuming and requires expertise. A tool that can handle routine mixing decisions—grouping instruments, applying effects, and fine-tuning levels—could speed up production workflows and make professional-quality mixing more accessible to producers without years of experience.

terms.meaning: collections of related tracks (like all drums or all vocals) that are mixed together as a unit before going to the final mix
a training method that teaches a system to prefer better outcomes by comparing different results rather than just copying examples
AI systems that can process multiple types of information at once, like both audio and text

papers.title: Derivation Depth Exposes Reasoning Failures in Tool-Augmented Music Analysis
papers.summary: Audio-language models remain unreliable at extracting basic musical properties from audio, motivating pipelines that place a music information retrieval (MIR) tool between the audio and the model. The tool reports measurements such as keys, chords, and structural similarity, and the model is expected to derive the answer. We test whether it can. Holding the musical information fixed, we vary derivation depth: the number of reasoning steps between the tool output and the answer. When the report states the conclusion, all five models score near 100%, and they follow it even when it is wrong. One step away, accuracy drops. On modulation, open models fall to 57-81%, although they answer that single step correctly when asked directly, and reach 0% at greater depths. Frontier models degrade less, but still degrade. Adding the audio does not recover the loss. The bottleneck in tool-augmented music analysis is not access to musical information but reasoning from it, so tool design must account for how much derivation it leaves to the model.

explain.tldr: Audio-language models struggle to reason through multiple steps from music analysis tool outputs, even when given correct information.
explain.plain: When researchers tested whether AI models could use music analysis tools (which measure things like keys and chords), they found a surprising problem: the models work great when the answer is stated directly, but fail when they need to reason through even one or two steps to get there. For example, on questions about musical modulation (key changes), open-source models dropped from near-perfect accuracy to 57-81% accuracy with just one reasoning step needed. The issue isn't that the models can't access the musical information—it's that they can't reliably think through what to do with it.
explain.why: This matters because it shows that simply feeding AI models better music analysis tools won't automatically make them better at music understanding. If you're building systems that use these tools, you need to design them so the model doesn't have to do complex reasoning—the tool should do more of the thinking for you.

terms.meaning: Software that automatically analyzes audio to extract specific musical facts like key, tempo, or chord progressions
The number of reasoning steps a model must take to get from tool output to final answer
An AI system trained to understand both sound and text, able to answer questions about audio

papers.title: KunSet: A Corpus and Benchmark for Lyrics Alignment and Rhyme Retrieval in Kunqu Opera
papers.summary: Kunqu is one of the oldest extant forms of Chinese opera, yet its digitization remains scarce and difficult to annotate, with two challenges standing out: first, close analysis of Kunqu performance demands syllable-level lyrics alignment; second, analyzing Kunqu pronunciation requires its phonological attributes (e.g., rhyme) to be linked with each syllable. To address these challenges, we present KunSet, the first Kunqu performance corpus comprising 482,164 fine-grained annotations of syllable-level lyrics and phonological attributes in total media duration of 155.2 h with 106.3 h annotated. To ensure annotation quality, KunSet was preannotated by an iterative ML-assisted pipeline and corrected by over 200 trained annotators via a purpose-built online annotation system under a two-round review process. To assess KunSet as a music information retrieval (MIR) benchmark, we evaluate two tasks: lyrics alignment, by finetuning a forced-alignment model with an acoustic anchor decoder; and same-rhyme retrieval, using frozen Chinese HuBERT features. Models built with KunSet outperform their baselines. We release KunSet and model checkpoints to support MIR research on traditional-music corpora.

explain.tldr: A dataset and benchmark for matching Kunqu opera lyrics to audio and finding rhyming syllables.
explain.plain: Kunqu is an ancient Chinese opera form that's rarely digitized. The researchers created KunSet, a large collection of Kunqu performances with detailed annotations linking each syllable of lyrics to the audio and marking phonological features like rhyme. They built and tested two systems: one that automatically syncs lyrics to audio, and another that finds syllables with matching rhymes. Both systems performed better when trained on KunSet than on existing methods.
explain.why: This work preserves and makes analyzable a centuries-old musical tradition that's at risk of being lost. For musicians and producers interested in traditional music, it demonstrates how to systematically document and computationally analyze opera with syllable-level precision—useful for transcription, analysis, and potentially new creative applications.

terms.meaning: automatically matching spoken or sung words to their exact timing in an audio recording
sound-based properties of language, like which syllables rhyme or share similar pronunciation patterns
a machine-learning model that converts audio into numerical representations capturing speech and sound characteristics

papers.title: Resonance and Depth: Composing Timbral Identity and Spatial Form in an Artist-in-the-Loop Co-Creative Multi-Agent Percussive Performance
papers.summary: This research-creation artistic report presents Resonance and Depth, a 9-minute immersive electroacoustic/acousmatic performance that treats timbre and space as primary compositional materials. Built from live electronic percussion and a personal corpus recorded, curated, and composed by the author, the work investigates how timbral identity and musical form can emerge through real-time recombination, spatialisation, and performer-system interaction rather than conventional harmonic development. The performance is realised as an artist-in-the-loop co-creative multi-agent system integrating MACAT, MACataRT, a MIDI-based musical agent, a spatialisation layer, and a conductor agent. These components recombine and transform the performer's material through concatenative synthesis, audio mosaicing, symbolic mediation, physically inspired synthesis, and object-based spatialisation. The work approaches spatialisation as an active compositional process in which position, trajectory, depth, diffusion, width, and apparent size participate in musical phrasing and form. Through this practice-based framework, Resonance and Depth examines how performer identity can be retained, transformed, and redistributed across human, algorithmic, timbral, and spatial processes within an immersive co-creative performance ecology.

explain.tldr: An electroacoustic performance where AI agents and a live percussionist collaborate to create music by transforming sounds and positioning them in space.
explain.plain: This is an artistic work that uses timbre (tone color) and spatial positioning as the main building blocks instead of traditional harmony. A percussionist performs live while multiple AI agents listen and respond in real-time, recombining the performer's sounds in new ways and moving them around in 3D space. The system treats the performer and the algorithms as equal creative partners, allowing the musician's identity to flow between human playing, computer processing, and spatial effects.
explain.why: This shows how live performers can collaborate with AI systems as creative partners rather than just tools, and demonstrates that space itself can be a compositional element as important as melody or rhythm. It's relevant if you're interested in how technology can expand what's possible in live performance or how to maintain artistic identity when working with algorithmic systems.

terms.meaning: Creating new sounds by cutting up and reassembling pieces of existing recordings in different orders
Covering or replacing a sound by finding similar small pieces from a sound library and stitching them together
Placing individual sounds as distinct objects in 3D space rather than mixing them into stereo channels

papers.title: Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR Technical Report
papers.summary: We present Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR, a family of audio-language models that builds upon its predecesor Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR with improved speech recognition and expanded capabilities in speaker-diarized transcription and general audio understanding. The family retains support for 30 languages and 16 Chinese dialects, together with instruction-controlled capabilities including historical-context conditioning, hierarchical hotword customization, and native transcription polishing. Speaker-diarized ASR produces structured outputs containing speaker labels, timestamps, and recognized text, maintaining consistent speaker labels across turns and the representation of overlapping speech. The general audio understanding capabilities cover audio-, speech-, and music-captioning, temporal grounding and sound event detection, as well as audio question answering and multiple-choice reasoning. These tasks broaden the application scope from recognizing spoken words to interpreting speakers, acoustic events, and their temporal relations. To accommodate different deployment requirements, the family includes variants for asynchronous file transcription, low-latency streaming, interactive voice input, and non-streaming recognition, with speaker-diarized transcription and general audio understanding available in certain variants. Evaluations span conventional ASR, multilingual and dialectal speech, speaker-diarized transcription, and general audio understanding, demonstrating the capabilities of the Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR family across transcription and broader audio analysis tasks.

explain.tldr: Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR improves speech recognition and adds speaker identification, music captioning, and sound event detection across 30 languages.
explain.plain: This is an upgraded speech-to-text system that does more than just convert spoken words to text. It can now identify who is speaking (speaker diarization), describe music and sounds, detect what acoustic events are happening, and answer questions about audio. The system works in multiple languages and dialects, and comes in different versions—some for quick file processing, others for real-time streaming conversations. The researchers tested it on standard speech recognition tasks as well as these new capabilities.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this matters because it can automatically transcribe sessions with multiple speakers while identifying who said what, caption your music and sound design work, and detect specific acoustic events—useful for organizing recordings, creating documentation, or building interactive audio applications.

terms.meaning: automatically identifying and labeling different speakers in an audio recording, so you know who said what
generating text descriptions of what's happening in audio, similar to how image captioning describes pictures
identifying and locating specific sounds or acoustic events in audio, like detecting when a drum hits or a door slams

papers.title: Transformer-Based Plate Parameter Estimation with Differentiable and Particle-Swarm Refinement
papers.summary: We present two Transformer-based methods for Task A of the 1st DAFx Parameter Estimation Challenge, which requires estimating six effective physical parameters of a synthetic plate-reverb model from its impulse response (IR). Method A1 combines an Audio Spectrogram Transformer encoder and Transformer regressor with differentiable IR refinement. Method A2 uses the same encoder to condition a continuous normalizing flow and refines sampled candidates using particle swarm optimisation (PSO) and gradient polishing. Both methods preserve the absolute IR scale to recover surface density. On a synthetic holdout set of 100 IRs, both refinement procedures reduce waveform and parameter errors by more than three orders of magnitude relative to the unrefined neural outputs. The PSO-based pipeline achieves the lowest errors, indicating near-perfect recovery in this matched synthetic setting.

explain.tldr: Two AI methods estimate physical parameters of plate reverb from its sound using neural networks and optimization refinement.
explain.plain: Plate reverb is a classic effect that simulates sound bouncing in a metal plate. The challenge is figuring out the physical settings (like plate size and material density) just by listening to how it affects sound. This paper uses Transformer neural networks—a type of AI good at processing audio—combined with two different refinement techniques: one using calculus-based optimization and another using particle swarm optimization (a nature-inspired search method). Both approaches dramatically improved accuracy, with the particle swarm version achieving near-perfect results on test data.
explain.why: If you could automatically measure a plate reverb's physical properties from its sound, you could better recreate classic reverb tones, design new reverbs more precisely, or understand how different physical designs affect the sound you hear.

terms.meaning: The sound a reverb produces when given a very short click; it captures the complete character of the effect
A neural network architecture that's particularly good at learning patterns in sequences, including audio
A search algorithm inspired by how bird flocks move, used to find the best solution by testing many candidates

papers.title: Sound Matching with a Differentiable Karplus-Strong Algorithm
papers.summary: We present a self-supervised, event-based sound matching model using a differentiable extended Karplus-Strong algorithm. To avoid relying on external onset and fundamental frequency detectors, we explore training methodologies combining parameter losses on synthetic data with audio losses. We demonstrate that time-domain fractional delay interpolation provides gradient accuracy comparable to frequency-sampling while avoiding time-aliasing in highly resonant time-varying scenarios. Through systematic gradient analysis, we reveal that standard spectral losses provide no meaningful directional gradients for onset times, heavily degrading joint training. Training exclusively with parameter losses on synthetic data effectively learns fundamental frequency, timbral parameters, and onset times, but struggles to generalise to monophonic studio recordings of plucked guitar. External detectors combined with audio losses generalise best, isolating the model to timbre optimisation. While our Karplus-Strong decoder recovers interpretable parameters and naturally captures the transient characteristics of plucked guitar, Harmonics plus Noise baselines yield higher reconstruction fidelity by most metrics.

explain.tldr: A differentiable Karplus-Strong algorithm learns to match plucked string sounds by predicting onset times, pitch, and timbre without external detectors.
explain.plain: The researchers built a system that can analyze plucked guitar sounds and recreate them by controlling parameters of a Karplus-Strong synthesizer—a classic algorithm for modeling plucked strings. They trained it using synthetic data and real audio, discovering that certain loss functions (ways of measuring how close the match is) work better than others. The model successfully learns when notes start, their pitch, and their tone color, though it works best when combined with external pitch detection. While simpler methods sometimes sound more accurate, this approach has the advantage of producing interpretable, musically meaningful parameters.
explain.why: This matters because it offers a way to automatically analyze and re-synthesize plucked string sounds using a model that produces understandable parameters—useful for sound design, music analysis, or building tools that let you edit recorded guitar tones by tweaking synthesis parameters rather than working with raw audio.

terms.meaning: A simple synthesis method that models plucked string sounds by filtering and feeding back noise through a delay line
Training a model without hand-labeled data by having it learn from the structure of the data itself
Designed so that gradients (directional information for learning) can flow backward through it, allowing the algorithm to be trained like a neural network

papers.title: MiCLA: Mixture-to-Constituent Latent Alignment for Polyphonic Audio Representation Learning
papers.summary: Real-world audio typically contains concurrent sound events, yet standard self-supervised methods treat each clip as an isolated training unit without explicitly modeling mixture--constituent relationships. We propose Mixture-to-Constituent Latent Alignment (MiCLA), a two-stage self-supervised pre-training framework that uses synthetic log-mel mixing to align mixture representations with their constituent clips. Stage 1 structures single-clip representations via masked self-distillation and contrastive regularization. Stage 2 introduces bidirectional alignment: for a synthetic mixture, MiCLA suppresses the component aligned with one constituent and aligns the residual with the other, using projective residualization on patch tokens and sample-adaptive soft residualization on the global class token. In downstream evaluations, MiCLA achieves 43.2% mean average precision (mAP) on AS-20K and 50.3% mAP on AS-2M under fine-tuning, and achieves the highest mAP among evaluated models on both AudioSet settings under frozen Convex Gated Probing (CGP). Furthermore, a Joint Semantic Retrieval diagnostic shows that MiCLA improves simultaneous retrieval of both constituent classes over target-averaging baselines. These results indicate that directional mixture-to-constituent alignment provides an effective pre-training signal for polyphonic audio representation learning.

explain.tldr: A training method that helps AI models better understand audio with multiple overlapping sounds by learning how mixtures relate to individual sources.
explain.plain: Most audio in the real world has multiple sounds happening at once, but standard AI training methods ignore this. This paper proposes MiCLA, which trains models by creating synthetic mixtures of sounds and teaching the model to understand how the mixture relates to each individual sound component. They test it on large audio datasets and find it performs better than existing methods at identifying sounds in complex audio, and can better retrieve both sounds when they're mixed together.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this matters because better AI understanding of polyphonic audio could improve tools for source separation, audio tagging, and music analysis—tasks that currently struggle when multiple instruments or sounds play together.

terms.meaning: Training an AI model on unlabeled audio data by creating its own learning targets, rather than needing humans to label everything
A way of converting audio into a visual representation that mimics how human ears perceive loudness and pitch
Audio containing multiple simultaneous sounds or musical voices playing at the same time

papers.title: Steering intonational tunes in text-to-speech synthesis
papers.summary: Text-to-speech systems built on residual vector quantization often generate audio in two stages: a transformer backbone emits the first level of each frame's token stack, and a smaller depth model generates the rest autoregressively. We ask which components of such a model are responsible for prosodic intonation, more precisely for generating the English nuclear tune (for instance, the falling pitch melody that distinguishes an assertion from a question's rising melody), and whether interventions on those components can be used to control intonation. Prompt-based control mostly fails; only a final question mark is a reliable lever. Interchange interventions in CSM and S2 locate the tune: the backbone's hidden state carries it to the waveform through the depth model, and the first level of the stack carries little or none of it. Steering the backbone state with a difference-of-means vector computed on new material generated with a final period or question mark moves the tune, but the push toward an assertion degrades the voice. Steering vectors computed instead from the backbone states associated with human imitations of theoretically-specified tunes, whose text carries no punctuation, and applied inside the generation loop, move most recordings to the other condition in both systems (even when fitted without the speaker being steered), at a small cost in predicted naturalness. These imitation-derived vectors are aligned with the one obtained from the two punctuated conditions far beyond a shuffled-label null, so the backbone state of a punctuated prompt already represents intonation. The steered recordings broadly become falling or rising, according to the intent, but the edge tone moves more coherently than the pitch accent, and the target tune cannot be selected precisely beyond this broad tendency.

explain.tldr: Researchers identify and steer the pitch patterns (intonation) in AI speech synthesis by manipulating hidden neural states.
explain.plain: Text-to-speech systems generate speech in stages, but it's unclear which parts control intonation—the pitch patterns that make speech sound like a question versus a statement. The researchers found that the main neural network (backbone) carries intonation information to the final output, while punctuation marks alone don't reliably control it. By computing 'steering vectors' from recordings of human speakers imitating specific pitch patterns, they could push the synthesized speech toward rising or falling melodies, though the control isn't perfectly precise.
explain.why: This matters because musicians and producers using text-to-speech tools could gain finer control over the emotional tone and naturalness of synthesized vocals. Understanding how AI models handle intonation helps make synthetic speech sound more expressive and intentional.

terms.meaning: A technique that breaks audio into discrete tokens (like a musical alphabet) in layers, allowing the model to generate speech step-by-step
A mathematical direction computed from examples that, when applied to a neural network's internal states, nudges the output toward a desired characteristic
The main pitch melody pattern at the end of a spoken phrase that conveys meaning (like rising pitch for questions)

papers.title: pyFDN: A Python Toolbox for Feedback Delay Network Design, Analysis, and Optimization
papers.summary: Feedback delay networks (FDNs) provide a compact representation of recursive audio systems for artificial reverberation and decorrelation. Their practical use spans structured matrix design, acoustic decay shaping, numerical simulation, and modal analysis, increasingly combined with differentiable optimization. We present pyFDN, an open-source Python toolbox that brings these operations into a common workflow. The library combines numerical design and analysis routines with block-based time-domain processing and integration with FLAMO for frequency-domain differentiable processing. Explicit network builds and JSON presets connect design, optimization, rendering, and reuse. This paper describes the software architecture, representative capabilities, and reproducibility mechanisms of version 0.5.0, providing a reference for research and teaching that use the toolbox.

explain.tldr: A Python tool for designing, analyzing, and optimizing feedback delay networks used in digital reverberation.
explain.plain: Feedback delay networks (FDNs) are a way to create artificial reverb and other effects by routing audio through interconnected delays. Researchers and producers have been using them in different ways—designing the network structure, shaping how sound decays, simulating it digitally, and now optimizing them automatically. This paper introduces pyFDN, a shared toolkit that puts all these operations together in one place, so musicians and researchers can design, test, tweak, and save their reverb designs more easily.
explain.why: If you make reverb plugins or study how reverb works, this toolbox could speed up your workflow by combining design, testing, and optimization in one system. It also makes research reproducible and easier to teach, since everyone uses the same tools.

terms.meaning: A digital audio system that creates reverb-like effects by feeding delayed copies of sound back into itself through a mixing matrix.
Automatically tuning parameters of a system by calculating how small changes affect the output, allowing computers to find better settings on their own.
Examining the natural resonant frequencies and decay patterns of a reverb system to understand how it colors sound.

papers.title: Point2Acoustic: Efficient Room Acoustic Parameter Estimation from 3D Geometry and Material Properties
papers.summary: Scene-adaptive immersive audio rendering requires rapid estimation of acoustic parameters that reflect the surrounding environment. For repeated runtime scene updates, performing a detailed geometric-acoustic simulation for every update can be computationally costly. We present Point2Acoustic, a learning-based framework for direct estimation of six-band reverberation time ($RT_{60}$) and reverberant-to-direct ratio (RDR) from 3D scene geometry and acoustic material properties. Each scene is represented by a surface-sampled point cloud with spatial coordinates and frequency-dependent absorption and scattering coefficients, and encoded using PointNet or PointNet++. We train and evaluate the framework on a synthetic furnished-room dataset with varied geometry and acoustic materials, using geometric-acoustic simulation to obtain reference targets. Point2Acoustic achieves accurate multi-band prediction with millisecond-scale inference, and ablation results indicate that explicit global room descriptors and semantic surface labels provide no consistent benefit. The proposed formulation supports efficient scene-adaptive acoustic rendering in extended reality (XR).

explain.tldr: A machine learning system that quickly predicts how rooms sound from their 3D shape and materials.
explain.plain: When you want immersive audio in virtual environments, you need to know how sound behaves in a space—things like how long echoes last and how much direct sound reaches you versus reflected sound. Calculating this precisely for every scene update is slow. This paper trains a neural network to predict these acoustic properties directly from a 3D model of a room and its materials, running in milliseconds instead of minutes. They tested it on synthetic rooms and found it makes accurate predictions across different frequencies.
explain.why: For musicians and producers working with spatial audio, VR, or interactive music, this means real-time acoustic simulation becomes practical. You could hear how your mix sounds in different virtual spaces instantly, without waiting for heavy computation.

terms.meaning: How long it takes for sound to fade away in a room, measured in seconds. A longer RT60 means more echo.
A 3D representation of a space as a collection of points with coordinates, like a digital point-based model of a room's surfaces.
A neural network architecture designed to process point clouds directly, learning patterns from spatial point data.

papers.title: MuLaCover: Flexible Cover Song Generation via Symbolic Tonal Control
papers.summary: A cover song re-renders an existing piece, most commonly by preserving its tonal content -- melody and chord progression -- while reshaping other musical attributes. This suggests a natural formulation for generative cover synthesis with pretrained music language models: explicitly control tonal content, while specifying lyrics and style through text. Existing approaches condition on frame-level features, tightly coupling generation to the reference's timing and structure, and limiting flexibility such as tempo variation, structural rearrangement, or partial conditioning. To this end, we present MuLaCover, a cover generation model that conditions a pretrained text-to-song foundation model on an editable symbolic lead sheet. Our design enables alignment-free control: generated outputs preserve the tonal signature of the source without frame-level alignment, allowing flexible timing, structure, and segment-level generation. We further introduce a training curriculum with partially mismatched audio-symbolic pairs, improving diversity and robustness. We evaluate MuLaCover with objective metrics, standard subjective ratings, and in-depth expert interviews that provide fine-grained diagnostic insights. Experiments show that MuLaCover achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source systems and is competitive with leading commercial models such as Suno-v5.5. Audio samples and code are available at our project page: https://mulalabs.ai/mulacover/

explain.tldr: A system that generates cover songs by letting you control melody and chords while specifying lyrics and style through text.
explain.plain: Cover songs typically keep the original's melody and chord progression but change other elements like tempo or arrangement. This paper presents MuLaCover, which uses a pretrained AI music model to generate covers from an editable lead sheet—a simple notation of melody and chords. Unlike previous approaches that lock generation to the original's timing, MuLaCover lets you freely adjust tempo, rearrange sections, or generate only parts of a song. The system was trained with mismatched audio-symbol pairs to make it more flexible and diverse. Tests show it performs competitively with commercial tools like Suno.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this means more creative control when generating cover versions—you can experiment with different tempos, structures, or partial re-recordings without being locked to the original's timing. It could speed up arranging or demoing cover ideas.

terms.meaning: A simplified musical notation showing the melody line and chord symbols, without audio or timing details
Matching generation to specific time points in the original recording, which restricts flexibility
An AI model trained on large amounts of music data beforehand, then adapted for specific tasks like cover generation

papers.title: AudioScorer: Learning Question-Aware Token Relevance for Large Audio Language Models
papers.summary: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) reason over speech, environmental sounds, music, and other acoustic information. However, their audio encoders produce dense token sequences that make long-form audio costly to process. Existing audio pruning methods reduce this cost using heuristics such as attention, representation similarity, or temporal sampling, but do not explicitly learn which tokens are most useful for a given question. We propose AudioScorer, a lightweight model that scores audio tokens according to the user question. It is trained by distilling the ranking of audio tokens under the frozen LALM's answer-gradient saliency, together with downstream answer supervision. Compared with other pruning methods, AudioScorer achieves the best or tied-best result at 10% token retention on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks, including speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification.

explain.tldr: A method that learns which parts of audio matter most for answering specific questions, reducing processing costs.
explain.plain: Large audio language models process audio by breaking it into many small pieces (tokens), which is expensive for long recordings. Most existing methods decide which pieces to keep using simple rules. AudioScorer instead learns what's actually relevant by training on what the model thinks matters for answering each specific question. They tested it on tasks like recognizing speech, emotions, and sounds, and found it works better than other methods while keeping only 10% of the audio tokens.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this could make AI audio tools faster and more practical—whether you're using them for analysis, transcription, or sound design. It means these tools could work better on longer recordings or run on less powerful hardware.

terms.meaning: a small chunk of audio data that a model processes; think of it like breaking a song into tiny pieces
removing unnecessary parts of data to make processing faster and cheaper
a measure of how important or noticeable something is to a model's decision

papers.title: Structural Context from Audio and Lyric Evidence for Music Structure Analysis Using the New SheetSage-MSA Dataset
papers.summary: Music structure analysis (MSA) aims to identify functional labels and their boundaries in music. Despite recent progress, three challenges remain. First, fine-grained annotations for MSA are scarce. Second, existing systems often share one encoder between boundary detection and functional labeling despite their different information requirements. Third, most end-to-end systems are audio-only and ignore structural cues from lyrics. To address these issues, we construct SheetSage-MSA, an MSA dataset derived from SheetSage, containing 13,880 cleaned excerpt annotations from 9,010 songs and approximately 82.5 hours of annotated audio. We further propose SCALE (Structural Context from Audio and Lyric Evidence), which uses separate task-specific audio pathways to model local transitions and long-range structural context, and incorporates timestamped lyrics and lyrical recurrence to refine chorus predictions. On the HarmonixSet benchmark, SCALE outperforms the existing state-of-the-art SongFormer by 3.5 and 4.2 percentage points in HR.5F and HR3F, respectively, while improving ACC by 0.9 points. An interactive demo page containing the source code is also available at https://multimodal-music-research-lab.github.io/SCALE/.

explain.tldr: New dataset and AI system that identifies song sections (verse, chorus, etc.) using both audio and lyrics.
explain.plain: Music structure analysis means automatically labeling different parts of a song—like verses and choruses—and finding where they start and end. Current systems struggle because good training data is limited, they use the same approach for two different tasks that need different information, and they ignore lyrics. This paper introduces a large dataset of 9,010 songs with detailed section labels, and proposes SCALE, a system that uses separate audio pathways for different structural tasks and adds lyric information to better recognize repeated sections like choruses.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, better automatic song structure analysis could help with music organization, remixing, or generating accompaniment. For music software makers, this work shows how combining audio and lyrics improves accuracy, which could improve features in DAWs or music analysis tools.

terms.meaning: Automatically identifying and labeling the functional sections of a song (like intro, verse, chorus, bridge) and where they occur.
A neural network component that converts raw input (like audio) into a useful internal representation the system can work with.
When the same lyrics or similar lyrical patterns repeat in a song, which often signals repeated musical sections.

papers.title: Applicability and Generalization of Audio Fingerprinting Methods to Speech
papers.summary: Audio fingerprinting methods identify audio based on its content, even when the content has been possibly corrupted. Despite their applicability and usage in the speech domain, research and advancements in audio fingerprinting traditionally focus on music and are almost exclusively evaluated on music. We provide insights into speech-oriented audio fingerprinting by benchmarking the best performing audio fingerprinting models on speech data while taking into consideration the effects of noise, reverberation, temporal changes, pitch modifications, and lossy compression. Our findings indicate that audio fingerprinting methods based on self-supervised learning outperform classical approaches on speech data, while the performance of these models on speech is inferior compared to the performance that they achieve on music. Results also include an analysis of false positives, showing that fingerprinting methods are more likely to match with an audio of the same speaker rather than an audio of the same text, when mismatches occur.

explain.tldr: Audio fingerprinting methods work worse on speech than music, with self-supervised learning performing best.
explain.plain: Audio fingerprinting is a technique that identifies audio content even when it's been damaged or altered. Most research focuses on music, but fingerprinting is also used for speech. This paper tests leading fingerprinting methods on speech data while adding challenges like noise, echo, pitch shifts, and compression. They found that newer machine-learning-based methods outperform older techniques on speech, but still don't work as well as they do on music. Interestingly, when fingerprinting makes mistakes on speech, it tends to match the wrong audio if it's from the same speaker rather than the same words.
explain.why: If you're working with speech—podcasts, voice recordings, or vocal samples—understanding how fingerprinting performs on your material matters. This research shows the current limitations and suggests which methods might be more reliable for speech-based applications.

terms.meaning: A compact digital summary of audio content that lets you identify a recording even if it's been altered, compressed, or played through noisy conditions.
A machine-learning approach where a model learns patterns from raw data without needing humans to label examples, often by predicting parts of the data from other parts.
Incorrect matches—when the fingerprinting system says two different audio clips are the same when they actually aren't.

papers.title: Whistle and Wrong Lyrics: Synthetic Queries Are Not Enough for Real-World Query-by-Melody
papers.summary: People look up a song by humming it, but also by whistling it or singing it with the wrong words. Published query-by-humming systems and benchmarks focus on hums and sung queries, and no public dataset pairs whistles or wrong-lyrics singing with song recordings. We study both query types with a melody-only retrieval system: a key-normalized pitch track embedded by a 5.2M-parameter contour encoder, with a spectral-peak tracker for whistles. First, a physics-grounded generator renders synthetic whistles and nonsense-syllable singing from the vocal melodies of 11,083 songs. Training on them raises top-1 retrieval of held-out synthetic queries against an 11,050-song gallery from 0.180 to 0.251 for whistles and from 0.193 to 0.264 for wrong-lyrics singing, but the gain does not transfer: on the MLEnd test performers the best synthetic-only model gets 210 of 339 real whistles right at top-1, against 214 for the baseline. Second, a closed-set fine-tune on real MLEnd whistles with performer-disjoint splits raises whistle-to-hum top-1 from 0.631 (95% CI 0.581-0.681) to 0.673 (0.622-0.723), on known songs only. Third, two further generations of synthetic queries also fail to transfer: melody-conditioned whistles and la-la singing from a commercial neural music model leave real-whistle top-1 at 0.631, and an open-source pipeline (YingMusic-Singer-Plus singing with partly wrong, mumbled or nonsense lyrics, a DDSP whistle synthesizer, and a melody-error model fitted on real performers) gives at best 0.619 (paired difference -0.012, 95% CI -0.038 to +0.015). Across physics-based, commercial neural and open-source neural synthetic data, nothing transferred to real whistles, which points to collecting real queries as the missing step. Code is public; models and data will be released.
