explain.tldr: Synthetic whistles and wrong-lyrics singing don't help train systems to recognize real whistles or wrong-lyrics queries.
explain.plain: Musicians search for songs by humming, whistling, or singing with wrong words. Researchers built a system to find songs from these queries using pitch tracking and neural networks. They tried training it on artificially generated whistles and wrong-lyrics singing, but found this synthetic data didn't improve performance on real whistles and wrong-lyrics from actual people—suggesting real recordings are needed instead.
explain.why: If you want music apps that recognize whistles or imperfect singing as search queries, this work shows that synthetic training data alone won't work. It highlights the practical gap between lab-generated audio and how people actually hum, whistle, and sing.

terms.meaning: a sequence of musical notes extracted from audio, showing the melody without timbre or harmony
a neural network that converts the shape of a melody into a compact numerical representation for comparison
a tool that finds the dominant frequencies in audio, useful for isolating a whistle's pure tone from background noise

papers.title: TOMORI: A Tool-Orchestrated Mixing Operator for REAPER Interaction
papers.summary: Code-based agents can operate creative software, but mixing requests often describe an intended sound without specifying the edits needed to achieve it. We present TOMORI, a code-based mixing-agent harness for native digital audio workstation (DAW) control. Custom plugins provide REAPER project inspection, optional audio measurement, and execution of model-generated Lua code. All observations return as text; delivery includes an editable project and rendered audio. TOMORI-BENCH pairs 110 human-reviewed reference edits with three instruction forms and evaluates native DAW execution end to end through operation structure, parameter precision, and rendered-audio outcomes. Across 990 cases from three primary models, explicit instructions yield high reference agreement, while abstract requests reduce project agreement and audio improvement. Paired ablations show that the full workflow improves explicit execution over a single submission. Prompted audio measurement succeeds in all 28 selected abstract cases but yields no clear overall improvement on the reference-based metrics and increases tool calls. These results expose the gap between executable DAW control and precise realization of perceptual mixing goals.

explain.tldr: A system that lets AI agents control REAPER to execute mixing tasks by writing code, tested on real mixing requests.
explain.plain: Mixing engineers often describe the sound they want without knowing exactly which knobs to turn. This paper presents TOMORI, a tool that lets AI models control REAPER (a popular DAW) by writing code to make mixing changes. The system can inspect projects, measure audio, and run the AI's instructions. They tested it on 110 real mixing tasks in different ways: when given specific instructions (like "boost the bass"), the AI did well; when given vague requests (like "make it sound better"), it struggled more. Adding audio measurement didn't clearly help overall.
explain.why: This matters because it shows both the promise and limits of AI-assisted mixing. If you're curious about AI in music production, this reveals why AI can follow explicit technical steps but still struggles to understand what "better" means—a key challenge for future mixing tools.

terms.meaning: Software for recording, editing, and mixing music, like REAPER, Pro Tools, or Logic
A programming language that REAPER uses to automate tasks and control its mixing tools
How closely the AI's edits matched the human expert's preferred way of solving the same mixing problem

papers.title: ShlokaDhara: A Multi-Speaker Sanskrit Speech Corpus for Learning Meter-Aware Prosody in Text-to-Recitation
papers.summary: Sanskrit verse recitation is governed by $\textit{Chandas}$, a strict prosodic framework defined by rhythmic $\textit{Laghu}$ (light) and $\textit{Guru}$ (heavy) syllables. Because existing Sanskrit speech datasets prioritize ASR or conversational TTS, they lack the metrical fidelity required for authentic verse synthesis. We introduce $\textbf{$\textit{ShlokaDhara}$}$, a 43-hour, multi-speaker Sanskrit speech corpus capturing diverse meters, recitation styles, and melodic variations. We specifically focus on $\textit{Text-to-Recite}$, a synthesis task explicitly requiring both prosodic accuracy and metrical correctness. Benchmarking state-of-the-art TTS architectures via an automated UTMOS (neural MOS) predictor demonstrates that XTTS-v2 achieves the highest perceptual quality. We further validate the XTTS-v2 generated samples using two paradigms: subjective assessments by 16 Sanskrit experts and novel empirical metrics, specifically, syllable-level $\textit{Laghu-Guru}$ duration analysis to objectively quantify structural metrical awareness. Ultimately, this work establishes a robust dataset and evaluation benchmark for prosody-aware computational Sanskrit recitation. Generated Samples: https://shlokadhara.vercel.app/

explain.tldr: A Sanskrit speech dataset and benchmark for synthesizing verse recitation with correct rhythmic meter.
explain.plain: Sanskrit poetry follows strict rules about which syllables should be short or long—like a metrical pattern. Existing speech datasets for Sanskrit don't capture this properly, so computer-generated recitations sound wrong. This paper introduces a 43-hour collection of recorded Sanskrit verse in different styles and meters, then tests whether modern text-to-speech systems can generate recitations that respect these rhythmic rules. They found that one system (XTTS-v2) worked best, and they created new ways to measure whether generated recitations actually follow the correct meter patterns.
explain.why: If you're interested in how music and language interact, this shows how computational tools could eventually help preserve and teach Sanskrit recitation traditions. It also demonstrates methods for evaluating whether AI-generated speech respects cultural and linguistic structure—ideas that could apply to other musical or poetic traditions.

terms.meaning: The Sanskrit system of metrical rules that governs how syllables in verse should be timed—which ones are short (light) or long (heavy).
A speech synthesis task focused specifically on generating verse recitation rather than natural conversation, requiring both correct pronunciation and correct meter.
An automated system that estimates how natural or good-quality a generated speech sample sounds, without needing human listeners each time.

papers.title: MOMO: Human Motion from Moving Sounds
papers.summary: Human responses to sound depend not only on its semantic content, but also on the evolving spatial relationship between source and listener, conveyed through spatial audio and its temporal dynamics. Modeling human reactions to such dynamic spatial audio is important for character animation, human behavior analysis, and robotics. As of yet, existing audio-driven motion generation methods primarily focus on non-spatial or static acoustic conditions, leaving this important problem largely underexplored. To bridge this gap, we formulate the novel task of dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation and introduce two motion-captured datasets. We introduce the Dynamic Spatial Audio and Motion dataset (DySAM) as the first dataset and benchmark for this task, providing synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motions, and moving sound source trajectories. Given the importance of dynamic spatial cues of sound sources, we further provide the Dynamic Spatial Audio Localization dataset (DySAL), an auxiliary binaural localization dataset that pairs diverse acoustic events with head poses and moving source trajectories to support spatial audio perception. For benchmarking, we propose MOMO for human Motion generation from Moving Sounds, a diffusion-based framework guided by three coupled principles: localization, understanding, and generation. MOMO performs localization by estimating head-centric spatial direction cues of the moving source directly from raw binaural audio, avoiding reliance on ground-truth source coordinates. It performs understanding by extracting frame-wise audio-content representations, and performs generation by conditioning motion diffusion on both semantic features and dynamic spatial cues. Experiments show that MOMO outperforms existing baselines in motion fidelity, audio-motion alignment, and physical plausibility.

explain.tldr: Generate realistic human motion from moving sound sources using spatial audio cues and machine learning.
explain.plain: When you hear a sound moving around you—like someone walking past—your body naturally responds by turning your head or shifting your posture. This paper tackles generating realistic human animations that react to moving sound sources, not just static audio. The researchers created two new datasets with synchronized recordings of spatial audio (binaural sound), human motion capture, and tracked sound source positions. Their method, called MOMO, learns to understand where a sound is coming from based on how it reaches both ears, what the sound means, and then generates believable body movements that match the audio's spatial dynamics.
explain.why: This matters for music producers and sound designers working on interactive media, games, or VR experiences where characters need to realistically react to spatial audio. It could also help musicians understand how listeners naturally respond to spatial sound design in immersive performances or installations.

terms.meaning: Sound recorded or mixed to simulate how both your ears hear a source, creating a sense of direction and space
A machine learning approach that generates motion by gradually refining random noise into realistic movement, guided by audio information
Recording the positions and movements of a real person's body to create digital 3D animation data

papers.title: SynerGest: Temporal-Spatial Synergistic Gesture Generation for Dyadic Conversations
papers.summary: Co-speech gesture generation in dyadic conversations for creating immersive virtual avatars remains highly challenging. Existing models often struggle to balance kinematic stability with rhythmic responsiveness and suffer from semantic entanglement, leading to either generic mean-pose regression or unnatural micro-jitters. To address these challenges, we propose SynerGest, a high-fidelity dyadic gesture generation framework grounded in Contrastive Flow Matching (CFM). Specifically, our CFM objective explicitly penalizes mismatched semantic pairs during training, discouraging spatial shortcuts and over-smoothed predictions while improving conditional semantic alignment. Furthermore, to overcome architectural bottlenecks, we introduce the Impulse-Trend Synergistic Attention (ITSA) module. Grounded in the key insight of decoupling "what moves" from "when it moves," ITSA models sharp, speech-driven rhythmic impulses separately from continuous kinematic trends, supporting precise audio-motion synchronization and global structural stability. Extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations on two public datasets demonstrate that SynerGest achieves state-of-the-art performance, delivering contextually responsive and kinematically fluid dyadic interactions.

explain.tldr: A system that generates realistic hand and body gestures for virtual avatars during two-person conversations.
explain.plain: When creating virtual avatars that talk to each other, making their gestures look natural is hard—they either move too smoothly and lose rhythm, or jitter unnaturally. This paper proposes SynerGest, which uses a technique called Contrastive Flow Matching to learn which gestures match which speech, and a special attention module that separately handles the timing of movements (when to move) versus the smooth motion itself (how to move). Tests on real conversation datasets show it produces gestures that feel more natural and stay synchronized with speech.
explain.why: If you're interested in music videos, virtual performances, or interactive music systems with animated characters, this work shows how to make avatars gesture convincingly during dialogue—useful for creating more engaging and realistic musical or conversational experiences.

terms.meaning: A training method that learns by comparing correct and incorrect pairings, helping the model understand which gestures belong with which speech
Smooth, natural-looking motion without jittering or unnatural jerks
Involving two people or entities interacting with each other

papers.title: Known Music, Unknown Response: Leakage-Audited Dynamic Arousal Forecasting With Scheduled Future Music
papers.summary: Dynamic music emotion recognition usually estimates concurrent or lag-aligned labels from audio that has already been observed. We instead forecast the change in consensus arousal when the upcoming music is scheduled but all later affect labels remain hidden. Evaluation holds out complete songs, encodes each eligible 4-s chunk independently, predicts arousal innovation, and compares the correct future with displaced segments from the same song. On PMEmo and a 1,494-song DEAM evaluation pool excluded from engineering development, a complete past/future MuQ representation raises concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) by 0.389--0.507 over recent affect and remains 0.268--0.382 above a calibrated nonlinear state model. A future-only trajectory contains no past or current audio and still exceeds that state model by 0.150--0.249. The earliest legal future chunk, which ends 5.5--11 s before the target, also remains informative. Correct placement exceeds an overlapping 5-s shift by 0.100--0.209 and the acoustic-nearest eligible same-song segment by 0.078--0.105, with positive song-cluster lower bounds. These results show that both scheduled content and its within-song position carry forecast information under the stated observation rules. The study provides a leakage-controlled reference for known-future music forecasting without treating predictive substitutions as causal interventions.

explain.tldr: Predicting how arousal will change when upcoming music plays, using only the scheduled music and its position in the song.
explain.plain: Usually, music emotion systems guess how you feel based on audio you've already heard. This paper does something different: it predicts how your arousal (energy/excitement level) will change when new music is about to play, but you haven't heard it yet. They tested this by hiding future emotional labels and seeing if the system could forecast arousal shifts just from knowing what music comes next and where it sits in the song. They found that knowing the upcoming music and its position in the track gives real predictive power—better than just tracking past emotional patterns.
explain.why: This matters because it suggests music's emotional impact isn't just about what you're hearing now, but also about what you know is coming. For producers and composers, it hints that song structure and sequencing choices have measurable effects on listener emotion, independent of moment-to-moment audio features.

terms.meaning: the energy or intensity dimension of emotion—how excited or calm you feel
a statistical measure of how well predictions match actual values, ranging from -1 to 1
when a machine learning model accidentally uses information it shouldn't have access to, making results look better than they really are

papers.title: MUB: An Identity-Masked Benchmark for Music Understanding in Multimodal Language Models
papers.summary: Evaluating musical perception in multimodal language models requires separating audio evidence from answers recoverable through metadata or external tools. We present the Music Understanding Benchmark (MUB), a locally assembled collection of 500 identity-masked recordings with existing annotations for tempo, key, time signature, and structural intervals. The collection covers all 24 major/minor key combinations, tempos of 47--180 beats per minute, and 4,676 annotated intervals. Original titles, artists, and platform identifiers are excluded from evaluation inputs. Relative to recent music question-answering and temporal-grounding work, MUB emphasizes scalar tempo prediction and full-recording interval outputs, together with a documented metadata-masking protocol. Saved baseline predictions yield 53.6\% tempo accuracy for a simple DSP estimator and 98.4\% time-signature accuracy for a constant 4/4 predictor. We identify important limitations, including an asymmetric legacy key metric, unverified independent annotation agreement, extreme metre imbalance, and unresolved recording-level rights clearance. No contemporary multimodal language model comparison has yet been completed. MUB is therefore an evaluation resource and protocol under validation, rather than a completed demonstration of model capabilities.

explain.tldr: A test dataset for evaluating whether AI music models can understand tempo, key, and structure from audio alone.
explain.plain: When testing whether AI models understand music, it's hard to know if they're actually listening to the audio or just looking up song titles online. This paper introduces MUB, a collection of 500 recordings where artist names and titles are hidden, along with human-verified information about tempo, musical key, time signature, and where sections start and end. They tested some basic music-analysis tools as a starting point—one could guess the time signature correctly 98% of the time by just assuming 4/4 for everything. The authors acknowledge the dataset still has issues to work out before it's ready for serious model testing.
explain.why: As AI tools become more common in music production and analysis, musicians need reliable ways to check if these models actually understand music or are just pattern-matching metadata. This benchmark helps ensure AI music tools are genuinely listening to what you create.

terms.meaning: AI systems trained on multiple types of information (like text and audio) that can answer questions about them
hiding identifying information like song titles and artist names so evaluation depends only on the audio itself
a simple computer algorithm that analyzes audio signals directly, without using machine learning

papers.title: Rethinking Magnitude Compression in Spectral Losses for DDSP Parameter Estimation
papers.summary: Spectral losses for differentiable digital signal processing (DDSP) commonly compress magnitudes, for example by using log-magnitude terms. Such compression mimics human perception, but whether it helps the optimization is less clear, and is usually found only by comparing trained models. In this work, we show that whether compression helps depends on the system's informative region: the region of its dynamic range that carries the information pointing toward the target. To indicate where this region lies without having to train, we introduce concordance, which measures how well a loss orders candidate parameter settings by their distance from the target. We then compare uncompressed, compressed, and combined losses by fitting a modal plate reverb and a subtractive synthesizer model to target sounds. A third system, selected for its low-energy informative region, tests the relationship in the opposite direction. In every system, the loss that matches the informative region performs best: the uncompressed one where the region lies at high energies, and the compressed one where it lies low. Surprisingly, the common combination of both log-magnitude and linear-magnitude terms performs best in none of the systems. Code and audio examples are available at https://github.com/superstem000/compression-analysis

explain.tldr: Magnitude compression in spectral losses helps DDSP parameter estimation only when the important signal information is in low-energy regions.
explain.plain: When training neural networks to estimate synthesizer or effects parameters from audio, researchers typically compress the audio spectrum using logarithms to match human hearing. This paper questions whether that's always best. They introduce a measurement called 'concordance' to predict where the important information lives in a sound's dynamic range without training. Testing on three different systems, they found that compressed losses work best when important details are quiet, while uncompressed losses work better when important details are loud. Surprisingly, using both compressed and uncompressed losses together—a common practice—didn't outperform either alone.
explain.why: If you're building tools that automatically estimate synthesizer settings or effects parameters from audio, this research suggests you should think carefully about whether to compress your loss function based on your specific sound. It could lead to faster, more accurate parameter estimation for music production tools.

terms.meaning: Differentiable Digital Signal Processing—a framework that lets neural networks learn to control audio synthesis and effects by treating them as trainable components.
A measurement of how different two sounds are by comparing their frequency content, used to guide training.
A metric that measures whether a loss function correctly ranks different parameter choices by how close they get to a target sound.

papers.title: D-Composer: Language Modeling for Simultaneous Drum Transcription and Sound Event Decomposition
papers.summary: Drum beats are often conceptualized and produced as arrangements of repeated single-drum sound events or one-shots. Drum Analysis-by-Synthesis (AbS) models combine this structural assumption with reconstruction-based training to perform MIR tasks such as drum transcription, drum source separation, and one-shot extraction, offering a flexible alternative to more traditional task-specific supervision. However, leading AbS approaches struggle to generalize to a broad range of drum timbres (e.g., electronic drum kits), rely on high-quality paired audio-transcription training data, and do not model intra-class timbral variation within a single arrangement (e.g., multiple kick sounds). To overcome these limitations, we propose D-Composer, an autoregressive language modeling framework that decomposes drum recordings into labeled sound events and their onset times. In drum transcription and one-shot extraction tasks, D-Composer performs comparably to or better than a state-of-the-art AbS system and task-specific baselines while generalizing to a broader range of drum timbres. Our results demonstrate that when equipped with abundant synthetic data and compact acoustic token representations, language modeling provides a simple recipe for unifying transcription and sound event decomposition.

explain.tldr: A language model that transcribes drums and separates individual drum sounds from recordings.
explain.plain: Drum beats are made from individual drum hits (kick, snare, etc.). This paper presents D-Composer, which listens to a drum recording and figures out what drum sounds happened and when they occurred. Unlike previous systems that struggle with different drum kit styles or need lots of paired training examples, D-Composer works better across electronic and acoustic drums, learns from synthetic data, and can handle when the same drum (like a kick) sounds different throughout a song.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this could improve tools for drum editing, remixing, and extracting individual drum sounds from recordings—useful for sample-based production or fixing timing issues in drum tracks.

terms.meaning: converting audio into a written representation—here, identifying which drums played and when
a machine learning approach that predicts the next item in a sequence one step at a time, like how autocomplete works
compact digital summaries of sound characteristics that the model uses instead of raw audio

papers.title: Hear, Localize, and Reason: Spatially Aware Scene Understanding for Audio-Visual LLMs
papers.summary: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) have made strong progress in multimodal understanding, yet most treat audio as monaural semantic content, limiting their ability to reason about where sounds originate and how they relate to the visual scene. Recent spatial audio-visual studies address parts of this problem, but often focus on specific abilities, such as spatial correspondence or direction and distance reasoning. In this work, we introduce HLR-AVSceneQA, a comprehensive benchmark with a hear-localize-reason hierarchy that evaluates whether models can recognize what is heard, localize sound sources in egocentric and allocentric views, and use these localized sources to reason about how they relate to the visual scene. We further introduce HLR-LLM, which augments a strong audio-visual foundation model with a binaural spatial audio branch alongside its monaural semantic audio pathway. We train HLR-LLM with a curriculum that incorporates final-stage chain-of-thought supervision for multi-step spatial reasoning. Experiments show that existing AV-LLMs remain limited in spatial grounding and relational reasoning, while HLR-LLM substantially improves spatial audio-visual scene understanding without compromising semantic audio-visual perception.

explain.tldr: A new AI model and benchmark that helps systems understand where sounds come from in videos and reason about spatial relationships.
explain.plain: Current AI systems that process both audio and video treat sound as just semantic content—they know what's being said or what sound it is, but not where it's coming from. This paper introduces a benchmark test (HLR-AVSceneQA) that checks whether models can do three things: recognize sounds, locate where they originate in a scene, and explain how those sounds relate to what's visible. They also built HLR-LLM, an improved model that processes spatial audio information (like stereo cues that tell you direction) alongside regular audio, trained with step-by-step reasoning guidance. Their results show existing systems struggle with spatial understanding, while their approach significantly improves it.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this matters because it could enable better tools for spatial audio production, immersive music experiences, and AI systems that truly understand the relationship between sound placement and visual content—useful for scoring, sound design, and interactive media.

terms.meaning: Audio recorded or processed using two channels (like stereo) in a way that preserves directional cues—the differences in timing and volume between left and right that tell your brain where a sound is coming from
Egocentric is from a first-person perspective (what you see from your position); allocentric is from an external viewpoint (like a camera looking at the whole scene)
Training an AI by showing it not just the final answer, but the step-by-step reasoning process needed to get there

papers.title: DuET: Note-Frame Dual Encoding for Piano Performance-to-Score Transcription
papers.summary: Transcribing expressive piano performances into scores requires interpreting individual note timings within an underlying metrical structure. However, score attributes are associated with notes, whereas beats may occur without coincident note onsets. We introduce DuET, a Dual-Encoder Transformer that jointly learns note-level performance MIDI-to-score (PM2S) transcription and frame-level beat and downbeat tracking. Bidirectional cross-attention connects note and frame encoders, while an autoregressive decoder alternates between their representations to predict structured score attributes. We further introduce TimeRoPE and Time-Pitch Rotary Positional Encoding (TPRoPE) to establish a shared performance-time reference and explicitly encode relative temporal and pitch relationships. Evaluations on ASAP, a classical piano dataset, and our curated Gangqinpu dataset, which spans multiple genres with a focus on popular piano music, demonstrate improvements in score timing and notated duration. Compared with the strongest baseline on each dataset, DuET reduces MUSTER mean error from 6.56% to 3.64% on Gangqinpu and from 11.30% to 11.22% on ASAP. Ablations support the benefits of frame-level context, time-based positional encoding, and decoder-history masking. Code, weights, and demos are available at https://github.com/wei-zeng98/DuET.

explain.tldr: A system that converts expressive piano recordings into written sheet music by tracking both individual notes and the underlying beat structure.
explain.plain: When a pianist plays, they don't always hit notes exactly on the beat—they add expression through timing variations. Converting this into sheet music requires understanding both *when* each note happens and *where* it fits in the musical meter. DuET uses two connected neural networks: one that focuses on individual notes and another that tracks the beat grid. They communicate with each other to produce accurate sheet music with correct note timings and durations. Tests on classical and popular piano music show it's more accurate than previous methods.
explain.why: This matters because automatic transcription of piano performances could help musicians quickly convert recordings into readable scores, speeding up the process of documenting or sharing performances. It's particularly useful for popular music and expressive playing styles where timing varies from the strict beat.

terms.meaning: Converting a digital recording of a performance (MIDI data) into written musical notation
A system that generates output one piece at a time, where each new piece depends on all the previous pieces it generated
A technique for telling a neural network about the order and spacing of events in time or pitch

papers.title: From Individual Songs to Music Corpora: Evaluating Explainable Harmonic Decision-Making on HookTheory
papers.summary: Automatic melody harmonization is often evaluated through individual compositions or data-driven corpus models. This study examines whether an explainable harmonic decision model developed for individual songs can be applied to independently collected human annotations without changing its rules. We evaluate a frozen Explainable Melody Harmonizer (EMH) on selected HookTheory excerpts containing aligned melody and chord annotations. EMH generates chord sequences from melody alone using explicit criteria for melodic compatibility, harmonic function, persistence, cadence, meter-aware segmentation, and Viterbi-like optimization. Human chords are withheld during generation and used only for post-hoc comparison. Nineteen excerpts yielded 439 evaluable harmonic segments. Exact chord agreement reached 20.50%, chord-root agreement 31.66%, and harmonic-function agreement 47.62%, with functions assessed relative to the key inferred by EMH. Decision-level analysis identified 203 segments (46.24%) where the human chord lay outside the model's candidate vocabulary and 146 (33.26%) where it was available but not selected. These findings distinguish representational limitations from differences in chord selection without treating the human reference as the only musically valid solution. The study demonstrates a reproducible, interpretable approach to corpus-based evaluation of harmonic decision-making.

explain.tldr: Tests whether a rule-based harmony system trained on individual songs works on real-world chord annotations without modification.
explain.plain: When musicians write melodies, they need to add chords underneath them. This paper tests a system called EMH that automatically suggests chords based on the melody, using explicit musical rules rather than machine learning. The researchers froze this system (didn't retrain it) and tested it on 439 chord segments from HookTheory, a real database of songs with melody and chord annotations. They found the system matched human chord choices exactly 20% of the time, but agreed on the harmonic function (the role the chord plays) 48% of the time. By analyzing where disagreements happened, they could tell whether the system simply didn't know certain chords or chose differently despite knowing them.
explain.why: This matters because it shows a transparent way to evaluate harmony suggestions—you can see *why* the system made each choice rather than just getting a yes/no answer. For producers and composers, this kind of interpretable system could help understand automatic harmonization tools and trust their suggestions more.

terms.meaning: the role a chord plays in the key—like tonic (home), dominant (tension), or subdominant—independent of which specific chord it is
an algorithm that finds the best sequence of choices by considering how each choice affects the next one
a large collection of real music data, like a database of songs with annotations

papers.title: MIDI-REPA: Improving Text-to-Music Generation with Symbolic Representation Alignment
papers.summary: State-of-the-art text-to-music models increasingly rely on scaling model capacity, data, and compute, while still learning musical structure directly from dense audio. Yet melody, rhythm, harmony, and structure can be represented compactly in symbolic form. We introduce MIDI-REPA, a representation-alignment framework that derives MIDI supervision from automatic music transcription (AMT) to align intermediate representations of a flow-matching DiT. Building on the 122M-parameter FluxAudio-S baseline from the 2026 ICME Academic Text-To-Music Challenge, we investigate what, where, and when to align. Aligning a MuScriptor-derived piano roll with an early DiT layer throughout the full flow trajectory performs the best. Without additional training data or techniques, MIDI-REPA remains competitive on the ATTM objective metrics while remaining trainable on a single RTX 3090 in about 31 hours. Our results highlight symbolic supervision as a simple and inexpensive learning signal for improving text-to-music generation. We release our transcription pipeline, JamendoMIDI, training code, and audio samples at https://midi-repa.vaclis.net.

explain.tldr: A method that uses MIDI transcription to help text-to-music models learn musical structure more efficiently.
explain.plain: Text-to-music AI models usually learn directly from raw audio, which requires lots of computing power. This paper proposes using MIDI—the symbolic music format—as an additional learning signal. They automatically transcribe music to MIDI and use it to guide what the model learns at intermediate stages. Testing on a baseline model, they found that aligning MIDI information early in the generation process works best, and the approach trains quickly on consumer hardware without needing extra data.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this could mean better text-to-music tools that understand melody, rhythm, and harmony more explicitly. Since MIDI is a format you already work with, this approach bridges symbolic music knowledge with AI generation in a way that might produce more musically coherent results.

terms.meaning: A type of AI model architecture that generates music by gradually refining random noise into coherent audio, guided by text descriptions
Software that listens to audio and converts it into MIDI or sheet music notation
Guiding an AI model's internal learned patterns to match a specific structure, like MIDI, during training

papers.title: SNOAR: Self-training with Noise filtering, Observation adding, and Remixing for Speech Denoising Without Clean References
papers.summary: Unsupervised speech denoising methods such as MixIT and noisy-target training can be trained directly on noisy recordings, avoiding the sim-to-real gap of synthetic training data, but remain well below supervised performance. Teacher--student self-training, as in RemixIT, narrows this gap by remixing a teacher's estimates into new mixtures that supervise a student; however, since the student is trained only toward the teacher's estimates, teacher errors, in particular over-suppressed speech, are never recovered and propagate as the teacher is updated from the student. We propose SNOAR, a self-training framework that corrects the teacher's estimates before use: the noise leaked into its speech estimate is removed by differential noise filtering (DNF), and part of the noisy observation is added back in to restore suppressed speech and attenuate artifacts. We show that the two corrections depend on each other, as without DNF the loop collapses to the identity mapping. Compared to RemixIT, SNOAR is more stable along training and outperforms it in signal-based, perceptual, and word error rate metrics, reaching 97\% of the SI-SDR improvement of a fully-supervised topline on WHAM!; on real CHiME-3 recordings, it improves every metric of three different teachers, while RemixIT degrades their perceptual quality.

explain.tldr: A method to denoise speech from noisy recordings without clean reference audio by correcting teacher model errors during training.
explain.plain: Denoising speech from recordings is hard without clean reference versions to learn from. This paper improves on RemixIT, a self-training method where a teacher model learns to separate speech from noise, then teaches a student by creating new training examples. The problem: the teacher makes mistakes (especially over-removing speech), and these errors get locked in and repeated. SNOAR fixes this by cleaning up the teacher's estimates before reusing them—removing noise that leaked into the speech estimate and adding back some of the original noisy recording to restore what was lost. They show this works better than RemixIT on standard tests and real recordings.
explain.why: Musicians and producers often record in noisy environments without perfect takes. Better unsupervised denoising means cleaner audio without needing expensive studio recordings or synthetic training data, making professional-quality cleanup more accessible.

terms.meaning: A technique where a model learns by training on its own predictions, improving iteratively without human labels
A metric that measures how well separated speech sounds compared to the original, commonly used in audio quality tests
The problem that models trained on synthetic or simulated data often perform worse on real-world recordings

papers.title: EEG-Based Prediction of Music Enjoyment Using Deep Learning with Explainable Temporal Analysis
papers.summary: Understanding why listeners enjoy music is difficult because the experience is subjective and changes as a piece unfolds. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive way to study neural responses during listening, yet earlier work has mostly treated music emotion as a categorical label or relied on black-box models. We formulate enjoyment prediction as a regression problem on the public MUSIN-G dataset, which contains 128-channel EEG from 20 listeners together with song-level enjoyment ratings. Six deep learning models were compared under a participant-wise protocol, in which 15 listeners were used for training and validation and 5 were held out for testing. DeepConvNet, CNN-LSTM and GNN-CNN reached the lowest mean absolute error (0.97 to 0.99 on the 1 to 5 scale), while the temporal convolutional network (TCN) had the highest Pearson correlation with the ratings (r = 0.21). Gradient-based and occlusion-based explanations, averaged over all held-out windows, identify the time segments within each two-second window that most influence the TCN predictions. The study provides a reproducible cross-listener benchmark for EEG-based enjoyment regression and shows how explainability analysis complements standard metrics.

explain.tldr: Deep learning models predict music enjoyment from brain signals, with explanations showing which moments matter most.
explain.plain: Researchers wanted to predict how much listeners enjoy music by analyzing their brain activity (EEG recordings) while they listen. They tested six different deep learning models on a dataset of 20 people rating songs. The best models achieved modest accuracy, and they used explanation techniques to identify which specific moments in the music most influenced the predictions. This approach treats enjoyment as a continuous scale rather than simple categories like 'happy' or 'sad.'
explain.why: This could help music producers and streaming platforms understand what makes listeners engaged, and the explainability aspect reveals which musical moments drive that engagement—potentially useful for composition and mixing decisions.

terms.meaning: A non-invasive method that measures electrical activity in the brain using sensors on the scalp
A machine learning approach that predicts continuous numerical values (like a 1-5 enjoyment score) rather than categories
Techniques that identify which parts of the input data (here, which moments in time) most influenced the model's predictions

papers.title: vst-bench-ml: Auditable Dataset Generation for Audio Plugins
papers.summary: Generating datasets with audio plugins requires preserving how each audio observation was produced. vst-bench-ml is a Python package that samples plugin parameters, coordinates rendering through a separately installed host, and records software identities, rendering settings, and output hashes for later verification. A sealed manifest binds this evidence and supports offline integrity checks without loading the plugin. A companion repository provides a sample-free VST3 test plugin, a deterministic offline host, and additional checks linking rendering attempts to recorded outputs. On a pinned macOS arm64 and Python 3.12 stack, functional validation of the pre-release versions reproduced package and host tests. Two runs in fresh processes reproduced the same render-plan hash and all eight expected output hashes, covering four sampled parameter configurations and two fixed MIDI signals; 12 negative cases also passed. Later licensed 0.1.0 release candidates passed producer-run continuous integration and local validation. Version 0.1.1 adds public Git source repositories, package-index installation, and user documentation; a separate release check reproduced the expected plan and output hashes. These checks establish integrity and repeatability within the tested setup; they do not establish portability, scientific suitability, or perceptual quality.

explain.tldr: A tool that generates reproducible datasets from audio plugins while verifying what produced each sound.
explain.plain: When you want to train machine learning models on audio, you need to know exactly how each sound was created—which plugin, which settings, which input. vst-bench-ml automates this by controlling plugin parameters, recording what happened, and creating a tamper-proof record (a manifest) of each rendering. The researchers tested it thoroughly and showed it can reliably reproduce the same outputs when run again, which matters because you need that consistency for trustworthy datasets.
explain.why: If you're building AI tools for music production, you need datasets where you can verify exactly how each audio example was made. This tool helps you create those datasets in a way that's auditable and reproducible—so other researchers can check your work and trust your results.

terms.meaning: A standard format for audio plugins that work inside music software; VST stands for Virtual Studio Technology.
A sealed record or log that documents what happened during rendering—which plugin, settings, and outputs—so you can verify it later.
A unique fingerprint of all the instructions and settings for generating audio; if the hash matches on a second run, the setup was identical.

papers.title: HRTF Upsampling and Personalization via Neural Operators
papers.summary: Head-related transfer function (HRTF) spatial upsampling from sparse measurements is a fundamental challenge in personalized binaural audio. We formulate HRTF upsampling as an operator learning problem and introduce SPARO, a neural operator that maps sparse measurements at a set of spatial directions to the HRTF field, a continuous representation that can be queried at arbitrary positions. SPARO projects the measurements onto a learned set of spherical latent modes, processes the latent modes with Transformer blocks, and decodes the resulting representations at query directions. On SONICOM, using the LAP24 measurement configuration, SPARO attains the best log-spectral distortion (LSD) and interaural level difference (ILD) error at every sparsity level from 3 to 100 measurements (18% lower LSD and 43% lower ILD error than the strongest baseline at 100 measurements) while remaining competitive in interaural time difference (ITD) error. It reconstructs a dense HRTF 15 to 373 times faster than the leading neural-field method RANF. We further validate the approach on HUTUBS, demonstrating its effectiveness across HRTF datasets.

explain.tldr: A neural network learns to fill in missing spatial audio measurements to create complete personalized 3D sound fields.
explain.plain: When recording how sound reaches your ears from different directions, you can't measure every angle—it's too time-consuming. This paper treats that problem as learning a continuous map from sparse measurements to a full 3D sound field. They built a neural network called SPARO that takes a few directional measurements, processes them through learned patterns, and can then predict what the sound would be like from any direction. Their method reconstructs complete spatial audio much faster than previous approaches and with lower error.
explain.why: This matters for spatial audio and VR: personalized binaural audio (custom 3D sound tailored to your ears) usually requires measuring many directions. Faster, more accurate reconstruction from fewer measurements means easier, cheaper personalization for headphone listening and immersive experiences.

terms.meaning: A measurement of how sound changes as it travels from a direction in space to your ears, accounting for your head and ear shape
Training a neural network to learn a function that maps one type of data (like sparse measurements) to another (like a complete field)
The difference in loudness between your two ears, which your brain uses to sense where a sound is coming from left or right

papers.title: MUSEBENCH: A Benchmark for AI-Generated Music Detection and Artifact Analysis
papers.summary: Advances in generative AI have made it possible to produce music that is nearly indistinguishable from human compositions, raising the question of whether such works can be reliably distinguished from human compositions. We present MUSEBENCH, a large-scale benchmark for AI-generated music detection and artifact analysis, comprising over 361K tracks. The dataset includes human compositions, stylistically matched music generated by ten state-of-the-art open-source and commercial models, such as Suno and Udio, as well as human-AI co-creations and variants processed with adversarial perturbations, compression, and acoustic post-processing. Using MUSEBENCH, we benchmark 11 automated detectors and evaluate their accuracy, generalization, and robustness, under default, out-of-domain, and transformed-variant experiment settings. We further conduct a comprehensive artifact analysis through acoustic feature inspection, identifying recurring signatures such as non-idiomatic harmonic progressions, upsampling induced spectral periodicities, and violations of physical performance constraints. Our findings reveal key strengths and vulnerabilities of existing detectors and provide practical insights for building more reliable AI music detection systems.

explain.tldr: A large dataset and testing framework to evaluate how well AI-generated music can be detected and what artifacts reveal its origins.
explain.plain: AI music generators are getting so good that it's hard to tell if a song was made by a human or a machine. This paper created MUSEBENCH, a collection of over 361,000 tracks—including human music, AI-generated music from popular tools like Suno and Udio, and hybrid human-AI creations. They tested 11 different detection systems to see how accurately they could identify AI music, including when the music was modified or came from unfamiliar sources. They also analyzed what acoustic fingerprints AI music leaves behind, like unusual chord progressions and digital artifacts from the generation process.
explain.why: As AI music tools become mainstream, musicians and platforms need reliable ways to identify AI-generated content for transparency, rights, and artistic integrity. Understanding what makes AI music detectable—and what tricks can fool detectors—helps both creators and listeners navigate this new landscape.

terms.meaning: small, intentional changes made to audio to test whether detection systems remain reliable or can be fooled
testing on music styles or generators the detector hasn't encountered before, to see if it generalizes beyond its training
repeating patterns in the frequency content of audio, often a sign of digital processing rather than natural sound

papers.title: Evaluating perceptual transparency of lossy music audio compression with Opus codec
papers.summary: Although the open-source Opus audio codec is widely used for digital audio streaming, its perceptual transparency threshold for high-bitrate music compression remains insufficiently evaluated. To establish this threshold, this study evaluates Opus across a two-phase ITU-R BS.1116-3 double-blind framework, analyzing Difference Grades using a Linear Mixed-Effects Model (LMM) and Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) for statistical equivalence. In a first phase with 21 qualified listeners and 23 music excerpts, 128 kbps achieves statistical in-distinguishability ($p = 0.456$) but narrowly fails strict equivalence to the uncompressed reference ($p = 0.064$). In Phase 2, Best Linear Unbiased Predictors (BLUPs) isolate the 10 most critical listeners and 8 most challenging samples for a stress-test. Under these worst-case conditions, 128 kbps is conclusively detected as degraded ($p = 0.030$), whereas 160 kbps successfully reaches perceptual transparency ($p = 0.747$) and strict statistical equivalence ($p = 0.024$). The study concludes that 160 kbps demonstrates perceptual transparency to uncompressed CD quality in critical listening environments. For reproducibility, we publicly release results for both phases, anonymized subject background info and sample characteristics.

explain.tldr: Tests whether Opus codec compression at different bitrates sounds identical to uncompressed music to trained listeners.
explain.plain: Opus is a popular codec for streaming music, but nobody had rigorously tested how much you can compress it before people hear quality loss. The researchers had trained listeners compare compressed versions at different bitrates to uncompressed originals using a standardized testing method. They found that 128 kbps showed some detectable degradation under strict conditions, but 160 kbps sounded transparent—meaning listeners couldn't reliably tell it apart from the original.
explain.why: If you're streaming or distributing music, knowing the exact bitrate where compression becomes audible helps you balance file size against quality. This gives producers and platforms concrete data for choosing compression settings.

terms.meaning: how much data per second is used to store or transmit audio; lower bitrate means smaller files but potentially lower quality
when compressed audio sounds identical to the original to human listeners, even under careful listening conditions
an international standard method for testing whether audio quality differences are noticeable to trained listeners

papers.title: CochlearMark: Audio Watermarking via Phase Locked Auditory Nerve Representations
papers.summary: Modern audio watermarks achieve strong robustness with learned encoder-decoder models, but their behavior under new processing is established empirically. CochlearMark is introduced as a training-free audio watermark that uses auditory-nerve phase-locking as its feature representation. A small waveform perturbation is optimized against a keyed random projection of this representation, and the same projection is used for detection, with no trained encoder or decoder. Because phase-locking represents temporal fine structure, the resulting robustness has a direct physiological interpretation: the mark is retained when this structure is preserved and lost when it is disrupted or rebuilt. Across speech, music, and environmental audio, CochlearMark achieves signal-edit robustness and imperceptibility comparable to trained neural baselines while requiring only a lightweight computational footprint. Among the evaluated training-free methods, CochlearMark is the only one to retain substantial detectability under neural-codec re-encoding.

explain.tldr: A watermarking method that hides data in audio using how the ear processes timing, without needing machine learning training.
explain.plain: Audio watermarking embeds hidden information in sound files—useful for copyright protection or authentication. Most modern methods use trained neural networks, which work well but are computationally heavy and unpredictable with new audio processing. CochlearMark instead uses phase-locking, a biological property of how the inner ear encodes sound timing. The method adds a tiny, imperceptible change to the audio that can be detected later using the same timing-based representation. It works across speech, music, and other sounds, stays hidden through various audio edits, and survives even when audio is re-encoded by neural codecs—something other training-free methods struggle with.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this matters because watermarks protect your work from unauthorized use or copying. CochlearMark is lightweight enough to run on modest hardware, making it practical for real-world deployment, while its biological basis means the robustness is predictable and interpretable rather than a black box.

terms.meaning: the inner ear's ability to lock onto the precise timing of sound vibrations, encoding when peaks and valleys occur
a machine-learning-based compression method that encodes audio into a compact form and can reconstruct it later
how well the watermark survives audio processing like compression, filtering, or re-encoding

papers.title: Designing Textual Interfaces To Enhance Llm Reasoning On Audio-Visual Question Answering
papers.summary: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has shown strong effectiveness for text-based LLMs and LLM systems, but its application to audio-visual understanding systems requires suitable textual interfaces through which multimodal reasoning can be exposed to text-based optimizers. We investigate how the design of textual interfaces affects prompt optimization for multimodal reasoning, on the audio-visual question answering task. We compare three interface designs, including a direct inference system consisting of a single omni-modal large language model (OmniLLM), a captioner-reasoner system, and an agentic architecture in which a primary agent orchestrates subagent OmniLLMs. Experiments with Qwen3-Omni and Gemini show that direct prompt optimization provides model-dependent gains; the captioner-reasoner system and the agentic system expose more interpretable optimization interfaces but are harder to optimize, where error analysis of cases affected by optimization is conducted. Our study highlights textual interface design as an important factor in making prompt optimization effective for omni-modal reasoning systems. Our implementation details are specified in GitHub repo.

explain.tldr: Study shows how different text-based interfaces affect prompt optimization for AI systems that reason about audio and video together.
explain.plain: When AI systems need to answer questions about audio and video content, researchers can improve their performance by automatically optimizing the text instructions (prompts) given to them. However, the way you structure the text interface—how you organize the information flowing between different AI components—significantly affects whether this optimization works well. The researchers tested three different interface designs and found that while direct optimization sometimes helps, more complex setups with multiple specialized components are harder to optimize but offer clearer insights into what's happening.
explain.why: This matters for musicians and producers working with AI tools for audio-visual content. Understanding how to structure AI systems for better audio-visual reasoning could lead to more reliable and controllable tools for music video creation, soundtrack generation, or interactive audio-visual installations.

terms.meaning: automatically improving the text instructions you give to an AI to get better results
AI's ability to understand and think about information from multiple sources at once, like audio and video together
a system design where one AI agent coordinates and delegates tasks to other specialized AI agents

papers.title: Soloist: A Generative Model for Blind Voice Separation in the Wild
papers.summary: Real-world voice separation must recover individual voices from overlapping speech, environmental noise, and music, yet isolated source recordings are rarely available for supervision. We introduce Soloist, a generative model for blind voice separation that autoregressively generates individual voice streams as audio-codec sequences conditioned on the mixture, without requiring a target-speaker query or a predefined voice count. We propose a two-stage training paradigm to learn from synthetic mixtures and adapt to real recordings. The first stage combines supervised separation on synthetic mixtures with isolated source targets and an auxiliary task that predicts speaker timelines from real recordings, learning who speaks when from natural acoustics. The second stage applies reinforcement learning to real recordings, with rewards supplied by a model judge that compares candidate separations based on voice purity and content preservation without isolated source targets. Across diverse scenarios, Soloist recovers clean speech from multi-speaker overlap and noisy recordings, and extracts singing vocals from music accompaniment while maintaining relatively high pitch accuracy and intelligibility. On real-world recordings with unknown voice counts, Soloist also separates voices well. Finally, we integrate Soloist into a full-duplex conversation processing pipeline that assembles separated outputs into continuous speaker tracks, demonstrating its practical utility in real conversations.

explain.tldr: A generative model that separates overlapping voices from messy real-world recordings without needing isolated training examples.
explain.plain: Voice separation—pulling individual speakers out of a crowded recording—is hard because real-world audio has noise, music, and unknown numbers of speakers, and you rarely have clean isolated recordings to learn from. Soloist tackles this by generating separated voices one piece at a time, learning first from synthetic mixtures paired with clean sources, then improving itself on real recordings using a scoring system that judges separation quality without needing those clean sources. The model can handle varying numbers of speakers and maintains intelligibility and pitch accuracy, even extracting singing from instrumental music.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this matters because it enables better vocal extraction and multi-speaker editing from messy recordings—useful for remixing, podcasting, live recording cleanup, and music production where isolated tracks aren't available.

terms.meaning: separating individual voices from a mixed recording without knowing in advance how many speakers there are or having clean isolated examples to learn from
an AI system that creates new audio by predicting what comes next, piece by piece, rather than just analyzing what's already there
training a system by giving it rewards or penalties based on how good its outputs are, rather than showing it correct answers directly

papers.title: Point-and-Play: Instrument Timbre Cloning from Music Mixtures
papers.summary: Neural instrument synthesizers can clone the timbre of a solo instrument, letting music producers make music with the sound they desire. However, an instrument of interest is often embedded in a fully produced, multi-instrument recording, beyond the reach of existing methods. Source separation before timbre cloning is an approach, but it may suffer from separation artifacts and is also likely a detour for the task. In this work, we propose Point-and-Play, a system that clones the timbre of a cued source directly from a polyphonic mixture and uses it to synthesize new pitches and velocities. To achieve this, we introduce a Cue-Gated Statistics Pooling (CGSP) module that extracts the timbre code of the cued instrument from adapted CLAP embeddings of the music mixture. This extracted timbre code is then used to condition a separately trained note synthesizer together with pitch and velocity inputs. Experiments show that our proposed system outperforms separate-then-clone baselines in terms of timbre fidelity and synthesis quality, achieving comparable performance with that cloned from a clean solo instrument.

explain.tldr: A system that extracts and clones an instrument's sound directly from a full music mix without isolating it first.
explain.plain: When you want to recreate an instrument's unique sound (its timbre), current methods require isolating that instrument from a full recording first—which can introduce unwanted artifacts. This paper presents Point-and-Play, which skips that step by pointing to the instrument you want in a full mix and directly extracting its timbre characteristics. The system then uses that extracted sound to synthesize the same instrument playing different notes and dynamics. Their experiments show this direct approach produces better-sounding results than the traditional separate-then-clone workflow.
explain.why: For producers and musicians, this means you could grab the exact sound of a specific instrument from any recording—even buried in a complex mix—and use it in your own productions without the quality loss that comes from trying to isolate it first.

terms.meaning: The unique color or character of a sound that lets you tell a violin from a trumpet, even playing the same note
A recording with multiple instruments playing at the same time
A machine learning representation that captures what a sound is, learned from pairing audio with text descriptions

papers.title: PhysicsSliders: Learning Physical Controls for Audio Foley Generation
papers.summary: Physical properties provide intuitive controls for sounds made by interacting objects. The challenge is to make a generative model respond predictably to these controls, both individually and in combination. We present \method\ (PXS), trained on simulated contact sounds with 15 material, geometry and contact parameters. Two separately trained variants accept direct parameter inputs or numerical captions. PXS controls hardness, size, speed and damping, supports room descriptions and produces spectrally distinct outputs at fixed targets. When controlling damping and size together, specifying thickness improves frequency accuracy and joint target delivery. Measurements from real recordings define effective-damping targets, which simulator inversion maps to generation inputs without real-audio fine-tuning. Across 18 impact classes from five real-audio datasets, PXS-Physical follows these targets with mean grouped Spearman correlation $ρ=0.976$ and class-median error 0.094 dex (a factor of 1.24).

explain.tldr: A generative model that creates realistic impact sounds by letting you control physical properties like material hardness, object size, and how much the sound decays.
explain.plain: Making sound effects for things like footsteps or objects hitting surfaces is tedious. This work trains a model on simulated impact sounds with different materials, shapes, and contact conditions. You can then control the output by adjusting physical parameters—like how hard or soft something is, how big it is, or how quickly the sound fades—and the model generates appropriate audio. The model stays accurate even when you adjust multiple controls together, and it can match target sounds from real recordings without needing to retrain on actual audio.
explain.why: For sound designers and producers, this means faster, more intuitive foley creation: instead of recording or hunting through libraries, you dial in the physical properties you want and get usable sounds. It bridges the gap between how we think about sound physically and how we generate it digitally.

terms.meaning: sound effects created to match on-screen action, like footsteps or objects colliding
an AI system trained to create new content (in this case, audio) based on learned patterns
how quickly vibrations or sound energy fade away over time

papers.title: FLOMSS: Generative Music Source Separation by Flow Matching
papers.summary: Music source separation (MSS) has been conventionally addressed by discriminative methods. Recently, flow matching has emerged as a strong generative paradigm for modeling complex data distributions, with successful applications across diverse domains. These advances motivate us to systematically investigate flow matching for MSS in a four-source (Vocals, Bass, Drums, Other) setting in full-band stereo. Specifically, we investigate prediction targets, flow paths, single-source versus multi-source modeling, and mixture consistency constraints. Beyond the signal-level metrics commonly used for MSS, such as signal-to-distortion ratio, we further evaluate MSS methods using embedding-based metrics, as well as a listening test, providing a comprehensive benchmark. On MUSDB18-HQ, our proposed model exhibits competitive performance in both objective and subjective tests, highlighting the potential of flow matching for generative MSS. Demo: https://ik4sumii.github.io/FLOMSS/

explain.tldr: A new generative method for separating music into vocals, bass, drums, and other instruments using flow matching.
explain.plain: Music source separation splits a mixed song into individual instrument tracks. Traditionally, this used discriminative methods (trained to classify/separate directly). This paper applies flow matching, a newer generative technique that learns to model complex data distributions, to this problem. They tested various design choices and found their approach performs competitively with existing methods on a standard benchmark, evaluated through both technical metrics and listening tests.
explain.why: Better source separation tools help musicians remix, produce, and remix existing music more flexibly. This work shows that generative approaches—a different paradigm from traditional methods—can work well for this task, potentially opening new directions for improving separation quality.

terms.meaning: A generative technique that learns to transform random noise into realistic data by following learned paths, similar to diffusion models but potentially more flexible
An approach that learns to create or generate new data (like separated instruments) rather than just classify or discriminate between existing categories
Evaluation methods that compare how similar separated tracks are to references using learned representations, rather than just raw audio measurements

papers.title: MSVAE: Rethinking Musical Semantics in Continuous Latent Spaces
papers.summary: Continuous latent representations underlie recent diffusion-based lyrics-to-song and text-to-music systems, yet aligning lyric conditions with these latents remains difficult: existing systems resort to generator-side machinery such as sentence-level timestamps, auxiliary alignment objectives, or semi-autoregressive decoding, while the latents they predict are still produced by autoencoders trained purely for reconstruction. We address this difficulty from the representation side. We propose MSVAE (Music Semantic Variational Autoencoder), which structures its continuous latent around two complementary semantic streams: work-level compositional content and lyric-level linguistic-vocal content. Partitioned dual-stream alignment makes both streams explicit by aligning disjoint latent subspaces with frozen lead-sheet and ASR references, while a semantic-first gated residual posterior derives its base from a frozen music-SSL encoder and admits acoustic information only through gated, bounded corrections. MSVAE achieves competitive stereo reconstruction and stronger MARBLE probing than continuous-autoencoder baselines, and improves downstream lyrics-to-song and text-to-music generation. Notably, with only an untimed phoneme prefix and no lyric timing, MSVAE yields the lowest phoneme error rate, whereas all baseline representations require sentence-level alignment to produce intelligible vocals.

explain.tldr: A new autoencoder that organizes music into separate semantic layers to better align lyrics with generated music.
explain.plain: When AI systems generate music from lyrics or text, they struggle to keep the lyrics properly aligned with the music. Current systems try to fix this by adding extra machinery during generation. This paper takes a different approach: they redesigned the underlying representation itself. They created MSVAE, which splits the music's internal structure into two parts—one for overall musical composition and one for lyrics and vocals. By training these parts to align with reference data (sheet music and speech recognition), the system becomes better at understanding how lyrics and music fit together, which helps downstream music generation work better.
explain.why: For musicians and producers using AI tools, this means lyrics-to-music and text-to-music systems could generate vocals that stay in sync with the music more naturally, without needing to manually specify timing information. Better alignment could make AI-assisted songwriting more practical.

terms.meaning: A compressed, abstract representation of music that an AI learns internally—like a hidden code that captures the essence of a song
A type of neural network that learns to compress data into a simplified form and then reconstruct it, often used for generating new variations
A pre-trained model that learns musical patterns from unlabeled audio without needing human annotations

papers.title: SpectralBridge: Adding High-Frequency Capability to Large Audio-Language Models
papers.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) have become highly capable on a wide range of tasks spanning speech, music, and environmental sound. However, many modern LALMs resample input audio to 16 kHz mono, making all frequencies above 8 kHz unobservable. We present SpectralBridge, a lightweight extension that gives such a model access to the 8-16 kHz band by joining low- and upper-band representations with time-aligned paired cross-frequency attention. Applied to Audio Flamingo Next, the method trains only a small adapter and rank-8 LoRA modules, while leaving the original audio encoder, audio projector, and base language model frozen. SpectralBridge improves both zero-shot transfer and downstream fine-tuning: it raises zero-shot balanced accuracy on the ESC-50 audio classification dataset from 75.5 to 90.5, and when fine-tuned on Insect-10, a 10-way insect species task we construct from InsectSet459 recordings, under the same budget as a LoRA fine-tuned baseline, it reaches 55.4 balanced accuracy against the baseline's 26.2. On a benchmark where the answer depends only on the 8-16 kHz band, it gains 30 mAP over the frozen model. Erasing the upper-band stream from the trained model removes these gains, showing that they come from the high-frequency signal itself rather than from extra tokens or the adapted prompt format.

explain.tldr: A method that lets audio AI models hear high frequencies they normally miss by adding a lightweight extension.
explain.plain: Large audio-language models typically process audio at 16 kHz, which means they can only hear frequencies up to 8 kHz—missing the crisp, bright sounds that make up the upper half of human hearing. SpectralBridge adds a small adapter that lets these models access the 8-16 kHz band by connecting high and low frequency information together. The results show significant improvements: on sound classification tasks, accuracy jumped from 75.5% to 90.5%, and on identifying insect species from recordings, it more than doubled performance compared to the baseline.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this matters because high frequencies carry important details—the shimmer of cymbals, the clarity of vocals, the presence of bright instruments. If AI tools analyzing or generating music can't hear these frequencies, they're working with incomplete information. Better high-frequency awareness could improve music recommendation systems, audio classification, and eventually generative models.

terms.meaning: An AI system trained to understand both audio and text, able to answer questions about sounds or describe what it hears
A technique for efficiently adapting large models by training only a small set of extra parameters rather than retraining everything
A mechanism that lets the model connect and compare information from different frequency ranges to understand them together

papers.title: PitchIn: Natural-Language Vocal Coaching from Unstructured Community Feedback
papers.summary: Effective vocal coaching connects performance issues with corrective advice, but recordings paired with expert diagnoses and advice are scarce. Online singing communities provide a potential source of supervision, but observations and advice are scattered across unstructured comments. We introduce PitchIn, audio-language models for natural-language vocal coaching, and the PeerCoach Dataset: 14,445 instruction examples covering Focused QA, Overall Feedback, and Recognition QA. We compare target combinations on Qwen2.5-Omni and train PitchIn on Focused QA and Overall Feedback using Qwen2.5-Omni and MOSS-Music. On VocalCoachBench, the proportion of requested diagnosis-correction pairs matching an expert issue with valid advice rises from 21.3% to 61.0% for Qwen2.5-Omni and from 31.4% to 51.2% for MOSS-Music. Direct training on source comments yields only 19.8% for Qwen2.5-Omni. For Qwen, Focused QA alone reaches 65.6%, but adding Overall Feedback improves alignment with expert reviews and human preference. Both models improve expert-review alignment over pretrained baselines and are significantly preferred for usefulness (92.0% and 67.3%, respectively). Demo examples are available at https://hayeonbang.github.io/PitchIn.

explain.tldr: AI system that learns from online singing community comments to give singers personalized vocal coaching advice.
explain.plain: Singers often need feedback to improve, but expert vocal coaching is hard to find and expensive. This paper uses comments from online singing communities—where people already give each other singing tips—to train AI models that can listen to a recording and offer helpful coaching. They created a dataset of 14,445 examples of real feedback and tested their system, finding it could correctly match singing problems with good advice much more often than baseline models.
explain.why: For musicians and singers, this could make vocal coaching more accessible by providing AI-powered feedback on recordings. It shows how real community knowledge can be turned into a useful tool, rather than requiring expensive expert instruction.

terms.meaning: AI systems that understand both sound (audio) and text, so they can listen to singing and respond with written or spoken advice
combinations of identifying a problem (diagnosis) and suggesting how to fix it (correction), like 'your pitch is flat—try singing from your diaphragm'
AI models that were trained on general data before this project, used as a comparison point to show improvement

papers.title: Predicting Audio Popularity: A Comparative Study of Metadata and Acoustic Features Across Music and Sound Effects
papers.summary: This study addresses the prediction of audio popularity on an online sharing platform by leveraging both metadata and acoustic feature representations. Two distinct categories of audio content are considered: music and sound effects. Popularity is formulated as a supervised classification task based on two target variables: the number of downloads and the average user rating. We conduct a comparative evaluation of multiple machine learning models, including Random Forest, XGBoost, and a Neural Network model. Experiments are performed across different feature sets, including metadata, platform-provided descriptors, and eGeMAPS acoustic features. Results indicate that metadata consistently provide the most informative representation for predicting popularity. Nevertheless, acoustic features alone achieve performance significantly above chance level, demonstrating that intrinsic properties of the audio signal contribute to popularity prediction.

explain.tldr: Researchers compared machine learning models to predict whether audio content becomes popular using metadata and acoustic features.
explain.plain: The researchers wanted to understand what makes audio files popular on sharing platforms. They tested whether they could predict popularity (measured by downloads and ratings) using two types of information: metadata like tags and descriptions, plus acoustic features—measurements of the actual sound itself. They tried several machine learning approaches and found that metadata worked best, but the acoustic features alone still predicted popularity better than random guessing, suggesting the sound itself matters.
explain.why: This research could help musicians and producers understand which sonic qualities resonate with audiences, and could inform platform algorithms that recommend music and sound effects to listeners.

terms.meaning: Numerical measurements extracted from audio signals, like loudness, brightness, or rhythm characteristics
A standardized set of acoustic measurements designed to capture perceptually relevant properties of sound
A machine learning approach where the algorithm learns from examples labeled with correct answers (like 'popular' or 'unpopular')

papers.title: MPASCNet: Magnitude-Phase-Aware Adaptive Spectral Compression for Compressed Music Restoration
papers.summary: Compressed music restoration aims to recover high-fidelity audio from lossy codecs such as MP3 by restoring missing spectral content and reducing coding artifacts. Recently, generative adversarial networks and band-split models have made progress in compressed music restoration. However, existing methods either operate without explicitly modeling phase or rely on predefined frequency partitions, which may limit restoration performance and the use of input-dependent frequency information. To address these issues, we propose MPASCNet, a Magnitude-Phase-Aware Adaptive Spectral Compression network. Instead of using fixed bands, MPASCNet combines magnitude and phase features to guide cross-attention, adaptively compressing full-resolution spectral features into compact tokens.
