These tokens are then processed by a spectro-temporal backbone to model spectral-temporal dependencies. Finally, separate decoder branches reconstruct the full-resolution magnitude and wrapped phase spectra. Experiments on MP3 restoration show that MPASCNet outperforms the Apollo and AEROMamba baselines across multiple restoration metrics while using only 6.49 M parameters. The code is available at https://github.com/xinghour/MPASCNet.

explain.tldr: A neural network that restores high-quality audio from MP3 files by intelligently handling both loudness and phase information.
explain.plain: MP3 and other compressed audio formats lose information to save file size, resulting in lower sound quality. This paper proposes MPASCNet, which uses artificial intelligence to recover that lost audio detail. Unlike previous methods that divide the audio spectrum into fixed sections, MPASCNet adapts its approach based on what's actually in the compressed file, paying attention to both the magnitude (loudness at each frequency) and phase (timing relationships between frequencies). Tests show it restores audio better than existing methods while using fewer computational resources.
explain.why: If you work with MP3s or other compressed formats, this could improve how your music sounds when restored to higher quality. It's also relevant if you're interested in how AI can enhance audio files or if you produce music that gets compressed for distribution.

terms.meaning: Two parts of sound at each frequency: magnitude is how loud it is, phase is the timing/alignment of the wave
Information about what frequencies are present in audio and how strong they are
A technique where the AI learns which parts of the input are most important for each output decision

papers.title: Controllable Mono-to-Stereo Upmixing using Reward-tilted Flows
papers.summary: We consider the problem of mono-to-stereo audio upmixing: generating a high-fidelity two-channel stereo signal from a single-channel recording. The task is fundamentally ill-posed i.e., many stereo signals are consistent with a given mono recording. An effective upmixer must therefore generate a realistic, musically coherent stereo image while preserving the underlying audio content. Previous approaches have relied on signal-processing driven decorrelation, ambience extraction and supervised learning, offering limited spatial control or requiring task-specific training. In response, we propose Aura (Audio Upmixing using Reward-tilted Flows), which reformulates upmixing as a generative inverse problem using a pretrained flow prior. To enable controllable spatial imaging, we design a reward-tilted posterior sampler whose reward penalizes divergences between generated and target distributions of inter-channel cues. Composing forward operators further enables joint restoration and upmixing without retraining or fine-tuning. Objective and subjective evaluations on real-world music recordings from MUSDB18-HQ demonstrate our method's effectiveness relative to several baselines.

explain.tldr: A method to convert mono audio to stereo while letting users control the spatial width and positioning of sounds.
explain.plain: Converting a single-channel recording to stereo is tricky because many different stereo versions could match the original mono. The researchers built a system called Aura that uses a generative model to create realistic stereo from mono while giving you control over how sounds are positioned in the stereo field. They tested it on real music and compared it to other approaches, finding their method works better and offers more creative control than previous techniques.
explain.why: This matters to producers and engineers who work with older mono recordings or want to remix material. Instead of manually panning and adding effects, you could use an AI tool that understands music and lets you dial in exactly how wide or narrow you want the stereo image to be.

terms.meaning: a pretrained AI model that has learned what realistic audio sounds like, used as a foundation for generating new audio
the differences between left and right speakers that tell your brain where a sound is positioned in space
working backwards from a result (mono audio) to find possible causes (stereo versions) that could have produced it

papers.title: TASTE: Taxonomy-Aware Symbolic Piano Generation from Textual Description
papers.summary: Text-conditioned symbolic music generation has attracted growing interest with the development of generative models. Yet two questions remain underexplored: what aspects of music the conditioning text should describe, and how the corresponding data should be collected and trained to improve controllability and text-music alignment. We address these challenges with TASTE, a taxonomy-aware framework for symbolic music generation with a main focus on piano pieces. First, we introduce a taxonomy of musical elements that specifies how a piece can be captured through textual description in a musically grounded way. The taxonomy comprises a set of metadata tags (genre, emotion, section plan, etc.) together with a free-form description of music imagery. This structure decomposes textual input to match the generation goal more coherently and precisely. Second, we build a data pipeline for collecting, annotating, and retrieving public symbolic piano resources, yielding a corpus of 432K MIDI files labeled at multiple levels of granularity. Finally, we design a staged training procedure that leverages this multi-granularity data across two model families: an autoregressive model and a non-autoregressive diffusion model. Both objective and subjective evaluations show that our models achieve superior musical-element control, text-description alignment, and overall music quality. We will release the full pipeline, all annotated datasets, and the model checkpoints.

explain.tldr: A system that generates piano music from text descriptions using structured musical categories and multi-level training data.
explain.plain: Musicians want to create piano pieces by describing them in words, but it's unclear what details matter most and how to train systems to understand those descriptions well. This paper proposes TASTE, which breaks down musical descriptions into specific categories (like genre, emotion, and structure) plus free-form imagery, then trains two types of AI models on 432,000 labeled piano pieces. Tests show their approach produces music that better matches what people ask for and sounds higher quality.
explain.why: This matters to composers and producers exploring AI-assisted creation: it shows how to make text-to-music tools more musically intelligent and controllable, rather than treating music as generic data. The released datasets and models could help others build better tools for describing and generating the specific sounds they want.

terms.meaning: Creating music as note sequences (like MIDI) rather than audio waveforms, focusing on what notes to play and when
An AI that generates music one note or token at a time, using previously generated notes to predict the next one
An AI that generates music by gradually refining random noise into coherent sequences, working on all notes somewhat simultaneously

papers.title: Harmonic Representations in Symbolic Music Transformers are Localized and Controllable
papers.summary: Transformer models trained on symbolic music have become remarkably capable. However, it is yet unclear how they represent music structure, and whether understanding their internal representations can be used to unlock methods for model control. We examine this through a case study of harmonic analysis: when a music transformer navigates a cadence, what does it internally "know" about its harmonic context, and can that knowledge be used to affect the generation? Using Aria, a LLaMA-based symbolic music transformer evaluated on Bach chorales, we find that harmonic decisions are causally localized progressively from middle layers onward. Linear probes show that mode becomes decodable in the same layer range where patching identifies growing causal effect, while key identity emerges later. We then confirm these representations are actionable for music generation control: steering via latent directions corresponding to harmonic changes reliably produces a deceptive or minor resolution, while preserving structural coherence and generation quality. This demonstrates that, at inference time, the model's internal harmonic knowledge can be directly manipulated to control the harmonic output.

explain.tldr: Researchers show that music transformers store harmonic knowledge in specific internal layers and can be steered to control chord progressions.
explain.plain: Music transformers are AI models trained on symbolic music notation that can generate new pieces. This study investigates how these models internally represent harmony—specifically, how they understand chord progressions and cadences. By analyzing a model trained on Bach chorales, the researchers found that harmonic decisions happen in middle layers of the model, and they discovered they could manipulate these internal representations to reliably change the output (for example, creating a deceptive cadence or shifting to minor) while keeping the music sounding coherent.
explain.why: This matters because it shows a path toward more controllable AI music generation. Instead of treating these models as black boxes, understanding where and how they make harmonic decisions lets musicians and producers guide the AI toward specific musical outcomes—like ensuring particular chord progressions or emotional qualities.

terms.meaning: music represented as discrete symbols (like note names and durations) rather than audio waveforms; essentially sheet music in digital form
a type of AI architecture that processes sequences (like notes in a piece) by learning which parts are most relevant to each other
abstract pathways within a model's internal representation that correspond to specific musical changes, which can be adjusted to steer generation

papers.title: High-Fidelity Song Generation with Joint Discrete and Continuous Modeling
papers.summary: Generating a full song from lyrics and a style description requires long-range musical planning without sacrificing vocal and instrumental detail. Low-rate discrete semantic tokens make this tractable, but quantization constrains the information available to acoustic rendering, while separately optimized stages prevent downstream generation objectives from shaping the planner. We propose joint discrete and continuous modeling for high-fidelity song generation. A VQ tokenizer supplies tokens for autoregressive planning, and a separately trained SSL-derived variational encoder supplies continuous semantic targets. Conditioned on the completed token plan and differentiable readouts of the planner's predictive states, a full-sequence flow model generates semantic features for acoustic rendering. Its flow-matching gradients reach the language model through the readouts, without differentiating through token sampling; the standard pathway keeps continuous features out of autoregressive feedback. On 192 shared prompts, its 48D configuration improves SongEval from 4.152 to 4.269 and reduces micro-PER from 20.26% to 14.47% relative to a discrete baseline, while receiving substantially higher expert listening scores. We further analyze the system through downstream semantic probes and conditioned reconstruction.

explain.tldr: A system that generates complete songs from lyrics and style by combining discrete planning with continuous acoustic detail.
explain.plain: Making full songs from text requires balancing two competing needs: planning the overall structure and maintaining fine details in vocals and instruments. This paper proposes using two complementary approaches together—discrete tokens for high-level planning (like a musical outline) and continuous features for acoustic quality (like the detailed sound). The key innovation is letting information flow between these two pathways so they improve each other. The results show better vocal clarity and higher quality ratings compared to using only discrete tokens.
explain.why: If this approach works well, it could enable musicians and producers to generate complete, high-quality songs from text descriptions or lyrics, potentially speeding up composition and arrangement workflows.

terms.meaning: A tool that converts continuous audio information into discrete symbols (tokens), like translating a smooth sound into a sequence of codes
A machine learning model that generates detailed audio features by gradually transforming random noise into structured sound information
Generating a sequence one step at a time, where each new step depends on all previous steps, like predicting the next note based on the melody so far

papers.title: FlowGRPO for Vocal Separation: From Reward Analysis to Reward Design
papers.summary: The Flow Matching objective supervises the velocity field at intermediate states, whereas waveform metrics are evaluated after decoding and may be non-differentiable. To align Flow Matching models with waveform-level and perceptual quality objectives during post-training, FlowGRPO optimizes their trajectories using endpoint rewards. In this work, we focus on music separation and use multi-resolution short-time Fourier transform (MRSTFT), scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio (SI-SDR), and Virtual Speech Quality Objective Listener (ViSQOL) as reward components. Before policy optimization, we analyze the relationship between data quality factors and the within-group gap between the maximum and mean rollout rewards for each component. This analysis motivates a revised ViSQOL reward that matches channel-wise root-mean-square (RMS) levels and evaluates the interval from the first to the last active frame, retaining inactive frames within that interval. We also apply a sample-quality filter based on predefined waveform checks. Together, the revised reward and quality filter enable FlowGRPO to improve the pretrained vocal separator in both separation performance and perceptual quality.

explain.tldr: A method to improve vocal separation by tuning AI models using quality-based rewards that match human perception.
explain.plain: Vocal separation AI models learn to generate clean vocals and backing tracks, but they're typically trained in ways that don't directly optimize for how good the results sound to human ears. This paper proposes FlowGRPO, which fine-tunes a pretrained vocal separator by rewarding it for producing results that score well on perceptual quality metrics—essentially teaching it what sounds better. They tested different reward signals and found that carefully designed rewards, combined with filtering out low-quality training examples, improved both the technical separation quality and how natural the results sound.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this means vocal separation tools could become more reliable at preserving vocal quality and natural sound. Understanding how to align AI models with perceptual goals is relevant to anyone developing or improving audio production tools.

terms.meaning: A machine learning approach that trains models by guiding them through intermediate steps, similar to gradually denoising a blurry image into a clear one.
A measurement of how similar a separated audio signal is to the original, ignoring differences in overall loudness.
An automated tool that predicts how natural and clear audio sounds to human listeners, based on perceptual characteristics.

papers.title: HMU-Bench: Hierarchical Music Understanding Benchmark for Omni Models
papers.summary: Music-understanding benchmarks should identify both the evidence available to a model and the operations a correct answer requires. We introduce HMU-Bench, a bilingual benchmark with notation and audio components. ABC Q&A contains 1,029 Chinese-English question pairs across six musical domains, labeled as extraction, single-step inference, or multi-step inference. Audio Q&A contains 460 question pairs on 92 recordings, spanning five scope-difficulty configurations. All music is Suno-generated, and questions and references are human-reviewed. Reference-based evaluation of seven omni models yields high notation scores for the strongest systems, but no model averages above 1.4 on the 0-4 audio scale. Notation and audio rankings show little correlation. A transposition case study also reveals octave errors missed by LLM grading. These findings motivate separate modality reporting and event-level checks for symbolic outputs. Data, annotations, evaluator prompts, and graded responses will be released at https://github.com/stepaudiollm/hmu-bench.

explain.tldr: A benchmark tests how well AI models understand music from both sheet notation and audio recordings.
explain.plain: Music understanding involves both reading notation and listening to audio, but existing tests don't clearly separate these skills. The researchers created HMU-Bench, a bilingual test with two parts: questions about musical notation (with 1,029 question pairs) and questions about audio recordings (460 pairs). They tested seven AI models and found they perform well on notation questions but struggle significantly with audio—no model scored above 1.4 out of 4 on average for audio. Interestingly, models that did well on notation didn't necessarily do well on audio, suggesting these are different challenges.
explain.why: This work matters because it reveals that current AI systems don't truly understand music holistically—they handle notation and sound separately. For musicians and producers, this shows where AI music tools have real limitations and where they might fail, helping you know when to trust or distrust their musical judgments.

terms.meaning: AI systems designed to handle multiple types of input (like both text and audio) in a single model
musical information represented as notation or structured data (like note names and durations) rather than sound waves
a type of input or output, such as audio, text, or sheet music notation

papers.title: AnyEdit: A Unified Framework for Speech and Singing Voice Editing with Real-World Environmental Consistency
papers.summary: We present AnyEdit, a unified, separation-free framework for speech and singing voice editing that preserves real-world acoustic environments, including noise, reverberation, and background music. Recent unified generative models already achieve strong speech and singing generation in clean conditions, but real-world vocal editing remains challenging because the model must revise content while simultaneously preserving speaker identity, prosody, and the surrounding acoustic scene. Directly modeling noisy audio end-to-end entangles semantic editing with environmental acoustics, weakening the core vocal generation capability. We therefore adopt a two-stage design that preserves clean-domain editing ability while deferring acoustic rendering to a separate stage: an instruction-guided autoregressive editor first predicts clean prosody and content-style tokens, supported by a teacher-student noise-robust prosody tokenizer that distills clean prosodic tokens from degraded recordings; a flow-matching acoustic model then performs in-context rendering conditioned on the source acoustic context, so the edited segment inherits surrounding noise, reverberation, and background sound while maintaining consistent speaker timbre. To stabilize unedited regions, we introduce unmodified-area-aware supervision; after pre-training, we further apply direct preference optimization on mined real-to-real singing pairs. We also release AnyEditBench, a benchmark covering both speech and singing voice editing under clean, simulated, and in-the-wild acoustic conditions. Experiments on Chinese and English speech and singing datasets showed that AnyEdit consistently outperforms strong baselines in content accuracy, subjective quality, and background consistency under noisy and reverberant conditions. Demo: https://any-edit.github.io/. AnyEditBench: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Ririiiii/anyeditbench.

explain.tldr: A system for editing speech and singing that keeps background noise, reverb, and other environmental sounds intact.
explain.plain: Editing vocals in real recordings is hard because you need to change what someone says or sings while keeping their voice recognizable and preserving all the background noise and room acoustics. Most editing tools work on clean audio, so they struggle with messy real-world recordings. AnyEdit splits the problem into two steps: first, it figures out what the new words or melody should be, then it adds back the original room sound and background noise so the edit blends seamlessly. The researchers tested it on speech and singing in multiple languages and found it outperforms other methods at keeping edits natural-sounding.
explain.why: If you record vocals in real spaces—bedrooms, studios with ambient noise, live settings—you can now edit what was said or sung without losing the authentic acoustic character of the original recording. This matters for producers fixing takes, musicians re-recording parts, and anyone working with imperfect recordings.

terms.meaning: The rhythm, timing, and intonation patterns of speech or singing—how something is said, not just what is said.
A machine learning model that generates audio by gradually transforming noise into realistic sound, guided by conditions like the surrounding acoustic environment.
Generating new audio that matches the acoustic properties (noise, reverb, background sounds) of the original recording it's being inserted into.

papers.title: Sori: Streamable and Controllable Model for Non-musical Audio to Symbolic Music Transformation
papers.summary: We introduce Non-musical Audio to Symbolic Music Transformation (NASMT), a novel task that converts non-musical audio into symbolic music representations. Unlike automatic music transcription, which assumes musical input and a unique correct score, NASMT is inherently one-to-many and requires evaluation along two axes: input correspondence and musicality. We present Sori, an encoder--decoder Transformer that addresses this task through domain adversarial training (DAT), which bridges the gap between musical and non-musical audio in the encoder's feature space, and classifier-free guidance (CFG) with a continuous parameter~$γ$ that controls the trade-off between correspondence and musicality at inference time. Across objective metrics and a listening study, Sori provides effective continuous control via $γ$ and compares favorably with instrument-agnostic transcription models. Sori supports real-time streaming on a consumer CPU. Audio examples are available at https://soridemo0320.github.io/sori-demo/.

explain.tldr: A system that converts non-musical sounds into sheet music notation with adjustable control over accuracy versus musical quality.
explain.plain: The paper tackles a new problem: turning everyday sounds (like traffic, speech, or nature recordings) into symbolic music—the kind you'd read as sheet music or MIDI. Unlike transcribing an actual performance, there's no single "correct" answer; the same sound could become many different pieces depending on how musical you want the output to be. The researchers built a model called Sori that lets you dial up or down how closely the output matches the original sound versus how musically pleasing it sounds, and it runs fast enough on regular computers to work in real time.
explain.why: This could open creative possibilities for producers and composers—turning found sounds or field recordings into playable musical material. It also suggests new ways to think about the relationship between sound and music notation, which matters for anyone interested in algorithmic composition or sound design.

terms.meaning: Music stored as notes, timing, and pitch rather than as audio waveforms—like MIDI or sheet music notation
A technique that trains a model to extract features that look similar whether the input is musical or non-musical audio, helping bridge the gap between the two
A method that lets you control a model's output at inference time by adjusting how much it follows a particular goal, using a single parameter

papers.title: The NPU-ASLP System for Music Restoration in the CCF-AATC 2026 Challenge
papers.summary: This paper presents the NPU-ASLP music restoration system developed for Track 1 of the China Computer Federation (CCF) Advanced Audio Technology Competition (AATC) 2026 Challenge. The task aims to recover clean music from mobile-device-captured recordings affected by coupled degradations from playback devices, acoustic propagation, environmental noise and recording terminals. System development is further constrained by limited and imperfectly aligned real data pairs and a strict model-complexity budget. In our system, we adopt TF-MoE as the backbone for its dual-axis modeling of cross-band and temporal dependencies, whose Top-1 routing activates a single expert per token to bound computation under the strict budget. We extend it with two task-specific adaptations: a scale-aware encoder and a complex mapping decoder. The former encodes normalized complex spectra jointly with per-band log-RMS to preserve the band-energy cues discarded by band-wise normalization. The latter directly estimates the clean complex spectrum rather than masking the input, thereby repairing coupled degradations. To address the limited, imperfectly aligned real recordings, we further build a challenge-calibrated playback--propagation--recording simulator that generates 1,572.12 h of sample-aligned data across 202 acoustic conditions. The final system contains 2.951M parameters and requires 82.659 GMACs for a 10-s input. On the official blind test, it achieved -49.067 dB SI-SNR, 1.273 LSD, 2.540 FAD, and 3.495 ViSQOL. It ranked third in LSD, FAD, and ViSQOL and received the third prize in the challenge.

explain.tldr: A system that cleans up music recorded on phones by modeling audio structure efficiently and simulating realistic degradation.
explain.plain: When you record music on a phone, it gets degraded by the device itself, room acoustics, background noise, and the microphone. This paper describes a system that tries to recover clean music from these messy recordings. The researchers used a neural network designed to understand how frequencies and time interact while staying computationally efficient. They also created a simulator that generates thousands of hours of training data by artificially degrading clean music in realistic ways, since real paired recordings are hard to get. The system ranked third in a competition and achieved measurable improvements in audio quality metrics.
explain.why: This matters if you're working with phone recordings or low-quality audio captures and want to restore them automatically. It shows how to build practical restoration tools that work within real computational constraints—useful for mobile apps or live processing.

terms.meaning: A neural network architecture that separately models how frequencies relate to each other and how sound changes over time, using 'experts' that activate selectively to save computation.
A representation of audio that captures both the magnitude (loudness) and phase (timing) of each frequency, rather than just loudness alone.
Different metrics that measure how well restored audio matches the original clean version, each focusing on different aspects of audio quality.

papers.title: JSIR: An Audio-Aligned, Multi-Task Dataset of Jazz Standard Recordings
papers.summary: Beat tracking, chord estimation, and structure analysis are staple tasks of music information retrieval. Their datasets are drawn largely from Western popular music, and jazz remains a repertoire on which state-of-the-art systems underperform. We present JSIR, the Jazz Standards dataset for Information Retrieval. Its 267 recordings of 44 jazz standards span 25.6 hours, 3.7 times the audio of JAAH, the closest existing resource. For each recording, we provide annotations for beat and downbeat positions, chords, and sections, all produced by a jazz musician and revised in several passes. In baseline experiments, models trained with JSIR also improve on other jazz datasets: the downbeat F-measure of a state-of-the-art beat tracker rises from 87.7% to 89.2%, and the seventh-chord accuracy of a pop-trained chord estimator on JAAH from 34% to 41%. We publicly release the annotations, the annotation tool used to create them, and a web application that displays them in sync with the audio.

explain.tldr: A new dataset of 267 jazz recordings with detailed annotations for beats, chords, and song structure to improve music analysis systems.
explain.plain: Jazz music has been underrepresented in datasets used to train music analysis systems, so existing tools don't work as well on jazz as they do on pop music. The researchers created JSIR, a collection of 267 jazz standard recordings with careful, expert annotations marking where the beats fall, what chords are played, and how songs are structured. When they trained systems on this new dataset, performance improved—both on jazz recordings and on other existing jazz datasets.
explain.why: If you work with jazz recordings or want to build tools that understand jazz music, better datasets and trained models mean more accurate automatic analysis of beats, harmony, and song form. This could help with transcription, remixing, or music discovery tools tailored to jazz.

terms.meaning: automatically detecting where the regular pulses (beats) occur in a recording
automatically identifying which chords are being played at each moment in the music
a score that measures how accurate a system is, combining how many correct detections it makes and how many false alarms it produces

papers.title: Gugak-VocalSet: A Multi-Genre Studio-Quality Dataset of Korean Traditional Singing with Sigimsae Annotations
papers.summary: We present Gugak-VocalSet, the first publicly available audio dataset for Korean traditional singing with dense annotations of sigimsae, a structured pitch contour system of vocal expressions. Gugak-VocalSet contains 24.5 hours of unaccompanied solo vocal recordings across 305 tracks of representative repertoire curated by the National Gugak Center, performed by 20 professional singers in a controlled studio environment with fixed key and tempo. In addition to genre, lyrics, and mood/timbre tags, the dataset provides a unified sigimsae ontology and approximately 68,000 segments (71,700 instances including multi-label) of audio-grounded sigimsae annotations; the ontology adopts a functional-position-based hierarchy designed for consistent application across genres, and 14 expert annotators specializing in Korean traditional music performed segment-level labeling accordingly. Baseline experiments on sigimsae classification and event detection show that domain-informed F0 representations remain competitive with, and on classification surpass, frozen probing of a general-purpose music foundation model, while pitch and spectral cues play complementary roles in event-level detection. Companion page: https://www.danbinaerin.com/Gugak-VocalSet/

explain.tldr: A dataset of Korean traditional singing with detailed annotations of sigimsae vocal techniques for research and AI training.
explain.plain: Korean traditional singing (gugak) uses a specific system of pitch movements and vocal ornaments called sigimsae to express emotion and style. This paper introduces a new dataset of 24.5 hours of professional recordings labeled with about 68,000 examples of these techniques, created by music experts. They tested whether AI models could recognize sigimsae from audio, finding that pitch-focused representations work well, sometimes better than general music AI models.
explain.why: This dataset lets researchers and musicians study how Korean traditional singing creates its distinctive sound. It could help develop tools for analyzing, teaching, or even synthesizing these vocal techniques, and provides a model for documenting ornamental singing systems in other traditions.

terms.meaning: A structured system of pitch movements and vocal ornaments used in Korean traditional singing to express emotion and style
Different ways of encoding the fundamental frequency (pitch) of a voice for analysis by computers
A large general-purpose AI model trained on broad music data that can be adapted for specific tasks

papers.title: HE-NAC: High-Efficiency Neural Audio Coding via Hierarchical and Residual Multi-Band Quantization
papers.summary: High-fidelity audio coding requires faithful reconstruction of perceptually important high-frequency components, which are often lost due to the aggressive temporal decimation and quantization of neural codecs. State-of-the-art neural audio coding methods rely on adversarial learning to hallucinate these missing components, yielding perceptually plausible but imprecise reconstructions; a limitation for high-fidelity music applications. As a remedy, we propose high-efficiency neural audio coding (HE-NAC), which provides a multi-band extension of the popular residual vector quantization (RVQ) scheme. HE-NAC introduces an effective training mechanism that harmonizes a bitrate-free blind upsampling process, residual learning to compensate it with minimal bitrate, and a multi-head decoder architecture for band-specific reconstruction. As a result, HE-NAC achieves a balanced trade-off, reliably reconstructing the core-band ($\leq$ 3 kHz) component while preserving overall sound fidelity. Subjective listening tests and objective evaluations demonstrate that HE-NAC outperforms both the DAC baseline and MPEG HE-AAC at equal or lower bitrates.

explain.tldr: A neural audio codec that better preserves high frequencies and sound quality by processing different frequency bands separately with improved quantization.
explain.plain: Neural audio codecs often lose important high-frequency details when compressing audio, sometimes trying to fake them back in. This paper proposes HE-NAC, which handles different frequency ranges separately instead of treating all audio the same way. It uses a technique called residual vector quantization applied across multiple bands, plus a smarter decoder that reconstructs each band appropriately. Tests show it produces better-sounding audio than existing methods at the same file size.
explain.why: For musicians and producers working with high-quality recordings, this matters because it means compressed audio files could maintain more of the original sound's clarity and detail—important when you care about preserving the nuances of instruments and vocals.

terms.meaning: A compression technique that breaks audio into small pieces and represents each piece with a code, then refines the representation by encoding what was missed in the first pass
How many bits of data per second are used to store or transmit audio; lower bitrate means smaller file size but potentially lower quality
Dividing audio into separate frequency ranges (like bass, mids, treble) and processing each range independently

papers.title: Transfer Learning for Rhythm Game Chart Generation from Music Transcription and Across Games
papers.summary: Rhythm games ask the player to act in time with a recording, following a chart: a sequence of actions, each with a time and, depending on the game, a lane, type, or playfield position. Charts are hand-written per recording and difficulty. Automatic generation from audio has been studied with pipeline and end-to-end approaches, and recent work reuses pre-trained audio encoders, but never compares them with one trained from scratch. None of these targets automatic music transcription (AMT), yet most chart times are note onsets, which AMT models locate. We freeze a pre-trained audio encoder, an AMT model in particular, and train only a linear projection and a Transformer decoder on charts. With MuScriptor, this fits human charts more closely than encoders trained from scratch and places more accurate note types than MERT, a music encoder pre-trained without transcription labels. Joint training on three osu! modes raises event F1 on the mode with the fewest charts from 0.492 to 0.506, while charts from Clone Hero, similar in layout, lower it to 0.482. Transfer between games thus appears to depend on charting style and the music covered.

explain.tldr: Using pre-trained music transcription models improves automatic generation of rhythm game charts from audio.
explain.plain: Rhythm games like osu! require hand-written charts that tell players what to do and when. This paper tests whether using a music transcription model (which learns to find note onsets in audio) as a starting point helps automatically generate these charts. They froze a pre-trained transcription model and trained only a small additional layer on top of it. This approach matched human charts better than training from scratch, though transferring between different rhythm games had mixed results depending on how similar the games' charting styles were.
explain.why: This matters because chart creation is currently manual and time-consuming. Better automatic generation could let rhythm game communities create charts faster, or help music producers understand how their songs might be interpreted as playable patterns.

terms.meaning: reusing a model trained on one task (like finding notes in music) as a starting point for a different but related task (like generating game charts)
a neural network that converts raw audio into a compact numerical representation that captures musical information
the exact moments in time when musical notes begin

papers.title: Explore This! Beat and Downbeat Tracking From a Learned Tatum Grid
papers.summary: State-of-the-art beat tracking is based on neural networks that model beats and downbeats as individual events, often followed by a separate Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN) enforcing musical consistency. We propose a novel architecture that combines deep learning with differentiable theory-based modules: Specifically, we design a system that first predicts a tatum grid, then groups tatum events to beats and downbeats, explicitly modelling multiple options for the current tempo and time signature in a bar-pointer-like fashion. Our approach improves continuity metrics compared to existing DBN-free systems and is more versatile than the de-facto standard DBN, but still falls behind the best DBN-based methods on average. Given the many design choices and hyperparameters involved, we assume we have not yet explored the full potential of this idea and publish our code and invite others to explore this further.

explain.tldr: A new system tracks musical beats by first finding a tatum grid, then grouping it into beats and downbeats.
explain.plain: Beat and downbeat tracking—figuring out where the pulse and measure boundaries are in music—is usually done by neural networks that treat beats as separate events, then add extra rules to keep them musically sensible. This paper tries a different approach: predict the underlying tatum grid first (a finer rhythmic subdivision), then intelligently group those grid points into beats and downbeats while considering different tempo and time signature possibilities. The results show better continuity than some existing methods, though not quite as good as the current best systems, but the authors think there's more room to improve with different design choices.
explain.why: Better beat and downbeat tracking helps music software stay locked to the right pulse, which matters for beat-synced effects, tempo detection, and tools that need to understand a song's rhythmic structure. This approach is also more interpretable—it builds in musical knowledge explicitly rather than leaving it hidden in a neural network.

terms.meaning: A regular subdivision of time at the smallest rhythmic level a listener can perceive; a finer grid than individual beats
A mathematical model that enforces rules about how sequences should flow over time, used here to keep beat predictions musically consistent
Components that encode musical rules in a way that neural networks can learn from, combining hand-designed knowledge with machine learning

papers.title: PAG-Agent: Zero-Shot Personalized Music Album Generation via Aesthetic Profile Distillation
papers.summary: Large Music Models (LMMs) can synthesize high-fidelity audio and support increasingly flexible prompt control, yet modeling the subjective preferences of an individual listener remains underexplored. We present PAG-Agent, a zero-shot multimodal framework that uses an explicit Personal Aesthetic Profile to bridge user preference inference and music generation control. A multimodal LLM distills favorite-song audio and contextual user information into this structured representation, which a planning LLM translates into generation instructions for existing music synthesizers. We further introduce PA-Eval, which evaluates personalization through the Aesthetic Consistency Score (ACS) for target-user alignment and the Aesthetic Specificity Index (ASI) for cross-user specificity. Experiments with Personal-100 on multiple MLLM and music-generation backbones show consistent improvements over generic and direct conditioning. A 50-participant follow-up study further shows a correlation $r=0.64$ between ACS and subjective preference.

explain.tldr: A system that learns your music taste from songs you like and generates personalized albums without needing training data.
explain.plain: Making music AI that sounds generic is easy—making it match what *you* specifically like is hard. This paper presents PAG-Agent, which listens to your favorite songs and learns your aesthetic preferences, then uses that understanding to guide a music generator to create albums tailored to you. They tested it with 50 people and found their preference scores correlated well with what listeners actually preferred.
explain.why: If you make or produce music, this matters because it shows a path toward AI tools that could adapt to your personal style rather than defaulting to average sounds. It also suggests ways to evaluate whether personalization is actually working.

terms.meaning: the system works without being trained on examples of your specific taste—it figures you out from your existing favorite songs
the system processes multiple types of information together, like audio files and text descriptions, not just one type
a measurement of how well the generated music matches the target listener's taste

papers.title: Speech event detector: Timestamped detection of non-verbal vocalizations and background sounds for rich speech transcription
papers.summary: Automatic speech recognition produces words but drops the non-verbal content of a recording: the breaths, coughs, sighs and laughter of the speaker, and the horns, music or barking around them. We describe Speech Event Detector, a 5.8-million-parameter convolutional-Transformer model that outputs probabilities every 40 ms for 54 event classes (20 speaker vocalizations and 34 background sounds), together with post-processing that converts these probabilities into timestamped events and a procedure for merging the events into a Whisper transcript. The model is trained on material drawn from seven public datasets whose labels come in incompatible forms: single detected regions, free-text tags with timestamps, temporally strong ontology labels, symbols embedded in transcripts, isolated recordings and environmental recordings. We unify them using rule-based label mapping, recover timestamps for transcript-embedded labels through CTC forced alignment, locating 6,360 of 8,620 sounds, and combine about 168 hours of real annotated training recordings with synthetic mixtures and augmentation using real background noise. Per-class thresholds for two operating profiles are tuned on real held-out recordings, and performance is estimated using two-fold cross-validation. On whole held-out recordings from four datasets, considering the 48 classes with at least ten held-out events, the sensitive profile detects an average of 49 percent of a class's events, covering 67 percent of all 9,367 events, at a macro precision of 0.30. The balanced profile achieves a macro recall of 0.37 at a precision of 0.36, with macro event F1 scores of 0.32 and 0.33, respectively. The detector runs about 39 times faster than real time on eight CPU threads.

explain.tldr: A model that detects and timestamps non-verbal sounds in speech recordings like breaths, coughs, and background noise.
explain.plain: Speech-to-text systems capture words but lose everything else: the speaker's breaths, laughs, and coughs, plus background sounds like music or traffic. This paper describes a neural network model that listens to audio and identifies 54 different types of these sounds, pinpointing exactly when each one happens. The researchers trained it on seven different datasets with mismatched labeling systems, unified the labels, and combined real recordings with synthetic ones. The model catches about half of these events accurately and runs fast enough to process audio much quicker than real time.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this matters because it could preserve the expressive, human details in recordings—breaths, timing, room tone—that usually get lost when speech is transcribed. It could also help with podcast editing, music production with vocal samples, or any workflow where you need to know exactly when non-musical sounds occur in a track.

terms.meaning: A neural network that combines two types of pattern-recognition layers: one that looks at local details and one that understands relationships across longer stretches of audio.
A technique that matches a known transcript to an audio file to figure out exactly when each word (or in this case, sound) occurs.

Measures of accuracy that treat each sound type equally rather than favoring common ones; precision is how often the model is right when it makes a detection, recall is how many actual sounds it finds.

papers.title: Sonic-AMG: Streaming Human Motion Generation from Spatial Audio
papers.summary: Modeling human reactions to spatial audio requires understanding both what is heard and where it comes from. Prior work generates motion offline from complete acoustic and spatial input sequences. Humans, however, react to sounds without knowing what they will hear next. We present Sonic-AMG, to our knowledge the first framework for streaming human motion generation from spatial audio. The model encodes acoustic content and body-relative source geometry as separate tokens. Conditioned on these tokens, a causal transformer with a flow head generates continuous motion latents, from which a causal decoder reconstructs motion segments. Standard teacher-forced training derives motion histories and body-relative source locations from ground-truth motion, whereas streaming inference relies on generated motion for both, resulting in a training-inference mismatch. To reduce this history discrepancy, we introduce rehearsal training, which combines full-sequence teacher-forced supervision with supervised prediction along short autoregressive self-rollouts. To keep spatial conditioning consistent with generated motion, we propose spatial feedback, which recomputes body-relative source locations from generated root poses during both rehearsal training and inference. On SAM, Sonic-AMG achieves state-of-the-art FID and R-precision. It further supports real-time online generation of coherent reactions across sound events and source locations. Project page: https://jingchengni.com/sonic-amg/.

explain.tldr: A system that generates realistic human body movements in real-time while reacting to spatial audio from any direction.
explain.plain: When you hear a sound, you naturally react with body movements—turning toward it, swaying, gesturing. This paper tackles a tricky problem: generating these reactions as audio plays, without knowing what sound comes next. They built Sonic-AMG, which processes both what you hear (acoustic content) and where the sound comes from (spatial location), then predicts body motion continuously. The key innovation is 'rehearsal training'—a technique that helps the system learn to generate motion smoothly even when it's predicting its own movements rather than copying real ones, plus 'spatial feedback' that keeps the sound direction consistent with the generated body position.
explain.why: This matters for interactive music experiences, VR/AR applications, and avatar animation in music videos or games. It could help create more believable virtual performers or dancers that respond naturally to spatial audio in real-time, rather than pre-recorded choreography.

terms.meaning: sound that has a sense of direction and location around you, not just left-right stereo but full 3D positioning
a neural network that processes information in order, only looking at past data (not future), suitable for real-time streaming
metrics that measure how realistic and accurate the generated movements are compared to real human motion

papers.title: What Do Audio-Language Judges of Generated Music Listen For? Four Probes with Controls from Expert Ratings
papers.summary: Open audio-language models are used as judges of generated music: given a clip and its text prompt, the model rates the clip, and the judge is validated by how well its ratings correlate with expert ratings. The correlation does not show what the judge responds to: the music, the text prompt, or the way the question is asked. We propose four probes that test each of these, three of them read against a control computed from the human ratings: removing the audio, replacing the clip with another model's clip for the same prompt, swapping the order of two clips in pairwise judging, and rewording the instruction. We apply them to five open judges on all 2,748 clips of MusicEval, and the last two to the SongEval songs. Without audio, no judge exceeds what the prompt alone predicts from the human ratings, and for prompt alignment every judge falls below it. With audio, every judge follows the clip it hears when rating prompt alignment, two do when rating musical quality, and the strongest judge's quality score tracks the experts' alignment rating more than their quality rating. The pairwise verdicts of the four smaller judges follow the position of a clip in the pair (its slot) rather than its quality on both rating sets. For musical quality, rewording the instruction moves the correlation of most judges as much as changing the judge. MusicEval's prompt assignment bounds any prompt-only judge at the model level. We recommend reporting the four probes with every music judge.

explain.tldr: Researchers test what audio-language models actually listen to when rating generated music, finding they rely heavily on prompts and instructions rather than the audio itself.
explain.plain: When AI models judge generated music by comparing audio clips to text descriptions, we don't know if they're actually listening to the music or just reading the prompt. Researchers created four tests to figure this out: removing the audio entirely, swapping clips between prompts, changing the order of clips being compared, and rewording the instructions. They found that without audio, the models couldn't rate better than just reading the prompt alone, and most models were influenced more by how the question was asked than by what they actually heard.
explain.why: If you're using AI to evaluate your generated music or train music-generation systems, you need to know whether the AI is actually assessing your music or just pattern-matching on descriptions. This work shows current judges aren't reliable for that purpose, which matters for developing better music AI tools.

terms.meaning: AI systems trained to understand both sound and text, so they can answer questions about audio
how well a generated music clip matches what the text description asked for
a measure of how closely two sets of ratings match each other

papers.title: QC-MI-OVSEL: Benchmarking Query-Conditioned Multi-Instance Open-Vocabulary Sound Event Localization
papers.summary: We study query-conditioned multi-instance open-vocabulary sound event localization (QC-MI-OVSEL), where a system must recover all active physical sources matching a natural-language category query, including when the queried category is absent. We introduce the QC-MI-OVSEL benchmark, a 40,000-scene first-order Ambisonics benchmark with 80,000 balanced present/absent query views over 83 classes, including 17 novel classes excluded from training and development. Each frame is annotated with the activity and 3-D direction of every query-matching source, with up to three simultaneous targets. We further propose Q-RSet, which uses query-conditioned source slots and responsibility-based evidence aggregation for source-set prediction. Experiments show improved source recovery, localization recall, cardinality estimation, exact-set recovery, and absent-query suppression over complementary baselines. Analysis indicates that novel categories, paraphrased queries, and higher source multiplicity mainly impair source discovery and set completion, while directional accuracy remains comparatively stable for successfully recovered sources.

explain.tldr: A benchmark and method for finding and locating multiple sound sources in 3D space based on natural-language descriptions.
explain.plain: The paper tackles a specific audio challenge: given a text description (like "dog barking"), find all instances of that sound in a recording, pinpoint their 3D locations, and know when the sound isn't present at all. They created a large dataset with 40,000 audio scenes annotated with sound locations and directions, including sounds the system has never encountered before. They also built a system called Q-RSet that performs better than existing approaches at finding multiple sources, estimating how many are active, and correctly saying "that sound isn't here" when appropriate.
explain.why: This matters for spatial audio production, immersive recording, and audio post-production tools. Musicians and producers working with surround sound or spatial audio could use this to automatically detect and locate specific instruments or sounds in a mix, or to verify what's actually in a recording.

terms.meaning: A spatial audio format that captures sound from all directions around a point, allowing 3D localization of where sounds come from
The system can recognize and work with sound categories it wasn't explicitly trained on, not just a fixed list
The system's behavior changes based on a text query or description you give it, rather than detecting everything at once

papers.title: LiveSynth: A Streaming Neural Synthesizer for Instrument Cloning and Text-to-Instrument
papers.summary: Recently, generative neural synthesizers have enabled zero-shot instrument cloning from reference recordings and timbre generation from text prompts. However, existing systems generate complete audio segments offline, precluding their use as playable instruments. We present LiveSynth, a streaming neural synthesizer with flexible timbre control and interactive generation capabilities, including zero-shot instrument cloning and text-to-instrument synthesis. A feedback-free causal Transformer conditioned on MIDI events and a CLAP timbre embedding outputs continuous audio latents at 100 Hz, which a causal variational autoencoder decodes into audio. Frame-wise timbre conditioning enables continuous timbre morphing, while MIDI-conditioning dropout enables autonomous continuation from a performed prefix. On the NSynth and Slakh datasets, LiveSynth achieved timbre similarity and spectral reconstruction quality comparable to offline baselines. On an M3 MacBook Air, LiveSynth required 8.8 ms of computation per 10 ms audio frame (an RTF of 0.88) with 10 ms algorithmic latency, enabling real-time interaction with a performer.

explain.tldr: A real-time neural synthesizer that clones instruments from audio or text and plays interactively like a traditional synth.
explain.plain: Existing AI synthesizers generate complete audio files offline, so you can't play them like an instrument. LiveSynth solves this by processing audio in small chunks as you play, using MIDI input to control a neural model that generates sound in real time. It can mimic an instrument from a recording you give it, or create new timbres from text descriptions. The system runs fast enough on a laptop to respond to your playing with minimal delay.
explain.why: This bridges the gap between AI sound generation and live performance. Instead of rendering offline, you could use this as an actual playable instrument in a DAW or live setup, with the ability to morph between timbres or clone acoustic instruments on the fly.

terms.meaning: Processing audio in real time, one chunk at a time, without waiting for future data—like how a live microphone works, not like editing a finished recording
A learned representation of a sound's character (brightness, warmth, etc.) derived from text descriptions, allowing the model to understand timbre from language
A neural network that compresses audio into a compact code and can reconstruct it back, useful for efficient real-time generation

papers.title: Structural and Representational Agency in LLM-Driven Timbre Generation and Interpolation
papers.summary: Generative creative interfaces routinely report the user's position within a space of possibilities. Such displays imply that the quantities shown were measured from the artefact; in a growing class of systems they are instead predicted by a language model describing its own output, and the two are indistinguishable on screen. Most creative domains lack an agreed measurement against which such a self-report can be checked; audio admits one. In a measurement study of a working LLM-driven timbre interface, what a user can cause proves separable from what the interface reports. The first is exactly characterisable: the reachable set is a zonotope whose dimension increases by one per sound placed, so the space the model may act within is demonstrably the user's own. The second is inaccurate. The displayed position differs from measurement by approximately three times the width of that region, and the error has two independent sources: model-predicted coordinates, whose accuracy varies twofold between the two models evaluated, and the interpolation step, which arises from combining synthesiser parameters and is unaffected by model quality. End to end, 26 of 36 refinement instructions produced no perceptible change, and under the weaker model the facility performed no action while reporting convergence. Effective agency (what a user can cause) and epistemic agency (whether they can know it) are therefore separable and independently engineered: structurally enforced constraints survive model failure, whereas guarantees resting on the model's own report do not. The failure mode that remains is silence presented as success. We close with a short protocol for building and auditing such displays.

explain.tldr: LLM-based timbre interfaces show users a position in sound-space that often doesn't match what actually happens or what the model predicts.
explain.plain: When you use an AI-driven tool to explore and blend different timbres (instrument sounds), the interface typically shows you where you are in a space of possibilities. This paper measured a real system and found two problems: the displayed position was often wrong, and many user adjustments produced no actual sound change while the interface claimed success. The researchers discovered that what you can actually do (the real sounds reachable) is separate from what the system reports you're doing. The real reachable space is mathematically precise, but the display's accuracy depends on both the AI model's predictions and how sounds are blended together.
explain.why: If you're using or building AI tools for sound design, this matters because it shows the gap between what the interface tells you and what's really happening. Understanding this separation helps creators know when they actually have control versus when they're seeing false feedback, and it suggests ways to build more honest and reliable creative tools.

terms.meaning: A mathematical shape describing all the possible sounds you can reach by combining different timbres; it grows larger as you add more reference sounds
Whether you can actually know and understand what's happening when you use the tool
The process of blending between two sounds or settings to create intermediate results

papers.title: How Much Audio Is Left In An Embedding? An Inversion Audit Of Audio Encoders
papers.summary: Pretrained audio encoders are reused for downstream tasks that are often unknown when the encoder is trained, so their usefulness depends partly on which signal properties survive the pretext objective. We study this retained information through paired source reconstruction. Using a shared Stable Audio Open latent diffusion decoder, we reconstruct five-second, 44.1-kHz stereo music from frozen representations produced by supervised classifiers (VGGish, ConvNeXt), an audio-text contrastive model (CLAP), and a waveform-reconstruction model (EnCodec). These objectives impose different pressures to preserve source detail, while their exposed interfaces vary substantially in temporal and spectral resolution. Evaluating on the Million Song Dataset (MSD), we find clear differences in reconstructability across encoder families, while within encoder comparisons show improved recovery when finer temporal or spectral structure is exposed. Even compressed task oriented embeddings support reconstructions that preserve measurable source specificity and high level musical content.

explain.tldr: Researchers test how much original audio information survives in compressed representations from different audio encoders.
explain.plain: When audio encoders are trained for one task (like identifying instruments), they're often reused for completely different purposes later. This study asks: how much of the original audio information actually survives this compression? The researchers took five different audio encoders—some trained to classify sounds, one trained to match audio with text descriptions, and one trained to reconstruct waveforms—and tried to rebuild the original music from their compressed outputs using a shared decoder. They found that different encoders preserve different amounts of detail, and encoders that expose finer timing or frequency information tend to preserve more of the original audio.
explain.why: If you're using pretrained audio models for music production, analysis, or AI-assisted tools, this tells you what information is actually preserved versus lost in those compressed representations. It helps you understand the tradeoffs: some encoders might be better for tasks needing fine detail, while others might be sufficient for higher-level musical understanding.

terms.meaning: a compressed numerical representation of audio that captures its essential features in a smaller form
a tool that reconstructs audio from compressed representations by gradually refining random noise into realistic sound
the original training task an encoder was designed for (like classification or matching audio to text)

papers.title: STEMMA: Song-to-Stem Multi-Audio Reasoning for Large Audio Language Models
papers.summary: Music understanding often requires comparing excerpts and reasoning about relationships among songs, sections, and stems. However, existing large audio-language models (LALMs) and music question-answering datasets typically operate on single recordings or compare independently sampled tracks with no known production relationship. We introduce STEMMA, a multi-audio music question-answering framework built around production provenance: whether excerpts originate from the same track or section, and which stems belong to which mixtures. Because such relations are sparse under conventional audio-first sampling, STEMMA adopts a relation-first construction strategy: it first specifies a target relation and then queries the catalog for excerpts that satisfy it and hard negatives that do not. Labels are determined directly from catalog provenance rather than generated by a language model from metadata. We build STEMMA-Bench for evaluation and a track-disjoint training set, STEMMA-Instruct. Fine-tuning two LALMs on STEMMA-Instruct improves multi-audio reasoning, with the largest gains on structural relations directly determined by the catalog, while preserving single-audio music understanding.

explain.tldr: A framework teaching AI models to understand relationships between different parts of songs by comparing stems and sections.
explain.plain: Music understanding often requires knowing how different parts relate—like which vocals belong to which mix, or which sections come from the same song. Existing AI music models struggle with this because they typically look at single recordings in isolation. This paper introduces STEMMA, which builds training data by deliberately selecting related audio excerpts (like different stems from the same track) and comparing them. The researchers tested their approach on two existing AI models and found it improved their ability to reason about these relationships, especially for structural connections, without hurting their ability to understand individual recordings.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this matters because AI tools that understand production relationships could better assist with remixing, stem separation, arrangement analysis, or music production workflows where knowing which elements belong together is crucial.

terms.meaning: Individual audio tracks that make up a song, like separate vocal, drum, or guitar recordings that get mixed together
AI systems trained to understand and reason about audio content, similar to how language models understand text
Information about where audio came from and how it was created—like which stems were mixed to make a final track

papers.title: CloudEar: Integrating Perceptual, Diagnostic, and Cross-Modal Evidence for Music Evaluation
papers.summary: Evaluating generated music requires modeling perceptual quality, technical audio quality, and prompt alignment. Existing methods often overlook signal-level defects, produce compressed quality scores, and miss fine-grained musical attributes in text prompts. We propose CloudEar, a pairwise framework for evaluating musicality and prompt alignment. It comprises three components: i) a Perceptual Expert for song-quality assessment; ii) a Diagnostic Expert for learned and signal-level quality analysis; and iii) a Cross-modal Expert for prompt-song alignment based on musical attributes. Experiments show that CloudEar outperforms the compared baselines in pairwise preference accuracy and score correlation.

explain.tldr: A system that evaluates AI-generated music by checking sound quality, technical problems, and how well it matches the original request.
explain.plain: When AI generates music from a text description, you need a way to judge if it's good. CloudEar does this by looking at three things: how the music sounds to human ears, whether there are technical audio problems, and whether the generated music actually matches what was asked for. The system compares two pieces of music against each other to decide which is better, and tests show it's more accurate than existing evaluation methods.
explain.why: If you're using AI tools to generate music, you need reliable ways to judge the results without listening to everything yourself. This matters for producers testing music generation tools and for researchers building better AI music systems.

terms.meaning: how often the system correctly picks the better song when comparing two options side-by-side
technical problems in the raw audio itself, like clicks, distortion, or dropout
connecting information from different types of input—here, matching text descriptions to actual audio

papers.title: Reference-Free Singing Pitch Correction via Music-Constrained Sequence Editing
papers.summary: Existing singing pitch correction approaches rely on target melodies or accompaniment tracks, which may be unavailable in practice. We formulate reference-free singing pitch correction as a music-constrained sequence editing task that determines whether and how each note should be corrected from the input performance alone. A pretrained symbolic music encoder with lightweight singing-domain adapters produces contextual representations of the singing MIDI. Based on these representations, two lightweight correction heads jointly model correction necessity and signed pitch modification through a factorized pitch-editing distribution. An input-dependent tonal prior derived from the estimated key distribution then reranks the candidate offsets, favoring tonally compatible corrections without target melodies or ground-truth key annotations. Experiments on real paired amateur and professional singing recordings show that the method improves note-level pitch accuracy from 73.25 to 83.43, outperforming a context-based baseline by 3.99 percentage points while balancing error correction and preservation of correctly performed notes.

explain.tldr: A system that fixes off-pitch singing notes without needing a reference melody or accompaniment track.
explain.plain: Singing pitch correction usually requires either a target melody to match or an accompaniment track to reference. This paper proposes a different approach: analyze the singer's performance alone to decide which notes need fixing and by how much. The system uses a pretrained music model to understand the context of each note, then predicts both whether correction is needed and how much to adjust the pitch. It also uses the estimated musical key to favor corrections that sound musically appropriate. Testing on real amateur and professional recordings showed it improved pitch accuracy from 73% to 83%, and worked better than simpler baseline methods.
explain.why: This matters for musicians and producers because pitch correction is often needed in recording, but you don't always have a clean reference track available—especially when recording rough demos, live takes, or when working with limited resources. A tool that can intelligently fix pitch from the vocal alone could make the correction process faster and more accessible.

terms.meaning: A machine learning model pretrained to understand music represented as discrete notes and timing (like MIDI), rather than audio waveforms
A musical constraint based on the estimated key of the song, used to guide corrections toward notes that fit the harmonic context
A statistical model that separately predicts two things: whether a note needs correction, and if so, by how many cents (hundredths of a semitone) to shift it

papers.title: SepGen: Multi-Stem Audio-Video Separation and Generation in a Single Model
papers.summary: A 4D audio-visual scene comprises a video, the dynamic geometry it depicts, and the sound sources that populate it, each with its own position and trajectory. Rendering such a scene from a novel viewpoint requires that every source be available as an individual waveform, so that it can be localized in the scene and propagated to the observer before the signals are mixed. Joint audio-video generators can synthesize the video and its soundtrack, but the soundtrack is emitted as a single audio-mix in which the sources are not individually accessible. We present SepGen, which extends a pretrained audio-video generator to emit the video, the mixed soundtrack, and one waveform per captioned source in one joint sampling run. SepGen supports two complementary modes: generation and separation. In generation mode, each source caption specifies what its stem contains. A two-speaker dialogue, for example, comes out as one stem per speaker in the original turn order. In separation mode, the input audio-mix remains clean while the captions specify what to extract, so the model can decompose a recording from a free-text description. We evaluate generation on scenes synthesized from text, and separation on scenes rendered by other generators and on real recordings of speech, music, and sound effects. Given an audio-mix and captions that carry the spoken lines, SepGen outperforms language-conditioned separators, most clearly on speech, and it keeps the lead when the lines are removed from the captions. Code, checkpoints, and datasets are available at https://sepgen.github.io/

explain.tldr: A model that separates audio into individual stems or generates them from descriptions, using video and text captions.
explain.plain: When you have a video with multiple sound sources (like dialogue, music, and effects all mixed together), it's hard to work with each sound separately. SepGen takes a trained audio-video model and extends it to output not just the mixed soundtrack, but also individual audio stems—one for each sound source. It works two ways: you can feed it a mixed recording and tell it what to extract (separation mode), or you can describe what sounds you want and it generates them separately (generation mode). The researchers tested it on speech, music, and sound effects, and found it works better than existing methods, especially for separating dialogue.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this means better tools for remixing videos, extracting individual instruments or voices from recordings, or creating new soundtracks where you can control each element's position and level independently.

terms.meaning: Individual audio tracks or waveforms for separate sound sources (like one track for vocals, one for drums, etc.)
A video along with its associated sounds, treated as a unified 3D space where sounds have positions and movements
A model that takes written or spoken instructions to control what it does

papers.title: Breaking the Group Size Barrier: Parameter-Efficient Group Dance Generation with Chain-of-Dancers
papers.summary: Group dance generation aims to synthesize coordinated multi-dancer choreography from music, with broad applications in animation and interactive content creation. This task requires modeling dense inter-person dependencies to ensure spatial coordination, while naturally preserving individual dancer identities. Existing approaches model all dancers jointly with end-to-end transformers, which tie the architecture to a fixed group size and entangle per-dancer identities across frames. We propose ChainDance, a scalable framework that reformulates group dance generation as a Chain-of-Dancers: a sequential decomposition over per-dancer conditional distributions, allowing a single model to scale across variable group sizes without retraining and naturally preserving per-dancer identity. Built on a frozen single-dancer diffusion backbone, ChainDance introduces two lightweight modules: a Role-Aware Text Encoder (RATE) for per-dancer semantic conditioning, and a Group-Aware Motion Encoder (GAME) that aggregates previously generated dancers via a distance-weighted graph convolutional network, and incorporates a training-free noise optimization procedure at inference time to enforce global spatial coherence. Experiments on AIOZ-GDance demonstrate that ChainDance achieves state-of-the-art motion quality and group coordination while structurally preserving per-dancer identity, with $3$-$4\times$ fewer parameters and requiring $3$-$6\times$ less training time compared to prior approaches.

explain.tldr: A system that generates coordinated group dances from music that works with any number of dancers without retraining.
explain.plain: Group dance generation creates choreography for multiple dancers moving together to music. The challenge is keeping dancers coordinated in space while maintaining each dancer's unique style. Instead of treating all dancers as one big problem, this approach generates dancers one at a time in sequence, where each new dancer sees what the previous ones did. The system uses a smaller, pre-trained single-dancer model as its foundation and adds lightweight components to handle group coordination and per-dancer instructions. Tests show it produces good results with fewer parameters and faster training than existing methods.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this matters because it could enable easier creation of synchronized group choreography for music videos, games, or live performance visuals—without needing to retrain models for different group sizes.

terms.meaning: A pre-trained foundational model that generates motion step-by-step by gradually refining random noise into realistic movement
A neural network that processes relationships between connected elements (here, dancers) by treating them as nodes in a graph
Breaking down group dance generation into a sequence where each dancer is generated one after another, conditioning on previously generated dancers

papers.title: Randomized Scores and Diverse Timbres: Augmenting Automatic Music Transcription with Online-Generated Data
papers.summary: Automatic music transcription (AMT) is limited by the scarcity of audio recordings paired with precise symbolic annotations. Synthetic data can provide supervision at scale, but it remains unclear whether effective transfer depends on realistic score structure or broad timbral coverage. We study these factors separately through an online sampler--renderer pipeline. A unified corruption sampler ranges from unmodified MIDI clips through partial corruption to deeply randomized note-event distributions. The renderer converts these events to audio while independently controlling instrument and timbral coverage. A fixed transcription model is trained jointly on offline recordings and newly rendered examples. Controlled ablations reveal an asymmetry between the two factors: moderate corruption of the note-event distribution does not impair transfer and can improve it, whereas broader renderer-side timbral support consistently improves out-of-domain generalization under a fixed note-event distribution. Finally, online-rendered examples complement real and existing synthetic data in a strong combined-data regime. These results suggest that synthetic AMT data should prioritize coverage of note-level attributes and their timbral realizations over realistic joint score structure.

explain.tldr: Synthetic training data helps music transcription more through diverse instrument sounds than realistic note patterns.
explain.plain: Automatic music transcription—converting audio to sheet music—struggles because there aren't enough recordings paired with accurate written scores. The researchers created synthetic training data by generating audio from MIDI in two ways: they either kept note patterns realistic or scrambled them, and they varied which instruments and sounds were used. They found that scrambling note patterns didn't hurt the transcription model's performance, but using many different instrument sounds consistently made it work better on unfamiliar music. This suggests that for synthetic training data, variety in how notes sound matters more than having perfectly realistic musical structure.
