explain.why: If transcription software trains better on diverse timbres than realistic scores, it means producers and musicians could improve transcription tools by generating training data that covers many instrument sounds—potentially making automatic transcription more reliable across different musical styles and instruments.

terms.meaning: Software that listens to audio and converts it into written musical notation or MIDI data
Artificially generated training examples (in this case, audio created from MIDI) rather than real recordings
The characteristic color or quality of a sound—what makes a trumpet sound different from a violin playing the same note

papers.title: MiDashengLM-Spatial: Unifying General Audio Understanding and Spatial Awareness
papers.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) have achieved strong performance in general audio understanding, yet most are designed for monaural input and discard the inter-channel cues essential for spatial perception. In contrast, existing spatial audio-language models are purpose-built for spatial tasks and fail to capitalize on the general understanding capabilities of monaural LALMs. We present MiDashengLM-Spatial, the first open-source end-to-end unified audio-language model, to our knowledge, which supports both general audio understanding and spatial awareness within a single architecture. It extends MiDashengLM with a spatial audio encoder, Spatial-Dasheng, integrated through a hierarchical semantic-to-spatial conditioning module that injects intermediate semantic representations into the spatial branch at multiple depths while preserving the original semantic pathway. To provide spatial audio-language supervision at scale, we develop a data synthesis pipeline that renders diverse spatial acoustic scenes with scene-level spatial descriptions and question-answer pairs. Experiments show that Spatial-Dasheng achieves strong performance on sound event localization and detection in real-world scenes, and that MiDashengLM-Spatial substantially outperforms existing LALMs on spatial understanding and reasoning benchmarks. Meanwhile, it remains competitive with state-of-the-art 8B-scale LALMs on diverse monaural benchmarks, demonstrating that spatial awareness can be acquired without compromising general audio understanding. The source code and model checkpoint are available at https://github.com/xiaomi-research/midashenglm-spatial and https://huggingface.co/mispeech/midashenglm-spatial.

explain.tldr: A unified audio AI model that understands both general sounds and spatial audio cues from multi-channel recordings.
explain.plain: Most audio AI models work with single-channel recordings and miss spatial information—where sounds come from in 3D space. This paper presents a model that combines general audio understanding with spatial awareness by adding a specialized spatial audio processor to an existing audio-language model. They created training data with spatial sound scenes and descriptions, and showed their model can locate sounds in space while staying competitive at general audio tasks.
explain.why: For musicians and producers working with spatial audio, immersive mixes, or spatial recording formats, this means AI tools could better understand and describe where sounds are positioned—useful for mixing feedback, spatial audio analysis, or creative applications.

terms.meaning: An AI system trained to understand audio recordings and respond to text questions or descriptions about them, similar to how image-language models work with pictures.
Differences between audio channels (like left and right speakers) that tell you where a sound is located in space.
Identifying what sounds are present in a recording and pinpointing where each one is coming from spatially.

papers.title: AutoSynth: Learning to Generate Editable Synthesizer Programs from Audio and Text
papers.summary: Audio generation models can translate natural-language descriptions into sound, but their outputs are typically waveforms. Their audio quality is constrained by audio compression, and their outputs do not readily support direct edits to notes, timbral parameters, or modulation relationships. We present AutoSynth, which represents MIDI performance events, fixed synthesizer parameters, and variable-length modulation routes as a unified sequence for a synthesizer, and learns their dependencies with an audio-conditioned autoregressive model. A single model supports both tasks. Given reference audio, the model directly predicts a synthesizer program; given text, it uses a pretrained audio generation model and converts the generated audio into a program. Training consists of two stages: supervised learning on large-scale audio-program pairs automatically constructed from a small set of native presets, followed by group-relative policy optimization with a mixed reward combining semantic similarity, pitch-related features, acoustic similarity, and sound usefulness. The pipeline requires neither paired text-target-program annotations nor a differentiable synthesizer. Experiments show that AutoSynth produces complete, editable synthesizer programs and achieves competitive results in both synthesizer inversion and text-driven generation. Audio demos and source code are available at https://auto-synth.github.io/.

explain.tldr: A system that converts audio or text descriptions into editable synthesizer programs instead of just waveforms.
explain.plain: Most AI music tools turn text or audio into sound waves you can't easily edit. AutoSynth instead creates complete synthesizer settings—including notes, knob positions, and modulation paths—that you can tweak afterward. It learns by studying pairs of audio and synthesizer programs, then gets refined through a training process that rewards programs that sound good and match what was requested. The result is editable, controllable synthesizer patches rather than locked-in audio files.
explain.why: This matters because it gives you back creative control. Instead of accepting whatever an AI generates, you get a synthesizer program you can adjust individual parameters, change notes, or modify how controls interact—just like programming a synth yourself.

terms.meaning: An AI that predicts one piece of information at a time in sequence, using what it predicted before to inform the next prediction
The process of figuring out what synthesizer settings and parameters would produce a given sound
The connections that let one synthesizer control move another (like an LFO controlling filter cutoff)

papers.title: Listen-to-Reason: Listen with Experts, Retrieve over a Graph, Reason with LLMs
papers.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) fuse an audio encoder into a large language model (LLM) through multi-stage training. This coupling means that a new domain or a stronger LLM requires retraining, and their answers cannot be traced to what the model heard: a chain-of-thought is a post-hoc account. We propose Listen-to-Reason (L2R), an interpretable-by-design pipeline that passes audio to the LLM through an explicit, human-readable tree: small heads on frozen expert encoders map each chunk of a clip to semantically meaningful nodes on the tree (for speech, music and environmental sound), and a frozen text-only LLM answers from these nodes and an ASR transcript without hearing the clip. Every answer can therefore be traced to the nodes and transcript it read, and the nodes are causal: replacing the deciding node with a distractor overturns 78% of correct answers on SAKURA. With a 7B reader, L2R outperforms all LALMs we compare against on SAKURA and trails them by 6-12 points on MMAU and MMAR, despite training about 1,400x fewer parameters on orders of magnitude less audio data. However, because any LLM can serve as the reader, we show that a stronger reader narrows this gap without retraining any audio component. A new domain is added with one small head: with five labelled clips per species, it outperforms QLoRA fine-tuning of an LALM on the same clips by 13-26 points.

explain.tldr: A system that makes audio AI interpretable by routing sound through labeled semantic nodes before answering questions.
explain.plain: Current audio-language models fuse audio processing directly into large language models, making it hard to understand what the AI actually heard or to adapt them to new domains. This paper proposes Listen-to-Reason, which instead maps audio chunks to human-readable semantic categories (like "speech," "drums," "traffic") organized in a tree structure, then feeds those labels plus a transcript to the language model. This way, every answer can be traced back to specific audio features the model identified, and you can verify the model's reasoning by swapping out nodes and seeing if answers change. The system works well on some benchmarks and can adapt to new audio domains (like bird species) with just a few labeled examples.
explain.why: Musicians and producers could benefit from AI tools that explain their decisions transparently—knowing *why* a system classified a sound or made a suggestion, rather than getting a black-box answer. This approach also makes it easier to customize AI for specific instruments, genres, or sound libraries without retraining everything from scratch.

terms.meaning: An AI system that combines audio processing with a language model, trained together so the audio encoder and text model are tightly integrated.
An audio processing component that is not updated during training; it stays fixed so you don't need to retrain it when switching to a new language model or domain.

A step-by-step explanation of how an AI arrived at an answer; here, the authors note that traditional models generate these explanations after the fact, whereas their system's reasoning is built into the structure.

papers.title: SAVU-BENCH: A Real-World Benchmark for Spatial Audio-Visual Understanding
papers.summary: Spatial audio-visual understanding requires models to recognize not only what is present, but also where events occur and how they relate across modalities. Existing benchmarks often rely on simulated scenes, evaluate isolated spatial skills, and provide limited diagnostic insight into failure modes. We introduce SAVU-Bench, a real-world benchmark that systematically evaluates spatial audio-visual understanding across three capability levels and seven evaluation tasks. We further introduce SAVU-Diag, a scene-linked diagnostic set that decomposes reasoning questions into their prerequisite grounding and alignment sub-tasks. Evaluation of 12 representative models on SAVU-Bench reveals that while visual spatial grounding is relatively mature, spatial perception involving audio remains a primary bottleneck. SAVU-Diag further demonstrates that most reasoning errors co-occur with failures on these prerequisite tasks, though reasoning gaps persist even when prerequisites are correctly resolved. Motivated by these findings, we introduce SAVU-EA, a training-free evidence-augmented baseline that makes spatial cues more explicit. While SAVU-EA substantially improves spatial grounding and joint matching, high-level spatial reasoning remains challenging. Our findings highlight the urgent need for both robust spatial audio perception and deeper integration of cross-modal spatial relations.

explain.tldr: A benchmark testing how well AI models understand where sounds and visuals occur together in real scenes.
explain.plain: When you watch a video, you naturally understand not just what you see and hear, but where sounds are coming from and how they match what's on screen. This paper creates a test called SAVU-Bench to measure how well AI models do this. They tested 12 different models and found that while visual location-tracking works okay, understanding where sounds come from is much harder. They also discovered that when models fail at complex questions, it's often because they struggle with basic audio-spatial tasks first.
explain.why: For musicians and producers working with spatial audio (like surround sound or immersive mixes), this research shows where AI tools currently struggle—particularly in connecting audio locations to visual content. Understanding these limitations matters if you're considering AI for soundtrack creation, spatial mixing assistance, or interactive audio-visual projects.

terms.meaning: recognizing not just what sounds and images are present, but where they're located in space and how they relate to each other
involving multiple senses or input types together (in this case, sound and vision working together)
connecting abstract concepts or events to specific locations or objects in a scene

papers.title: MIRA: A Musical Intent Refinement Agent for Aligning Text-to-Music Generation with User Intent
papers.summary: Text-to-music systems produce increasingly convincing audio, yet evaluation reveals little about whether the result matches user intent. A global text-audio relevance score can overlook the implicit intent in underspecified prompts and mask failures in specific requirements, such as instrumentation, structure, rhythm, or mood progression. To bridge this gap, we formulate text-to-music intent alignment as satisfying a per-request rubric of independently verifiable items covering both a request's explicit requirements and its implied musical intent. Scoring items individually makes evaluation diagnostic by intent source and musical dimension, rather than a single opaque score. We instantiate this as MuRA-Bench, a benchmark of real-world platform requests curated by music experts. We further propose MIRA (Musical Intent Refinement Agent), a test-time agent that first grounds a request's intent into rubrics, then searches over prompt revisions for a black-box generator under a bounded budget, iteratively generating music, verifying it against the rubrics, and using this feedback to guide a trajectory-aware tree search. Experiments across open-source and commercial backends show that MIRA improves intent alignment, enabling an open-source generator to achieve performance comparable to representative commercial systems (e.g. Suno and Mureka). Project page: https://mirareview.github.io/.

explain.tldr: A system that refines text prompts for music generation to better match what users actually want.
explain.plain: When you describe music you want in words, AI music generators don't always create what you had in mind—a single score can't tell you if it failed on instrumentation, rhythm, mood, or something else. This paper breaks down evaluation into specific musical dimensions (like "does it have the right instruments?" and "does the mood progress as intended?"). They built MIRA, an agent that takes your music request, converts it into a checklist of requirements, then automatically rewrites your prompt multiple times, generates music for each version, checks it against the checklist, and keeps refining until it finds a better match. Tests show this helps open-source music generators perform closer to commercial systems like Suno.
explain.why: If you use AI to generate music from text descriptions, this work could help you get results that actually match your vision instead of settling for close-enough. It also shows how to evaluate whether AI music tools are really doing what you ask.

terms.meaning: AI systems that create music audio based on written descriptions or prompts
how well the generated output matches what the user actually wanted
an algorithm that explores different options (like prompt variations) systematically to find the best one

papers.title: Toward Part-Aware Choral Transcription with singing voice assignment
papers.summary: Single-instrument automatic music transcription (AMT) has advanced substantially, yet choral applications require soprano, alto, tenor, and bass (SATB) to be transcribed as separate parts. Recent note-level choral AMT instead produces a single merged note track, limiting rehearsal, education, and score reconstruction. To address this limitation, we introduce Part-aware Choral Transcription (PawCT), to our knowledge the first end-to-end neural framework that identifies active SATB parts from choral audio and transcribes each into a separate note-level track. PawCT combines part-specific onset, offset, and frame prediction with part-presence estimation, union-level supervision, and structured training targets using a range prior (RP) based on SATB pitch ranges and its ordered-continuity (OC) extension, which adds within-part melodic continuity and cross-part pitch ordering. On YouChorale, PawCT-RP-OC achieves a macro part-aware note F1 of 0.225 at a 50-ms onset tolerance, outperforming an adapted choral baseline (0.165) by 36.4% relative and a two-stage post-hoc assignment pipeline (0.175). Its part-agnostic variant, PagCT, achieves a 50-ms onset F1 of 0.382, compared with 0.237 for the previous state-of-the-art choral AMT model. Cross-dataset evaluations on CSD and Cantoria further assess performance under dataset shift. These results demonstrate the benefit of jointly modeling note transcription and vocal-part assignment. Code and demos are available at https://hanyu-meng.github.io/Paw_Choral_AMT_Demo/.

explain.tldr: A neural system that transcribes choral music into separate soprano, alto, tenor, and bass note tracks from audio.
explain.plain: Existing music transcription systems struggle with choral music because they produce a single merged note track instead of separating the four vocal parts. This paper presents PawCT, a neural network designed to listen to choral audio, identify which vocal parts are singing, and write out the notes for each part separately. The system uses knowledge about typical pitch ranges for each voice type and expects parts to move smoothly and stay in their proper ranges. Testing shows it outperforms previous approaches at this task.
explain.why: For choral musicians and educators, having separate transcriptions of each vocal part makes it easier to learn arrangements, create sheet music, and rehearse individual lines. This could speed up the process of turning recordings into usable scores.

terms.meaning: software that listens to audio and converts it into written musical notes
the moment a note starts (onset) and stops (offset) in time
a measurement of accuracy that balances how many correct notes were found versus false alarms

papers.title: Direction-preserving Spatial Audio Signal Enhancement in The Spherical Harmonic Domain
papers.summary: Spatial audio signal enhancement (SASE) aims to separate a desired soundfield from interference and noise while preserving its spatial cues. However, existing algorithms pay limited attention to preserving the spatial cues of the residual interference, which reduces their effectiveness in practical applications. In this paper, we propose a direction-preserving SASE algorithm based on multi-output beamforming. The proposed algorithm extracts the desired soundfield while preserving the spatial cues of both the desired soundfield and the residual interference soundfield. The simulation study shows that the proposed algorithm achieves performance comparable to the existing SASE algorithm in terms of estimation error, while it better preserves the spatial cues of the residual interference within a region of interest, in a noisy and reverberant environment.

explain.tldr: A method to clean up spatial audio recordings while keeping directional information about both desired sounds and remaining noise.
explain.plain: When recording spatial audio (like immersive or surround sound), you want to isolate the main sound while removing interference and noise. Most existing methods focus only on preserving where the desired sound comes from, but ignore where the unwanted sounds are coming from. This paper proposes a new approach using multi-output beamforming that keeps directional cues for both the desired sound and the leftover interference. Tests show it performs as well as existing methods at reducing errors while better maintaining spatial information about the remaining noise.
explain.why: For immersive audio production and spatial recording, knowing where sounds come from is as important as how loud they are. This technique could improve how natural and realistic cleaned-up spatial recordings sound, since listeners can still perceive where background noise is coming from rather than it sounding artificially removed.

terms.meaning: A mathematical way to represent spatial audio that describes sound coming from all directions around a listener, like a 360-degree recording.
A technique using multiple microphones to focus on sounds from a specific direction while rejecting sounds from other directions.
The information in audio that tells you where a sound is coming from in 3D space.

papers.title: Tracing Inputs, Verifying Outputs: Validating Attribution in Music Generation
papers.summary: How can we verify whose music contributed to an AI-generated output? This paper demonstrates how input-based attribution can provide verifiable evidence of which audio sources were used in a generation and whether they shaped the output. To do so, we condition the generation solely on audio without any text input, then trace the inputs behind each output, and establish their musical effect. In prompt adherence tests and controlled input swaps, the stems generated by our generator, MixAudio, follow the prompt audio in timbre and the context audio in harmony. Yet these outputs may still reproduce training data not supplied as inputs. We therefore audit memorization with our musical version identification model, musicDNA, and find few reproductions outside the input records. On human-judged cases within the flagged pool, it achieves higher precision and recall than the other tested memorization detectors. The two evaluations suggest that input records and output analysis provide complementary evidence for attribution, on which rights-holder reporting and compensation can draw as the AI music economy takes shape. Audio examples are available at https://neutune.github.io/attr2027demo/

explain.tldr: A system that traces which audio sources influenced AI-generated music and detects if training data was reproduced.
explain.plain: When AI generates music, it's hard to know which input sounds actually shaped the output or whether the AI is just replaying something from its training data. This paper presents MixAudio, a music generator that works from audio prompts alone, and musicDNA, a tool that checks whether generated music matches known training recordings. They tested whether the generator actually follows the input audio's characteristics and whether it reproduces memorized training data. They found the generator does follow input audio in certain ways, and their detection tool catches reproductions better than other methods tested.
explain.why: As AI music tools become commercial, musicians and rights-holders need to know whether their work influenced generated outputs and whether they're owed credit or payment. This work provides a way to verify those connections and catch unauthorized reproductions of training material.

terms.meaning: identifying which source materials contributed to or influenced a generated output
when an AI system reproduces exact or near-exact copies of training data rather than creating something new
individual audio tracks or layers (like drums, bass, vocals) that can be mixed together

papers.title: CASM: Context-Aware Semi-Markov Post-Processor for Beat Tracking
papers.summary: In music beat tracking, model-predicted activations must be decoded into a discrete, musically coherent event sequence. Direct peak picking closely follows local evidence but can retain spurious peaks or miss weak beats. Dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs), a widely used structured post-processor, improve sequence consistency under predefined global tempo, meter, and transition constraints, but their behavior can depend strongly on these settings. We introduce CASM, a context-aware semi-Markov decoder that instead conditions its temporal constraint on local activation evidence. CASM also accounts for ambiguity among competing periodic interpretations, including half- and double-tempo alternatives. Deterministic safeguards prevent implausible outputs and preserve beat-downbeat consistency. Applied to fixed activations from three neural beat trackers (BeatThis, MSCNN, and TCN), CASM improves temporal continuity while preserving event-level F1 across the GTZAN and SMC datasets, without backbone retraining or dataset-specific retuning. Further analysis shows that CASM is less sensitive than the DBN baseline to the composition of the calibration data.

explain.tldr: A smarter post-processor that converts beat-tracking predictions into musically sensible beat sequences without needing manual tuning.
explain.plain: Beat tracking systems predict where beats occur in music, but their raw predictions often include mistakes—missed weak beats or false peaks. Current methods use fixed rules about tempo and meter to clean up these predictions, but those rules need careful tuning for different music. This paper introduces CASM, which adapts its rules based on what the prediction actually looks like, and also considers whether the beat might be at half or double speed. When tested on three different beat trackers, CASM produced more consistent beat sequences while maintaining accuracy, and worked better across different types of music without needing retuning.
explain.why: Better beat tracking helps music production tools, DJ software, and music analysis systems work more reliably. If a beat tracker can produce cleaner, more musically coherent output automatically, it makes these tools more practical and requires less manual correction by users.

terms.meaning: A method that predicts sequences of events (like beats) while allowing flexible timing between them, rather than assuming fixed intervals
The raw numerical predictions from a neural network showing how likely a beat occurs at each moment in time
A statistical model that enforces rules about how sequences should behave over time, like maintaining a steady tempo

papers.title: Towards AI-Generated Music Plagiarism Detection as a Version Identification Problem
papers.summary: The rapid expansion of text-to-music generative models challenges traditional paradigms of music creation and intellectual property. Plagiarism in this context is rarely an absolute mathematical binary, but an ambiguous threshold negotiated over harmonic structure, melodic contours, or overall perceived stylistic character. In this work, we test the transferability of state-of-the-art music version identification architectures from the human-to-human cover domain to the human-to-AI plagiarism setting. To evaluate this task, we introduce COPYCAT, a benchmark derived from real-world plagiarism cases and extended through generative re-synthesis and digital signal processing obfuscations, yielding 350,654 evaluation pairs. We show that scalar distance thresholding collapses under generative re-synthesis, while a supervised framework leveraging coordinate-wise embedding shifts recovers the dispersed plagiarism signal, raising overall $F_{0.5}$ from $0.612$ to $0.803$.

explain.tldr: Researchers adapt music cover-detection technology to spot AI-generated songs that plagiarize human compositions.
explain.plain: As AI music generators become more common, detecting plagiarism gets harder—it's not always a clear yes-or-no, but depends on similarities in harmony, melody, and style. The researchers tested whether existing systems that identify human cover songs could work for spotting AI plagiarism. They built a large test dataset called COPYCAT using real plagiarism cases and created variations of songs using AI re-synthesis and audio processing tricks. Simple similarity matching failed, but a more sophisticated machine-learning approach that tracks how embeddings shift between songs worked much better, improving detection accuracy significantly.
explain.why: As AI music tools become mainstream, musicians and rights holders need better ways to protect original work and detect unauthorized copies. This research shows a path toward practical plagiarism detection that could help enforce intellectual property in an AI-generated music landscape.

terms.meaning: automatically recognizing when two songs are the same piece despite differences in performance, arrangement, or production
a numerical representation of a song's characteristics that a machine-learning model learns to create, useful for comparing songs
intentional changes to audio (like pitch-shifting or filtering) that disguise the original while keeping core elements recognizable

papers.title: WorldSonus: Bringing Sound to Worlds
papers.summary: Recent advances in world models have enabled increasingly realistic visual synthesis. However, these generated environments remain largely silent. Bringing sound to world models poses three core challenges: real-time generation to keep pace with interactive video streams, interactive control to respond to mid-stream sound instructions, and spatially aligned stereo to reflect scene geometry and camera motion. To address these demands, we introduce WorldSonus, an interactive video-to-audio framework designed for real-time spatial sound synthesis in world models. For real-time generation, WorldSonus employs a streaming causal autoregressive diffusion architecture that synthesizes audio chunks at a low real-time factor (RTF) of 0.41. For interactive control, we incorporate an audio-centric captioning pipeline with chunk-indexed prompt scheduling, enabling dynamic manipulation of sound events during generation. For spatial alignment, we leverage high-quality stereo supervision curated from diverse stereo and ambisonic data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that while tailored for world models, WorldSonus generalizes effectively to open-domain video-to-audio benchmarks, matching or outperforming state-of-the-art bidirectional models in both acoustic quality and spatial alignment. Project page: https://noizai.github.io/WorldSonus/

explain.tldr: A system that generates realistic spatial sound in real-time for AI-created video environments with interactive control.
explain.plain: AI can now create realistic videos, but those videos are silent. This paper tackles adding sound to these generated worlds in three ways: making it fast enough to keep up with video playback, letting you control what sounds appear mid-generation, and making the sound match the scene's geometry and camera movement. They built WorldSonus, which generates audio in chunks using a streaming approach, responds to text instructions about sounds, and creates stereo audio (left and right channels) that aligns with the visual scene.
explain.why: This matters because interactive audio-visual environments—whether for games, VR, film, or music composition tools—need synchronized, controllable sound. As AI-generated video becomes more common, having matching spatial audio opens new creative possibilities for producers and composers working with synthetic media.

terms.meaning: A type of AI model that generates audio by gradually refining noise into clear sound, similar to how some image generators work
Training data where the AI learns from real stereo recordings (separate left and right channels) to understand how sound should differ between speakers
A measure of speed: an RTF of 0.41 means the system generates audio 2.4 times faster than real-time playback

papers.title: Sobolev Norms in Neural Embeddings Measure Audio Morphing Regularity
papers.summary: Morphing has recently gained renewed interest with the emergence of generative models, particularly in audio and image generation. In musical sound synthesis, morphing can generate intermediate sounds between two targets, helping musicians and sound engineers explore new sounds with interesting perceptual properties. As morphing is inherently defined in perceptual terms, evaluating this task is challenging. In this work, we introduce Sobolev Distances to Ideal Morphing (SDIM), a novel objective metric to quantify the regularity of audio morphing trajectories in perceptually relevant audio embedding spaces. Leveraging a physics-based sound synthesizer, we evaluate the discriminative power of SDIM on controlled morphing trajectories with varying degrees of regularity and compare it with that of existing audio morphing metrics. Results show that, contrary to state-of-the-art metrics, the proposed metric reliably discriminates desirable trajectories from adversarial ones.

explain.tldr: A new measurement tool that evaluates how smoothly audio morphing transitions between two sounds.
explain.plain: When generative models morph between two sounds, musicians want the transition to feel natural and perceptually smooth—not jumpy or weird. The researchers created a metric called SDIM that measures this smoothness by analyzing how the sound changes in a perceptual embedding space (a mathematical representation of what sounds actually mean to our ears). They tested it against existing metrics and found their approach better identifies smooth, desirable morphing paths versus awkward ones.
explain.why: Musicians and producers using AI tools to explore sounds between two targets need reliable ways to judge if the morphing sounds good. This metric could help generative models create more musically useful transitions and give sound designers better feedback on their morphing results.

terms.meaning: A mathematical representation where sounds are positioned based on their perceptual qualities, so similar-sounding things are close together
A mathematical way to measure smoothness of transitions by looking at how quickly things change
The path a sound takes as it gradually transforms from one target sound to another

papers.title: Restore, Separate, Restore: A Modular Framework for Music Source Restoration
papers.summary: Music Source Restoration (MSR) seeks to recover original, unprocessed instrument stems from mixed, mastered, and possibly degraded recordings. Unlike conventional source separation, which treats the mixture as a linear sum of clean sources, MSR must additionally invert nonlinear production effects, such as equalization and compression, and transmission-related degradations, such as codec artifacts. We propose a three-stage framework built around this distinction: (1) a mixture restoration model that addresses degradation before separation, (2) a single model that separates the restored mixture into eight target stems (vocals, guitars, keyboards, synthesizers, bass, drums, percussion, and orchestra), and (3) stem-specific restoration experts fine-tuned on the separator's own residual artifacts. Each stage improves restoration quality over the previous one on the MSR Challenge test set. We release code and models to support future research in MSR at https://github.com/theMoro/music_source_restoration.

explain.tldr: A three-stage system that cleans up recordings, separates them into instrument stems, then fixes remaining artifacts.
explain.plain: When you extract individual instruments from a finished recording, you're fighting against two problems: the mixing process itself (EQ, compression, effects) and degradation from compression or streaming. This paper proposes handling these separately instead of all at once. They clean the recording first, then separate it into eight instrument types, then use specialized tools to fix whatever artifacts the separation created. Each step improves the final result.
explain.why: Musicians and producers working with stems from existing recordings—whether for remixing, sampling, or restoration—could get cleaner, more usable individual tracks. This matters if you're trying to extract stems from mastered songs or degraded sources where traditional separation struggles.

terms.meaning: the process of splitting a mixed recording into individual instrument tracks or 'stems'
unwanted distortions or noise introduced when audio is compressed for storage or streaming (like MP3 compression)
leftover errors or unwanted sounds that remain after processing, like glitches from the separation step

papers.title: Geometric Representations for Transformed Pattern Matching in Music
papers.summary: We review the notion of representing music using point sets and argue that such representations are better adapted than sequential representations for matching patterns in unvoiced, polyphonic music, such as keyboard music. Musical transformations such as transposition, inversion, diminution, augmentation and retrograde can be modelled by geometric transformations in pitch-time representations that combine translation with scaling parallel to and reflection in the time axis. We identify eight types of geometric pitch-time representation that use chromatic pitch, morphetic pitch, morph or chroma to represent pitch and either onset time or midtime to represent time. We illustrate how these types of representation allow us to characterise different types of musical transformation. For example, by using midtime instead of onset time, we can precisely characterise certain retrograde relationships; and by using morph and chroma pitch representations we can characterise transformations involving octave displacements and duplications. We present the concept of a transformation class and consider the three specific classes, $F_{\mathrm{2STR}}$, $F_{\mathrm{2STRMod7}}$ and $F_{\mathrm{2STRMod12}}$. We introduce the notion of an inter-pattern transformation graph for a set of patterns, $S$, and a transformation class, $F$. Each vertex in such a graph represents a pattern in $S$ and there is an edge in the graph from pattern $P_1$ to pattern $P_2$ if and only if $P_1$ can be mapped onto $P_2$ by a transformation in $F$. We show, with the aid of such graphs, that the musical relationships between the occurrences of the HAYDN theme in Ravel's Menuet sur le nom d'Haydn can be precisely described in terms of transformations in $F_{\mathrm{2STR}}$, $F_{\mathrm{2STRMod7}}$ and $F_{\mathrm{2STRMod12}}$ within the pitch-time representations considered.

explain.tldr: Using geometric shapes to find musical patterns that have been transformed like transposed or inverted.
explain.plain: Finding the same musical idea when it's been changed—moved to a different key, played backwards, sped up—is hard in keyboard music with multiple notes playing together. Instead of thinking of music as a sequence of notes, the authors represent it as points in a geometric space (pitch and time). Musical transformations like transposition or inversion become geometric operations like shifting or flipping. They tested this approach on a famous theme from Ravel's music that quotes Haydn, showing they could precisely identify all the different versions of that theme.
explain.why: This matters if you're interested in music analysis tools, composition software, or understanding how composers reuse and transform musical ideas. It could help music software better recognize when you've used a melodic idea in different forms.

terms.meaning: moving a melody up or down in pitch while keeping the same intervals between notes
playing a melody backwards, from the last note to the first
a way of representing pitch that distinguishes between different octaves, unlike chroma which treats all C's as equivalent

papers.title: CTAG-FX: Reinterpreting Synthesizer Parameter Spaces for Expressive Tone-Shaping Audio FX Design
papers.summary: Recent text-guided audio FX research has focused on translating natural-language descriptions into parameters or chain configurations within existing FX systems. However, comparatively little attention has been paid to how the internal control space of an individual FX processor can itself be constructed. To address this gap, we propose CTAG-FX, which functionally reinterprets the roles of 78 parameters in a text-conditioned synthesizer configuration as controls of a tone-shaping FX processor. Each synthesizer configuration defines a fixed tone-shaping processor that can be repeatedly applied to new audio inputs rather than producing only a one-off rendered output. The text-conditioned synthesizer configurations are generated using A&R-CTAG, a retrieval-enhanced extension of CTAG. We evaluate CTAG-FX through signal-level analysis, together with a scrambled-mapping ablation in which parameter-to-control assignments are randomly permuted to assess the contribution of the proposed role assignment. Role-based mapping produces prompt-distinct spectral and nonlinear behavior, whereas scrambling reduces this prompt-specific differentiation and yields a more prompt-insensitive nonlinear profile. Overall, these results suggest that synthesizer parameter spaces can serve not only as sound-generation spaces but also as design resources for constructing new audio-FX control spaces. Audio samples are available at https://taylor3527eg-hub.github.io/ctag-fx-platform-demo/.

explain.tldr: Reusing synthesizer parameters as controls for audio effects processors guided by text descriptions.
explain.plain: Usually, audio effects are designed with their own fixed control layouts. This paper proposes taking the 78 parameters from a text-guided synthesizer and repurposing them as controls for an effects processor instead. By assigning meaningful roles to these parameters, they create an effects unit that responds to text descriptions and shapes incoming audio in prompt-specific ways. Testing shows that this thoughtful role assignment produces better, more consistent results than randomly shuffling the parameter assignments.
explain.why: This could open new ways to design custom effects with intuitive text control, letting producers describe the tone they want rather than tweaking knobs blindly. It also suggests synthesizer designs might be more flexible than we think—their internals could serve multiple creative purposes.

terms.meaning: A system that takes written descriptions as input to control its behavior, rather than just knob positions
The full set of adjustable controls in a synthesizer or effect, and how they relate to each other
A technique that looks up relevant examples or data to help guide the system's decisions

papers.title: Feature Encoding in VAE-based Audio Decoders: Effects of Input, Depth and Distribution
papers.summary: Neural audio synthesis models like the Realtime Audio Variational autoEncoder (RAVE) achieve impressive genera tion quality, yet how their internal representations encode musical features remains poorly understood. We present a systematic layer-wise and cross-layer cluster analysis of RAVE decoder activations across three models trained on different musical domains, tested with four stimulus types. We then evaluate architectural generalization with a general purpose EnCodec model. For RAVE, we find that synthetic stimuli are encoded well across models and audio features (pitch |\r{ho}|=0.45, 5.1x the null, BPM |\r{ho}| = 0.76, 8.6x the null). These results are reduced but still substantively apparent when using natural audio (mean across features |\r{ho}|=0.25, 2.8x the null). Natural audio sees a stronger encoding when nonlinear probes are used (mean across features R2=0.56, 18x the null, +0.152 nonlinear gain over the linear probe R2). Encoding strength varies throughout the layers of the decoder and an increased ability to joint-encode in the middle layers is seen across all audio features (\b{eta}2 all negative, p < 0.05). The general purpose EnCodec decoder also sees similar strong synthetic responses across audio features, similar nonlinear gains for natural audio joint encoding and similar depth profiles. We find the best cross-layer cluster improves the strength (r = 0.65, p = 0.006) and prevalence (r = 0.75, p = 0.001) of BPM encoding when compared against the best whole layers within the same section, with no effect for joint encoding. These findings advance the interpretability of neural audio models and inform targeted control strategies for neural synthesis.

explain.tldr: Researchers analyzed how neural audio synthesis models internally represent musical features like pitch and tempo.
explain.plain: Neural audio synthesis models like RAVE can generate realistic audio, but it's unclear how they actually process and store information about musical features internally. The researchers examined what happens at different layers inside these models when they process audio with known properties (pitch, tempo, etc.). They found that the models encode these features reasonably well, especially when given synthetic test sounds, and that different layers specialize in different ways—with middle layers being particularly good at handling multiple features together.
explain.why: Understanding how these models represent musical information could help producers and musicians better control neural synthesis tools, making it easier to manipulate specific aspects of generated sound rather than treating the model as a black box.

terms.meaning: A type of neural network that learns compressed representations of audio by encoding it into a smaller form and then reconstructing it
The internal numerical patterns that emerge as data flows through the decoding part of the network
A testing method that can capture complex, curved relationships between internal representations and musical features, rather than just straight-line relationships

papers.title: ARIA: Audio-Driven Melody-Tone Relation Modeling for Cantonese Lyric Authoring
papers.summary: Cantonese lyric writing requires close alignment between lexical tones and melodic pitch. Existing melody-guided lyric generation methods typically rely on symbolic melody to generate lyrics. However, in real songwriting scenarios, melodies are often expressed as raw singing audio or hummed recordings, where pitch is implicit, noisy, and unstructured, making these methods difficult to apply directly. To address this limitation, we propose ARIA, a two-stage audio-driven melody-tone relation modeling framework for Cantonese lyric authoring that generates Cantonese lyrics from singing recordings with provided character-level timestamps. Specifically, we first design a Tri-Stream Relation-Aware Tone Estimator (TRATE) to predict 0243 sequences from timestamped singing audio by modeling multi-stream acoustic cues and relational tonal structure. We then propose a Decoupled Retrieval-Augmented Tone-Conditioned Lyric Generator (DRA-TCLG) to generate fluent lyrics conditioned on predicted tonal plans with retrieval-enhanced lexical guidance. Moreover, we construct a large-scale aligned audio-Jyutping-0243 dataset from real Cantonese singing recordings to support this new task. Experimental results demonstrate that ARIA achieves strong performance in both 0243 prediction and tone-consistent lyric generation, validating the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

explain.tldr: System that generates Cantonese lyrics from sung audio by predicting tones and matching them to melody.
explain.plain: Writing Cantonese lyrics is tricky because the language's tones must match the melody's pitch. Most existing tools work with written musical notation, but real songwriting often starts with hummed or sung recordings where the pitch is messy and unclear. This paper presents ARIA, which takes a singing recording and timestamps for where words should go, then figures out what tones the melody implies and generates lyrics that fit those tones. They built a new dataset of real Cantonese songs to train and test the system.
explain.why: For Cantonese musicians and lyricists, this could make it faster to write lyrics that naturally fit a melody you've already sung or hummed, rather than having to work from sheet music or manually adjust tones afterward.

terms.meaning: the pitch pattern of a syllable that changes its meaning—Cantonese has six main tones, and using the wrong one changes what the word means
a technique that looks up relevant examples from a database to help guide what the system generates
a romanization system for writing Cantonese sounds using Latin letters

papers.title: SkillFormer: Skill-Decomposed Adaptation for Audio Language Models
papers.summary: Audio language models must handle dozens of distinct skills, from pitch comparison and speaker counting to musical tempo estimation and emotion recognition. Joint training on all skills at once causes interference: gains on one skill often come at the cost of another. We propose \textbf{SkillFormer}, which decomposes audio understanding into skill-specific low-rank adapters and composes them at inference time through a learned router. The router examines the question to decide which adapters to activate and how much weight each should carry, so that a pitch query engages different parameters than a genre classification query. An alternating training schedule updates each adapter on its own skill cluster before jointly calibrating the router, preventing the gradient conflicts that arise in standard multi-task optimization. SkillFormer adds fewer than 4\% of the base model's parameters and requires no changes to the audio encoder or language backbone. Evaluated on three architecturally distinct models across MMSU, MMAU-Pro, and MMAR, it raises the average accuracy by 2.5 to 4.1 points, with balanced gains across perception, reasoning, and semantic subcategories.

explain.tldr: SkillFormer trains audio language models on multiple tasks without them interfering with each other by using specialized adapters.
explain.plain: Audio language models need to handle many different audio tasks—like identifying pitch, counting speakers, or detecting emotion—but training them all together causes problems: improving at one task often makes the model worse at another. SkillFormer solves this by creating separate, lightweight skill-specific modules (adapters) for different tasks, then uses a smart router that looks at each question and decides which modules to use and how much. The training process updates each skill separately before fine-tuning how they work together, which prevents the conflicting signals that normally happen. The result is better performance across all tasks without significantly increasing the model's size.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this means AI tools that understand audio could become more reliable at specific tasks you care about—whether that's analyzing a vocal's emotion, detecting tempo, or identifying instruments—without sacrificing performance elsewhere. This could lead to better music analysis and production tools.

terms.meaning: Small, efficient add-on modules that specialize in specific tasks without requiring the entire model to be retrained
A learned decision-maker that examines a question and determines which specialized modules to activate and how much to use each one
Training a model on multiple different tasks simultaneously, which can cause conflicts when improvements in one task hurt performance in another

papers.title: Adapting a Latent Audio Diffusion Model to Historical Guqin Recordings: A Listening-Driven Case Study
papers.summary: We report a small-data case study in adapting a pretrained latent audio diffusion model to the guqin, the seven-string Chinese zither, aiming at an "AI radio" that plays guqin-style music without end. From a library of historical recordings we curate 412 solo performances (42.5 h, 61 performers) and split them by composition. We fine-tune a rank-16 DoRA adapter on Stable Audio 3 Medium using its continuous latents, masking weighted towards continuation, captions that combine researched notes on each piece with mood tags and an automatically estimated pentatonic mode, and random-length crops, stopping when held-out loss stops improving. Seven blind listening studies by one expert listener guided every decision. The final adapter was rated highest for continuing unseen pieces (3.9/5, against 3.4 for the best earlier adapter) and 4.6/5 for generating from free-written scene descriptions. Negative results are equally informative: a from-scratch autoregressive model over the same latents produced no recognisable timbre, a signal-level friction-noise measure correlated with the listener's complaints in the wrong direction, and a pentatonic-fit measure tracked ratings overall but barely within a group of candidates. Chaining continuations for long playback exposed a silent tail on every generated clip and a loudness feedback loop, both with simple fixes. With one listener and at most ten clips per condition, no paired difference is statistically significant; we present an exploratory record of what helped, what did not, and why.

explain.tldr: Researchers adapted an AI music model to generate guqin music by fine-tuning it on historical recordings and using listening tests to guide improvements.
explain.plain: The guqin is a traditional Chinese instrument, and researchers wanted to create an AI system that could generate endless guqin-style music. They took a pretrained music generation model (Stable Audio) and adapted it using 412 historical guqin recordings, adding musical descriptions and mode information. They ran seven listening studies with an expert to test different approaches, finding that their adapted model could continue unseen pieces and generate music from written descriptions reasonably well. However, they also discovered what didn't work—like trying to build a model from scratch—and identified technical issues like silent gaps between generated clips.
explain.why: This shows how AI music tools can be customized for specific instruments and musical traditions, even with limited training data. For musicians and producers interested in AI, it demonstrates a practical, listening-focused approach to adapting general models to specialized sounds rather than relying only on automatic metrics.

terms.meaning: An AI system that generates audio by learning patterns from training data, working in a compressed representation rather than raw sound waves
A lightweight technique for customizing a pretrained model for a new task without retraining the entire model from scratch
A musical scale with five notes per octave, common in many non-Western musical traditions including Chinese music

papers.title: Smorph: Playable Sound Morphing with Diffusion Models
papers.summary: Sound morphing, generating intermediate sounds that transition from one sonic identity to another, can be a powerful tool for musical sound design. Existing diffusion-based morphing approaches entangle temporal structure and timbral identity, offering no mechanism to hold one fixed while transforming the other. We present smorph, a training-free guidance framework that preserves how a sound behaves over time while transforming what the sound is, allowing users to morph, for instance from brass to strings at a fixed pitch. We demonstrate across three morphing modes: prompt-to-prompt, audio-to-prompt, and audio-to-audio. Evaluations across diverse datasets show that smorph effectively produces smooth morph trajectories while substantially improving temporal-structure and source preservation over baselines, albeit with more conservative target-ward transformation in some settings. In an exploratory case study, musicians found smorph trajectories to be expressive and playable, suggesting structural anchoring can serve as a productive constraint for instrumental interaction.

explain.tldr: A tool that smoothly transforms one sound into another while keeping its timing and rhythm fixed.
explain.plain: Sound morphing creates intermediate sounds that transition between two different sonic identities—like gradually changing brass to strings. The problem is that existing approaches blur together how a sound evolves over time with what the sound actually is, so you can't control them separately. Smorph solves this by using a guidance framework that preserves the temporal structure (the rhythm and timing) while transforming the timbral identity (the character or color). Musicians tested it and found the morphing transitions expressive and playable.
explain.why: This matters to producers and sound designers because it gives you fine-grained control over sound design—you can experiment with new timbres without losing the rhythmic or melodic shape you want. It could also make real-time sound morphing more practical for live performance or interactive music.

terms.meaning: AI systems that generate new content by gradually refining noise into structured sound or images, often used for creative generation
the characteristic color or quality of a sound—what makes a trumpet sound different from a violin
how a sound evolves and changes over time, including its rhythm, timing, and dynamic shape

papers.title: UltraDub: Towards Authentic Dubbing by Unifying Visually-Steered Flow Learning and Trajectory Guidance
papers.summary: Visual voice cloning requires intelligible, speaker-consistent speech synchronized with visible articulation. However, sequential multimodal conditioning can disrupt previously established temporal and speaker cues, while imbalanced inference guidance can improve linguistic accuracy at the expense of lip synchronization. In this paper, we propose UltraDub, a Unifying Visually-Steered Flow learning and trajectory Guidance Dubbing framework that leverages vision in two ways: as continuous motion for multimodal context aggregation, and as structural rhythm for trajectory rectification. Specifically, we introduce the Motion-guided Dual-context Retrieving (MDR) module, which continually recalibrates linguistic and speaker-style retrieval through shared lip-motion query residuals, utilizing independent time-conditioned gates to regulate their contributions. Furthermore, we propose Rhythm-anchored Trajectory Guidance (RTG), a training-free mechanism that evaluates hierarchical multimodal corrections at a visual-only predictive midpoint, safely strengthening semantic conditioning while better preserving temporal alignment. Finally, we construct DiverseDub, a multi-scenario benchmark to evaluate video dubbing in the wild. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UltraDub achieves state-of-the-art performance across four datasets.

explain.tldr: A system that creates dubbed speech matching actors' lip movements while keeping voices natural and consistent.
explain.plain: When dubbing videos (replacing dialogue with new speech), you need the new voice to match the actor's lip movements, sound like the same person, and remain intelligible. The challenge is that trying to improve one aspect—like making words clearer—often breaks another, like lip sync. UltraDub uses visual information from the actor's mouth movements in two ways: to help the system remember both what words to say and what the speaker sounds like, and to guide corrections that keep timing aligned with the video. They tested it on multiple datasets and report it outperforms existing approaches.
explain.why: This matters for musicians and producers working on film, TV, or game localization—dubbing into different languages while keeping performances authentic. Better dubbing tools could make international content more natural-sounding and reduce the uncanny feeling of mismatched lips and speech.

terms.meaning: using multiple types of input information (like both audio and video) to guide what a system generates
matching the timing of spoken words to the visible movement of an actor's mouth
steering the system's output along a desired path by providing reference points or corrections during generation

papers.title: Relational Synthesis: Structure-Mediated Concatenative Synthesis for Foley and Retrieval-Augmented Audio Generation
papers.summary: We ask: given a retrieved source audio $S$ and a separate reference audio $R$, can we synthesize novel audio $Y$ out of this pair $(S,R)$ such that $Y$ remains acoustically consistent with $S$, while not persistently copying segments of $S$ or $R$? The first clause is a well-known goal in Foley audio production, and the second is a well-known issue in neural RAG when $S$ and $R$ are naively injected into neural generators. We show that both clauses can be addressed simultaneously using a method we coin relational synthesis, a variation of concatenative synthesis where target cost is replaced by a relational Gromov-like structural cost. Rather than imitating the content of $R$, relational synthesis exploits it from the "other side of the hill": it transfers the temporal structure and directed amplitude motion of $R$ to reorganize and concatenate the grains of $S$ in a novel manner that protects $S$'s acoustic information. Our experiments show that relational synthesis integrates naturally with neural RAG and produces Foley audio that performs well on metrics measuring temporal agreement, acoustic fidelity, and leakage persistence, while maintaining distribution-level quality and text alignment.

explain.tldr: A method that combines two audio sources to create new Foley sounds while preserving acoustic character and avoiding direct copying.
explain.plain: When making sound effects (Foley), producers often want to transform one sound using the structure or rhythm of another. This paper addresses two problems: keeping the original sound recognizable while borrowing the timing pattern from a reference sound, and preventing AI systems from just copying chunks of either source. They use a technique called relational synthesis that rearranges small pieces of the source sound according to the reference sound's rhythm and amplitude changes, rather than trying to imitate the reference directly. Tests show this produces Foley that sounds natural, maintains the original acoustic quality, and doesn't leak recognizable copies of the source material.
explain.why: This could help Foley artists and sound designers create variations of sounds more efficiently by automatically adapting one sound's character to match another's timing or motion. It also addresses a real problem in AI-assisted audio generation where systems tend to copy their inputs rather than creatively transform them.

terms.meaning: Building new sounds by cutting up and reassembling small pieces (grains) from existing audio
Sound effects created by recording or synthesizing everyday sounds for film, games, or other media
An AI approach that finds relevant existing examples and uses them to help generate new content

papers.title: Joint Estimation of Common-Slope Decay Rates and Spatial Amplitudes Using Parameterized Nonnegative Matrix Factorization
papers.summary: We formulate joint estimation of common-slope decay rates and amplitudes from room impulse responses (RIRs) as parameterized nonnegative matrix factorization with the Itakura--Saito divergence as the loss function (IS-NMF). Estimation at each short-time Fourier transform frequency bin produces detailed reverberation time (RT) curves directly from RIR powers with no backward integration needed. Standard space-alternating generalized expectation-maximization (SAGE) algorithm yields closed-form amplitude updates and a convex subproblem for each decay rate update. To accelerate estimation, we introduce contribution-weighted SAGE, which emphasizes observations where each component contributes strongly to the modeled power. Experiments with synthetic data show accurate recovery of well-separated decays and faster loss reduction than standard SAGE. Application to measured coupled-room RIRs yields frequency-dependent RT curves and reveals complementary space-time contributions of the shared decay components.

explain.tldr: A method to measure how sound decays in rooms by analyzing impulse responses using matrix factorization.
explain.plain: When sound bounces around a room, it decays at different rates depending on frequency and location. This paper presents a technique to estimate these decay rates and the strength of different sound paths directly from room impulse responses—the recordings that capture how a room affects sound. They use a mathematical approach called nonnegative matrix factorization, which breaks down complex data into simpler components. Their method produces detailed reverberation time curves at each frequency without needing extra processing steps, and they made it faster by focusing computation on the most important parts of the data.
explain.why: Understanding how sound decays in a room is fundamental for acoustic design, room correction, and realistic reverb simulation. This technique could help producers and acoustic engineers characterize spaces more precisely and model room acoustics more accurately in recordings or virtual environments.

terms.meaning: a recording that captures how a room affects sound by recording the echoes and reflections after a brief sound burst
a mathematical technique that breaks down a table of numbers into simpler components, where all values must be zero or positive
how long it takes for sound to decay to inaudible levels in a room, typically measured at different frequencies

papers.title: SheetSage2: Coherent Lead-Sheet Transcription with Synthetic Supervision
papers.summary: Transcribing music into a human-readable score requires a coherent understanding of rhythm, harmony, melody, and form. Two obstacles limit this goal: annotated recordings are scarce, and accurate local predictions can still produce inconsistent musical sequences. We present SheetSage2, a unified music transcription framework that combines synthetic data, task-specific structured decoding, and autoregressive distillation. Automatically annotated MIDI, rendered into audio, provides scalable supervision across music understanding tasks. Task-specific structured decoders integrate complementary musical cues and their temporal dependencies to produce musically coherent scores. Autoregressive distillation further retains transcription accuracy without task-specific dynamic programming at inference. Across eight benchmark collections, a single SheetSage2-AR model exceeds the listed prior systems on 12 of 15 benchmark--metric pairs in our evaluation, substantially improving over SheetSage1 and surpassing task-specific models on several benchmarks. Model weights and inference code are publicly available.

explain.tldr: A system that automatically transcribes music recordings into readable sheet music by learning from synthetic data and ensuring musical coherence.
explain.plain: Converting audio recordings into written sheet music is hard because there's limited training data and because getting individual notes right doesn't guarantee the result sounds musically sensible. SheetSage2 solves this by training on artificially created music (MIDI converted to audio), using a decoder that understands how musical elements like rhythm and harmony connect over time, and then simplifying the process for actual use. The system outperformed previous approaches across multiple test datasets.
explain.why: This matters because accurate music transcription could save musicians and producers hours of manual work when converting recordings or sketches into scores, and it could help music software better understand what you're playing or producing.

terms.meaning: artificially generated training examples (here, MIDI files converted to audio) rather than real recordings
a technique where a simpler model learns to replicate a complex model's predictions, making it faster to use while keeping accuracy
a decoding method that enforces musical rules and relationships rather than predicting each element independently

papers.title: Influence of Geometrical Acoustic Simulator Complexity on a Trained Multisource Localizer
papers.summary: Learning-based acoustic sound source localization and detection (SSLD) requires large labeled datasets covering diverse acoustic conditions. Since obtaining measured data is costly, training commonly uses simulated data, while practical devices must operate under real-world conditions. However, higher simulation complexity increases data-generation cost, and the complexity required for reliable generalization remains unclear. In practice, SSLD methods often rely on efficient geometrical acoustic simulation, typically the image-source method. This work investigates how geometrical acoustic simulation complexity affects the real-world performance of a common multi-source SSLD model. We train the model with simulators ranging from anechoic conditions to high-order image-source simulations, optionally including diffuse reverberation, array simulation, and randomized image-source positions, and evaluate them on three measurement-based test datasets. Results show that anechoic simulation is insufficient, while medium-complexity image-source simulations already provide strong real-world performance. Further increases in complexity yield only marginal gains, with the best performance obtained using the highest tested image-source order, array simulation, and randomized image-source positions. For this configuration, measured-domain performance approaches within-domain simulated performance, suggesting limited benefit from further increasing simulation complexity. These findings show how the complexity-performance trade-off can be exploited in future data-driven SSLD, and highlight image-source randomization as an efficient way to improve generalization.

explain.tldr: Training sound localization AI with moderately complex simulations works nearly as well as highly complex ones for real-world use.
explain.plain: Sound source localization—figuring out where sounds come from—is hard to train because real recorded data is expensive to collect. Researchers instead use simulated acoustic environments to train AI models. This paper tests whether more realistic, complex simulations actually improve performance on real recordings. They found that simple anechoic (echo-free) simulation doesn't work, but medium-complexity simulations already perform nearly as well as the most complex ones tested, with only small improvements from adding more realism.
explain.why: For musicians and producers using spatial audio tools or microphone arrays, this means faster development of sound localization features. Simpler training simulations mean companies can develop these tools more cheaply and quickly without sacrificing real-world accuracy.

terms.meaning: A way to simulate how sound bounces around a room by mathematically modeling reflections off walls
An environment with no echoes or reverberation, like a perfectly sound-absorbing room
How well an AI model trained on simulated data performs on real-world recordings it hasn't seen before

papers.title: A Multidimensional Model for Quantifying Tonal Strength: A Continuous Framework of Analyzing Tonal Evolution Beyond Tonal-Atonal Binary Classification
papers.summary: Tonality is a fundamental organizing principle of Western music. However, the gradual transition from common-practice tonality to atonality around the turn of the twentieth century cannot be captured by binary labels. To characterize intermediate tonal states and trace this evolution, we propose a multidimensional framework for quantifying tonal strength, grounded in tonal theory and mechanisms underlying tonal dissolution. This framework operationalizes the global statistical regularity, temporal coherence, and local perceptual alignment of tonal organization through three complementary features: pitch-class distribution uniformity, temporal stability of tonal centers, and local tonal clarity, respectively. To validate the model, we introduce two new datasets: a binary dataset comprising 196 tonal and atonal pieces, and a historical MIDI corpus of 1,561 compositions by 21 composers spanning the Baroque era to the early twentieth century. The proposed model achieves high discriminative performance on the binary classification task (F_1=0.985), and quantitatively reveals a continuous historical trajectory from established tonality through progressive weakening to eventual dissolution. Computational analysis of representative composers further confirms significant declines in tonal strength throughout the careers of late-Romantic and modernist figures. Additionally, analysis of EMOPIA dataset reveals a weak but statistically significant positive correlation between higher tonal strength values and positive emotional valence. This work establishes a unified quantitative model for analyzing tonal evolution and provides a continuous measure for future behavioral and neurophysiological investigations of the relationships among tonal organization, musical emotion, and cognition.

explain.tldr: A framework that measures how tonal music is on a continuous scale rather than just tonal-or-atonal, tracking how tonality weakened over time.
explain.plain: Western music gradually moved from strongly tonal (like Bach) to atonal (like Schoenberg) around 1900, but this shift can't be captured by simply labeling pieces as one or the other. The researchers built a system that measures tonality across three dimensions: how evenly distributed the pitches are, how stable the tonal center stays over time, and how clear the tonality sounds locally. Testing on 1,561 historical compositions, they found their system accurately distinguishes tonal from atonal music and reveals a continuous weakening of tonality through composers' careers during the late 1800s and early 1900s.
explain.why: This gives musicians and musicologists a precise way to describe and study the gradual evolution of tonality in music history, rather than forcing pieces into rigid categories. It could help producers and composers understand what makes music sound more or less tonal, and connects tonal organization to emotional response.

terms.meaning: how evenly or unevenly the twelve musical pitches are used in a piece; tonal music favors certain pitches, atonal music spreads them more equally
the home pitch or key that a piece feels anchored to; in C major, C is the tonal center
music that deliberately avoids organizing around a single home pitch or key

papers.title: Unheard but Recognizable: Ultrasonic Signatures for Musical Instrument Recognition
papers.summary: Musical-instrument recognition is a fundamental music information retrieval (MIR) task supporting transcription, source separation, and audio understanding. Despite significant algorithmic progress, there is still room for improvement in recognizing acoustically similar instruments, particularly in polyphonic mixtures. We examine the contribution of ultrasonic components, i.e., frequencies above the audible 0-20 kHz range. Although most of this content cannot be represented at conventional 44.1/48-kSPS sampling rates under the Nyquist criterion, it is available in high-quality 96-kSPS recordings. Using a 96-kSPS multitrack corpus covering 15 classes across performers, instruments, studios, and sessions, we compare full-band, low-pass, and ultrasonic-only inputs using classical machine-learning and deep-learning classifiers. Our results show that source-dependent ultrasonic extensions and broadband transients contain instrument-specific information that significantly improves isolated and polyphonic recognition and motivates wider-bandwidth studies of other MIR tasks.

explain.tldr: Ultrasonic frequencies above human hearing improve machine recognition of musical instruments in recordings.
explain.plain: Identifying which instruments are playing in a recording is useful for music transcription and analysis, but it's harder when instruments sound similar or play together. This research discovered that frequencies too high for humans to hear—above 20 kHz—contain unique patterns that help distinguish instruments. By analyzing high-quality recordings sampled at 96 kHz (instead of the standard 44.1 kHz), they found that these ultrasonic signatures, especially in the sharp attack sounds of instruments, gave machine-learning models better accuracy at recognizing instruments, both when playing alone and in mixtures.
explain.why: If instrument recognition improves, it could make automatic music transcription, source separation (isolating individual instruments from a mix), and other music analysis tools more reliable—potentially useful for producers, composers, and music software developers.

terms.meaning: A rule stating that to capture frequencies up to a certain limit, you need to sample at least twice that frequency; e.g., 44.1 kHz sampling captures up to ~22 kHz.
Audio where multiple instruments or voices play at the same time, rather than one at a time.
The field of extracting useful information from music recordings, like identifying instruments, detecting beats, or transcribing notes.

papers.title: AdaLoop: Adaptive-Depth Latent Reasoning for Audio Language Models
papers.summary: Large audio language models answer questions about speech, sound, and music, yet their accuracy drops sharply on tasks that need fine-grained acoustic analysis. Judging which of two speakers has the higher pitch demands iterative signal-level reasoning that a content question does not. Current models spend the same computational depth on both. We introduce AdaLoop, a lightweight recurrent module that learns how many latent refinement steps a given audio--question pair requires. A shared transformer block iterates over the audio representation, guided by the question, while a learned halting mechanism exits the loop once the representation is ready. AdaLoop adds fewer than 3\% of the base model's parameters and plugs into any audio encoder--language model pair without modifying either component. Evaluated on three architecturally distinct models across MMSU, MMAU-Pro, and MMAR, AdaLoop raises the average accuracy by 2.9 to 3.8 points, with the largest gains on perception-heavy subtasks where the model learns to apply deeper reasoning.

explain.tldr: AdaLoop adds adaptive reasoning loops to audio language models, spending more computation on hard acoustic tasks.
explain.plain: Audio language models—systems that answer questions about speech, sound, and music—struggle with tasks requiring careful listening, like comparing two speakers' pitches. The problem is that these models use the same amount of processing for every question, whether it's easy or hard. AdaLoop is a small add-on that learns how many times to refine its understanding of the audio for each specific question. It uses a learned stopping mechanism to exit when it has enough information, and tests show it improves accuracy by 2.9 to 3.8 percentage points, especially on perception-heavy tasks.
explain.why: For musicians and producers, this means AI tools for audio analysis could become more reliable at subtle acoustic judgments—like pitch comparison or timbre analysis—without slowing down simple tasks. It's also efficient: the add-on uses minimal extra parameters, so it could be deployed on existing systems.

terms.meaning: internal refinement steps where the model improves its understanding of audio without outputting intermediate answers
a learned decision-maker that tells the model when it has processed the audio enough and can stop iterating
the part of a system that converts raw audio into a numerical representation the model can work with

papers.title: "Spectral Harmony" Towards the Unification of Timbre and Speech: Resolution of the Young Mahler Schoenberg Dream
papers.summary: In this article, we present a method of spectral serialization envisioned by G. Mahler and A. Schoenberg between the late 19th and early 20th centuries that enables the selection of timbres rooted in musical structure.
